entries.exodus 21:7: A daughter sold into service was not released after six years the way male servants were. The law treated her situation differently because of how she might be taken as a wife.
entries.exodus 21:8: If her master chose her but then was not pleased with her, she had to be allowed to go free, and he could not sell her to foreigners. He had broken faith with her and could not just pass her on.
entries.exodus 21:9: If the master gave her to his son as a wife, she was to be treated with the full rights of a daughter in the family. She was not to be treated as less than family.
entries.exodus 21:10: If the man took another wife, he still had to provide the first wife with food, clothing, and marital rights. He could not neglect her needs just because he married someone else.
entries.exodus 21:11: If he failed to provide those three things, she could leave free with no payment owed. The law gave her a way out when she was being neglected.
entries.exodus 21:12: Anyone who struck another person so that they died was to be put to death. Human life was treated as serious and taking it deliberately carried the highest penalty.
entries.exodus 21:13: If a death was accidental and not planned, God provided a place of refuge for the person to flee to. The law distinguished between murder and an unintentional killing.
entries.exodus 21:14: If someone deliberately and deceitfully killed a neighbor, even the altar could not protect him; he was to be taken and put to death. Planned murder could not be excused by seeking sanctuary.
entries.exodus 21:15: Anyone who struck his father or mother was to be put to death. Violence against parents was treated as a serious offense against God's order for the family.
entries.exodus 21:16: Anyone caught kidnapping a person to sell them was to be put to death. Treating a human being as goods to be bought and sold was a capital crime.
entries.exodus 21:17: Anyone who cursed his father or mother was to be put to death. Speaking evil against parents was treated as a serious offense, not a small matter.
entries.exodus 21:18: This covers a fight where one man hits another with a stone or his fist but does not kill him, leaving him bedridden. The law then addresses what happens next.
entries.exodus 21:19: If the injured man recovers enough to walk outside with a stick, the one who struck him is not punished further but must pay for his lost time and see that he is healed. The offender had to make good the harm he caused.
entries.exodus 21:20: If a master beat his servant with a rod and caused death, the master was to be punished. Even a servant's life was protected under the law.
entries.exodus 21:21: If the servant survived a day or two, the master was not punished, since the servant was considered his property. This shows the law of that time did not give servants full equal standing.
entries.exodus 21:22: If a fight caused a pregnant woman to lose her child but she was not otherwise harmed, the man responsible had to pay whatever her husband set, as the judges decided. The law required payment for the harm done.
entries.exodus 21:23: If the woman herself was harmed, then the penalty matched the harm, up to a life for a life. The punishment was to fit the seriousness of the injury.
entries.exodus 21:24: The penalty was to match the harm done: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, and so on. This limited revenge so it could not go beyond the actual damage.
entries.exodus 21:25: The same matching principle applied to burns, wounds, and blows. The point was fair limits on punishment, not unlimited retaliation.
entries.exodus 21:26: If a master struck his servant's eye and destroyed it, he had to set the servant free to make up for the eye. Even a servant was owed something for serious injury.
entries.exodus 21:27: If a blow knocked out a servant's tooth, the servant went free in compensation. The law gave the servant freedom as payment for the loss.
entries.exodus 21:28: If an ox killed a man or woman, the ox was to be stoned and its meat not eaten, but the owner was not held responsible. The animal that caused the death was dealt with, but the owner was not blamed if he had no warning.
entries.exodus 21:29: If the ox had hurt people before and the owner knew but did not control it, and it killed someone, both the ox and the owner were to be put to death. Failing to act on a known danger made the owner responsible.
entries.exodus 21:30: If a payment was set for the owner's life, he had to pay whatever amount was fixed. The law allowed a ransom in place of the death penalty in this case.
entries.exodus 21:31: The same rule applied if the ox killed a son or a daughter. The penalty did not change based on the age of the victim.
entries.exodus 21:32: If the ox killed a male or female servant, the owner paid thirty shekels of silver to the servant's master, and the ox was stoned. The law set a specific payment for the loss of a servant.
entries.exodus 21:33: If a man dug a pit and left it uncovered, and an ox or donkey fell in and died, the man was responsible. Leaving a hidden danger open made him accountable.
entries.exodus 21:34: The owner of the pit had to pay the animal's owner, but the dead animal became his. He bore the cost of his negligence but kept what was left.
entries.exodus 21:35: If one man's ox killed another man's ox, the live ox was sold and the money split between them, along with the dead one. The loss was shared fairly between the two owners.
entries.exodus 21:36: If the ox was known to have hurt animals before and the owner did not control it, he had to give a live ox for the dead one, and the dead animal was his. A known dangerous animal made the owner fully responsible.
entries.exodus 23:1: Don't spread rumors or lies, and don't team up with someone who is doing wrong by backing up their false story. What you say about others matters, so refuse to pass on or support what isn't true.
entries.exodus 23:2: Don't let a crowd push you into doing wrong, and don't side with the majority just because they want an unfair outcome. Popular opinion is not the same as what is right, so decide for yourself what is true.
entries.exodus 23:3: Don't bend the rules in someone's favor just because they are poor. Being fair means treating everyone the same, whether rich or poor.
entries.exodus 23:4: If you find your enemy's animal wandering loose, you must return it to him. Kindness to an enemy's property is required, not optional.
entries.exodus 23:5: If you see an animal belonging to someone who dislikes you struggling under a heavy load, you must help it, even if you don't want to. Doing right doesn't depend on how you feel about the person.
entries.exodus 23:6: Don't deny justice to a poor person just because they are poor. Everyone deserves a fair hearing and a fair decision.
entries.exodus 23:7: Stay far away from anything dishonest, and never let an innocent person be condemned to death. God will hold the guilty accountable, so don't join in injustice.
entries.exodus 23:8: Don't accept bribes, because money can blind people to the truth and twist the decisions of those who should be fair. Even good people can be corrupted by a payoff.
entries.exodus 23:9: Don't mistreat foreigners living among you, because you know what it feels like to be a stranger in a strange land. Remember your own experience and treat them with kindness.
entries.exodus 23:10: For six years you may plant your fields and harvest what they produce. Work is expected, and so is enjoying what your work brings in.
entries.exodus 23:11: In the seventh year, let the land rest and don't plant it, so the poor can eat what grows on its own and wild animals can eat the rest. Do the same with your vineyards and olive trees, giving the land and the needy a break.
entries.exodus 23:12: Work for six days, but rest on the seventh day so your animals, your servants, and the foreigners among you can rest too. Rest is for everyone, not just for you.
entries.exodus 23:13: Pay attention to everything God has commanded, and don't even speak the names of other gods. Loyalty to God means keeping other gods out of your mind and your mouth.
entries.exodus 23:14: Celebrate three festivals to God each year. Regular times of worship and thanksgiving are meant to be part of your life.
entries.exodus 23:15: Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread at the set time in the month of Abib, eating bread without yeast for seven days, and don't come to God empty-handed. Remember how God brought you out of Egypt, and bring an offering when you come.
entries.exodus 23:16: Keep the Feast of Harvest with the first crops from your fields, and the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year when you have gathered everything in. Celebrate God's provision at the beginning and end of the harvest.
entries.exodus 23:17: Three times a year, all the men are to appear before the Lord God. Worship is not a one-time event but a regular commitment.
entries.exodus 23:18: Don't offer the blood of a sacrifice together with bread that has yeast, and don't keep the fat of a festival offering until morning. Offerings to God are to be handled properly and promptly, not carelessly.
entries.exodus 23:19: Bring the best first crops of your land to the house of the Lord your God, and don't cook a young goat in its mother's milk. Give God your best, and treat even small customs with care and respect.
entries.exodus 23:20: God is sending an angel ahead of you to guard you on the way and lead you to the place he has prepared. You are not left to find your own way; guidance is provided.
entries.exodus 23:21: Pay attention to the angel and obey him, because he carries God's authority and won't excuse your wrongdoing. Listening to God's guidance matters, and disobedience has consequences.
entries.exodus 23:22: If you truly listen to God's voice and do what he says, he will oppose those who oppose you and fight those who fight you. Obedience brings God's protection and help.
entries.exodus 23:23: God's angel will go ahead of you and bring you into the land of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hivites, and Jebusites, and God will remove them. God goes before his people and clears the way.
entries.exodus 23:24: Don't bow down to the gods of those peoples or copy their practices; instead, destroy their idols and smash their sacred pillars. Don't adopt the wrong ways of the culture around you; remove them instead.
entries.exodus 23:25: Worship the Lord your God, and he will bless your food and water and take sickness away from among you. Putting God first brings blessing and health.
entries.exodus 23:26: No woman in your land will miscarry or be childless, and God will give you a full life. God's blessing includes fruitfulness and long life.
entries.exodus 23:27: God will send his fear ahead of you, throwing into panic all the peoples you encounter so that your enemies turn and run. God himself prepares the way and defeats opposition.
entries.exodus 23:28: God will send hornets ahead of you to drive out the Hivites, Canaanites, and Hittites. God uses even small means to clear the way for his people.
entries.exodus 23:29: God will not drive them all out in a single year, so the land doesn't become empty and wild animals don't multiply against you. God's timing is wise, even when it feels slow.
entries.exodus 23:30: God will drive them out little by little until your numbers grow and you can take possession of the land. Progress may be gradual, but God is still at work.
entries.exodus 23:31: God will set your borders from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines and from the desert to the Euphrates, and give the peoples of those lands into your hands. God's promises are specific and generous.
entries.exodus 23:32: Make no treaty with those peoples or with their gods. Agreements that pull you away from God are dangerous, so keep your distance.
entries.exodus 23:33: Don't let them live in your land, or they will lead you into sin against God, and worshiping their gods will become a trap to you. Bad influences close at hand can pull you away from God, so guard against them.
entries.exodus 25:1: God begins speaking to Moses on the mountain, giving him instructions for the people. This shows that what follows comes directly from God, not from Moses' own ideas.
entries.exodus 25:2: God asks the people to bring gifts for building the tabernacle, but only if they genuinely want to give. Giving to God should come from a willing heart, not from pressure.
entries.exodus 25:3: The first materials listed are valuable metals: gold, silver, and bronze. These were costly items that would be used to build something lasting and beautiful for God.
entries.exodus 25:4: The people were to bring colored fabrics, fine linen, and goat hair. Each material had a purpose in the tabernacle, showing that ordinary skills and goods matter in serving God.
entries.exodus 25:5: This verse lists tanned animal skins and acacia wood. These practical materials remind us that God uses everyday resources, not just precious ones, for his work.
entries.exodus 25:6: Olive oil was needed to keep lamps burning, and spices were for making sacred anointing oil and incense. These items supported worship and the daily life of the tabernacle.
entries.exodus 25:7: Precious stones were to be set into the priest's special garments. These gems marked the high priest's role as someone set apart to represent the people before God.
entries.exodus 25:8: God's goal was a sanctuary where he could live among his people. He wanted to be close to them, not distant, and this place made that presence possible.
entries.exodus 25:9: Moses was to follow God's exact pattern for the tabernacle and its furnishings. God cares about how he is worshiped, and the details were not left to human invention.
entries.exodus 25:10: The first item is the ark, a chest made of acacia wood with specific dimensions. It was the most sacred object, the center of God's presence among the people.
entries.exodus 25:11: The ark was to be covered with pure gold inside and out, with a gold border around it. Its beauty and value reflected the holiness of what it contained.
entries.exodus 25:12: Four gold rings were attached to the ark's feet for carrying it. This design allowed the ark to be moved without anyone touching it directly.
entries.exodus 25:13: Poles of acacia wood were made and covered with gold. These matched the rings and were the means by which the ark was carried.
entries.exodus 25:14: The poles were inserted through the rings so the ark could be lifted and carried. This made the sacred chest portable for the people's journey.
entries.exodus 25:15: The poles were to stay in the rings permanently and never be removed. This ensured the ark could always be moved properly and treated with respect.
entries.exodus 25:16: Inside the ark, Moses was to place the tablets of the covenant God would give him. The ark served as a container for God's own words to his people.
entries.exodus 25:17: A solid gold cover, called the atonement cover, was made to fit exactly on top of the ark. This cover was where God's presence would meet the people.
entries.exodus 25:18: Two cherubim, angelic figures, were to be hammered from gold and placed at each end of the cover. These figures guarded and marked the place of God's presence.
entries.exodus 25:19: The two cherubim were made as one piece with the cover, one at each end. They were not separate decorations but part of the sacred object itself.
entries.exodus 25:20: The cherubim's wings were spread upward over the cover, and they faced each other and the cover. Their posture showed reverence and guarded the place where God would speak.
entries.exodus 25:21: The cover was placed on the ark, and the covenant tablets were put inside. Together these formed the heart of the tabernacle, holding God's law and his mercy seat.
entries.exodus 25:22: God promised to meet Moses between the cherubim and speak with him there. This was the place where God gave his commands for Israel, showing he speaks to his people.
entries.exodus 25:23: A table of acacia wood was made with specific measurements. It held the bread of the Presence and stood in the holy place as part of Israel's worship.
entries.exodus 25:24: The table was overlaid with pure gold and had a gold rim around it. Its craftsmanship showed honor for the God it served.
entries.exodus 25:25: A frame the width of a hand was made around the table, with a gold border. This detail kept the table's contents secure and added to its beauty.
entries.exodus 25:26: Four gold rings were placed at the four corners, near the table's legs. These rings were for the carrying poles, just like those on the ark.
entries.exodus 25:27: The rings were fixed under the frame to hold the poles for carrying the table. This made the table movable without being touched directly.
entries.exodus 25:28: Wooden poles covered with gold were made to carry the table. They matched the rings and allowed the table to be transported safely.
entries.exodus 25:29: Gold dishes, pans, pitchers, and bowls were made for the table's service. These vessels were used in the tabernacle's worship and were all of pure gold.
entries.exodus 25:30: The bread of the Presence was to be kept on the table before the Lord at all times. This constant offering showed the people's ongoing dependence on God.
entries.exodus 25:31: A lampstand of pure hammered gold was made, with a base, shaft, and decorative cups and flowers. It provided light in the holy place and was a work of great skill.
entries.exodus 25:32: Six branches extended from the lampstand's sides, three on each side. This gave the lampstand its distinctive shape and held the lamps that lit the tabernacle.
entries.exodus 25:33: Each branch had three cups shaped like almond blossoms, with buds and flowers. These decorations echoed the beauty of creation and added to the lampstand's splendor.
entries.exodus 25:34: The central shaft had four cups shaped like almond flowers, each with buds and flowers. This matched the branches and made the whole lampstand a unified work of art.
entries.exodus 25:35: A bud was placed under each pair of branches, made as one piece with the lampstand. This detail held the branches together and kept the design consistent.
entries.exodus 25:36: All the buds and branches were hammered from one piece of pure gold. The lampstand was a single, unified object, not assembled from separate parts.
entries.exodus 25:37: Seven lamps were made for the lampstand and placed so they would light the area in front of it. The light served the priests as they ministered in the holy place.
entries.exodus 25:38: The wick trimmers and trays used with the lampstand were also made of pure gold. Even the small tools were treated with care and honor.
entries.exodus 25:39: A whole talent of gold, a large amount, was used for the lampstand and its tools. This shows the great value and importance of this object in worship.
entries.exodus 25:40: Moses was told to follow the pattern he had seen on the mountain exactly. God gave the design, and Moses was responsible for carrying it out faithfully.
entries.exodus 27:1: God told Moses to build a square wooden altar for sacrifices, about seven and a half feet on each side and four and a half feet tall. It was to be a sturdy, practical structure for the worship God had commanded.
entries.exodus 27:2: The altar had horn-like projections at its four corners, all covered in bronze. These horns were part of the altar's design and were used in the sacrificial rituals.
entries.exodus 27:3: All the tools used with the altar—pots for ashes, shovels, bowls, meat forks, and fire pans—were made of bronze. Everything connected to the altar's work was to be durable and ready for use.
entries.exodus 27:4: A bronze grating with four bronze rings was made to fit the altar. This grating was part of the altar's structure, likely for the fire and the carrying of the altar.
entries.exodus 27:5: The grating was placed under the altar's ledge so it reached halfway up the altar. This shows the careful, detailed construction God required.
entries.exodus 27:6: Wooden poles covered in bronze were made for carrying the altar. These poles allowed the altar to be moved as the people traveled.
entries.exodus 27:7: The poles were inserted through the rings on both sides of the altar so it could be lifted and carried. The altar was designed to be portable for the journey.
entries.exodus 27:8: The altar was to be hollow and made of boards, following the exact pattern God showed Moses on the mountain. God gave precise instructions, and Moses was to follow them exactly.
entries.exodus 27:9: A courtyard was to surround the tabernacle, with fine linen curtains on the south side stretching about 150 feet. This created a set-apart space for worship.
entries.exodus 27:10: The courtyard curtains hung on twenty bronze pillars set in bronze bases, with silver hooks and bands. Each material had its place in the structure God designed.
entries.exodus 27:11: The north side was built the same way, with curtains, twenty bronze pillars and bases, and silver hooks and bands. The courtyard was symmetrical and carefully ordered.
entries.exodus 27:12: The west side of the courtyard was fifty cubits wide, with ten pillars and ten bases. The dimensions and counts were all specified by God.
entries.exodus 27:13: The east side was also fifty cubits wide. The courtyard was laid out with exact measurements on every side.
entries.exodus 27:14: On one side of the entrance were curtains fifteen cubits long, hung on three pillars and three bases. The gateway area was carefully framed.
entries.exodus 27:15: The other side of the entrance matched, with curtains fifteen cubits long on three pillars and three bases. The entrance was balanced and orderly.
entries.exodus 27:16: The entrance itself had a twenty-cubit curtain of fine linen embroidered in blue, purple, and red, hung on four pillars and four bases. This colorful screen marked the way into God's courtyard.
entries.exodus 27:17: All the pillars around the courtyard had silver bands and hooks, with bronze bases. The same pattern was followed all the way around.
entries.exodus 27:18: The whole courtyard was a hundred cubits long and fifty wide, with curtains five cubits high, all of fine linen on bronze bases. The space was large, enclosed, and set apart for worship.
entries.exodus 27:19: Every tool used in the tabernacle's service, along with all the tent pegs for the tabernacle and courtyard, was made of bronze. Even the smallest hardware was included in God's instructions.
entries.exodus 27:20: God told the Israelites to bring pure olive oil so the lamp would burn continually. The people were to provide what was needed to keep the light burning before God.
entries.exodus 27:21: Aaron and his sons were to tend the lamp from evening to morning in the Tent of Meeting, outside the curtain before the ark. This was a lasting rule for Israel from generation to generation.
entries.exodus 26:1: God told the people to build him a special tent using ten curtains of fine linen in blue, purple, and red, decorated with pictures of winged beings. This shows that worshiping God was meant to be beautiful and carefully done, not sloppy or casual.
entries.exodus 26:2: Each curtain had to be the same size, about forty-two feet long and six feet wide. God cared about the details, which tells us that doing things well for him matters.
entries.exodus 26:3: The curtains were sewn together in two groups of five. This was practical planning so the whole tent could be put together and taken apart as the people traveled.
entries.exodus 26:4: They made blue loops along the outer edge of each group of curtains. These loops were the starting point for joining the two halves together.
entries.exodus 26:5: Each edge had fifty loops placed so they lined up with each other. The matching loops show how the two halves were designed to fit together as one.
entries.exodus 26:6: Fifty gold hooks connected the loops so the two groups became one single tent. Gold was the most valuable metal, showing this was a special place set apart for God.
entries.exodus 26:7: Over the decorated tent they made eleven curtains of goat hair to serve as a protective outer covering. This was a sturdy, practical layer to shield the inner tent from weather.
entries.exodus 26:8: These goat-hair curtains were each about forty-five feet long and six feet wide, all the same size. The extra length compared to the inner curtains let them hang down and cover the sides.
entries.exodus 26:9: Five of these curtains were joined and six were joined, with the sixth one folded over at the front entrance. This gave the tent a double layer at the doorway for extra protection.
entries.exodus 26:10: Fifty loops were put on the outer edge of each group of goat-hair curtains. These loops were where the two groups would be fastened together.
entries.exodus 26:11: Fifty bronze hooks joined the loops so the outer tent became one piece. Bronze was strong and practical, suited for the rougher outer layer that faced the weather.
entries.exodus 26:12: The extra half-curtain that hung over was left draping down at the back of the tent. This made sure the back was fully covered with no gaps.
entries.exodus 26:13: The extra foot of material on each side hung down over the sides of the tent as a cover. God's instructions made sure the structure was completely enclosed.
entries.exodus 26:14: Two more covers went on top: one of red-dyed ram skins and one of leather. These outermost layers protected the beautiful inner curtains from rain, sun, and wear.
entries.exodus 26:15: They made upright frames out of hard wood to form the walls of the tent. Wood was the sturdy framework that held the whole structure up.
entries.exodus 26:16: Each frame was about fifteen feet tall and two and a quarter feet wide. These tall, narrow boards formed the walls of the tabernacle.
entries.exodus 26:17: Each board had two pegs that fit into the board next to it, so the wall held together firmly. Good connections kept the whole structure stable.
entries.exodus 26:18: Twenty boards were used for the south wall of the tent. The south side was the longer side of the structure.
entries.exodus 26:19: Under those twenty boards they made forty silver bases, two under each board to hold its pegs. Silver bases gave the walls a solid, valuable foundation.
entries.exodus 26:20: Another twenty boards were used for the north wall, matching the south side. The tent was symmetrical, built to the same pattern on both sides.
entries.exodus 26:21: These boards also sat on forty silver bases, two under each one. Every board had its own secure footing, so no part of the wall was left unsupported.
entries.exodus 26:22: Six boards formed the back wall on the west side. This closed off the rear of the tent.
entries.exodus 26:23: Two more boards were made for the back corners to strengthen them. Corners need extra support, and God's design included that.
entries.exodus 26:24: The corner boards were joined at the bottom and held together at the top with a ring, making a solid corner. This kept the structure from coming apart at its weakest points.
entries.exodus 26:25: So the back had eight boards in total, resting on sixteen silver bases, two under each board. The count adds up to a complete, well-supported back wall.
entries.exodus 26:26: They made wooden crossbars, five for the boards on one side. These bars ran across the boards to hold the wall rigid.
entries.exodus 26:27: Five more crossbars went on the other side and five on the back wall. Every wall had the same bracing so the whole tent was equally strong.
entries.exodus 26:28: The middle crossbar ran through rings on all the boards from one end to the other. This one long bar tied the entire wall together.
entries.exodus 26:29: The boards and crossbars were covered with gold, and gold rings held the bars in place. Covering the plain wood with gold showed that this was a place of great honor for God.
entries.exodus 26:30: Moses was told to build the tent exactly according to the plan God showed him on the mountain. God's worship was to follow his instructions, not human ideas.
entries.exodus 26:31: A special curtain of fine linen in blue, purple, and red, decorated with winged beings, was made to hang inside the tent. This curtain marked off the most sacred inner room.
entries.exodus 26:32: This curtain hung from gold hooks on four wooden pillars covered with gold, standing in silver bases. The rich materials showed how seriously the people were to treat God's presence.
entries.exodus 26:33: The curtain was hung under the hooks, and the ark of the law was placed inside it. This curtain separated the holy place from the most holy place, the innermost room where God's presence was especially near.
entries.exodus 26:34: The cover was placed on the ark inside the most holy place. This was the most sacred spot in the whole tent, where atonement was made for the people.
entries.exodus 26:35: Outside the curtain they put the table on the north side and the lampstand opposite it on the south side. These furnishings were for the daily worship that happened in the outer holy room.
entries.exodus 26:36: A curtain for the entrance of the tent was made of fine linen with colorful needlework in blue, purple, and red. This doorway curtain was the way into God's dwelling place.
entries.exodus 26:37: Five wooden pillars covered with gold, with gold hooks and bronze bases, held up the entrance curtain. Bronze was used for the bases at the doorway, while gold was used where the curtain hung.
entries.exodus 31:1: God begins speaking to Moses again on the mountain. This reminds the reader that what follows comes directly from God.
entries.exodus 31:2: God chose a specific man, Bezalel, by name for a special job. It shows God picks ordinary people for His work and knows them personally.
entries.exodus 31:3: God filled Bezalel with His Spirit and gave him skill, understanding, and know-how for craftwork. The reader can see that practical talents are gifts from God.
entries.exodus 31:4: Bezalel was given ability to make beautiful things out of gold, silver, and bronze. This shows God cares about careful, skilled work done for Him.
entries.exodus 31:5: He could also cut and set stones and work with wood in every kind of craft. God gives people many different practical skills to serve His purposes.
entries.exodus 31:6: God chose Oholiab to work alongside Bezalel and gave skill to everyone else who was able. God works through teams, and He supplies the ability they need.
entries.exodus 31:7: The work included the meeting tent, the ark of the law, and its cover, plus everything for the tent. These were the central items where God would meet with His people.
entries.exodus 31:8: They were also to make the table and its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, and the altar for burning incense. Each item had a set purpose in worship.
entries.exodus 31:9: The list continues with the altar for burnt offerings, its utensils, and the basin with its stand. Even the practical washing items were part of the holy setup.
entries.exodus 31:10: They were to make the woven garments, including the holy clothes for Aaron and his sons to wear as priests. These clothes marked them out for their special role serving God.
entries.exodus 31:11: They were also to prepare the holy oil and the sweet-smelling incense for the holy place. Everything was to be done exactly as God commanded.
entries.exodus 31:12: God speaks to Moses again. This marks a new instruction that follows the building plans.
entries.exodus 31:13: God tells Israel to keep His Sabbaths as a lasting sign that He is the one who makes them holy. For the reader, rest is a visible reminder that God sets His people apart.
entries.exodus 31:14: The Sabbath was to be treated as holy, and breaking it carried the severe penalty of being cut off from the people. This shows how seriously God took this sign of belonging to Him.
entries.exodus 31:15: Work was allowed for six days, but the seventh was a day of complete rest holy to God, and working on it was punishable by death. The reader sees that God built rest into life and expected it to be honored.
entries.exodus 31:16: Israel was to keep the Sabbath through every generation as a permanent agreement. It was meant to be a lasting practice, not a one-time rule.
entries.exodus 31:17: The Sabbath was a permanent sign between God and Israel, rooted in God resting after creating the world. It reminds the reader that rest and delight are part of God's own pattern.
entries.exodus 31:18: When God finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, He gave him two stone tablets written by God Himself. This shows the law came from God directly, not from human opinion.
entries.exodus 28:1: God chose Aaron and his sons to serve as priests, the special people who would represent the nation to God. It means God picks who serves him, and that service is a serious calling.
entries.exodus 28:2: Aaron's clothes were to be made special and beautiful to show the honor of his role. The reader learns that what is set apart for God should be treated with dignity.
entries.exodus 28:3: God had already given certain craftsmen the skill and wisdom to do this work. It means God supplies the ability for the tasks he asks people to do.
entries.exodus 28:4: This lists the specific pieces of clothing the priests were to wear for their work. It shows that serving God involved careful, detailed preparation.
entries.exodus 28:5: The workers were to use valuable materials like gold and fine colored fabrics. It means the best was given for God's service, not leftovers.
entries.exodus 28:6: The ephod, a special vest-like garment, was to be made by skilled designers from the finest materials. It shows that beauty and craftsmanship mattered in worship.
entries.exodus 28:7: The ephod had shoulder straps sewn on to hold it together. This is a practical detail showing the garment was made to be worn properly.
entries.exodus 28:8: The decorative waistband was to match the ephod exactly in material and workmanship. It means the whole outfit was to be consistent and carefully made.
entries.exodus 28:9: Two precious stones were to be engraved with the names of Israel's tribes. It means the people were to be remembered and represented before God.
entries.exodus 28:10: Six tribe names went on each stone, listed in birth order. This shows careful order and that every tribe was included.
entries.exodus 28:11: A skilled jeweler was to carve the names into the stones like a seal, then set them in gold. It means the names were permanent and precious.
entries.exodus 28:12: The stones sat on the priest's shoulders as a reminder of the people before God. It means the priest carried the people with him when he came to God.
entries.exodus 28:13: Gold settings were to be made for the stones. This is a detail about how the precious stones were to be held securely.
entries.exodus 28:14: Two cords of pure gold, twisted like rope, were to attach to the settings. It shows the care and quality put into every part of the priest's clothing.
entries.exodus 28:15: The chest piece used for making decisions was to be made like the ephod, from the same fine materials. It means this important item matched the rest of the priest's holy clothing.
entries.exodus 28:16: The chest piece was to be square and folded double, about a hand-span in each direction. This gives its exact size and shape.
entries.exodus 28:17: Four rows of precious stones were to be set on the chest piece, starting with carnelian, chrysolite, and emerald. It shows the richness of what the priest wore before God.
entries.exodus 28:18: The second row was to hold a ruby, a sapphire, and an onyx. Each stone added to the beauty and value of the priest's chest piece.
entries.exodus 28:19: The third row was to hold a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst. The careful arrangement shows order and honor in worship.
entries.exodus 28:20: The fourth row was to hold a topaz, a beryl, and a jasper, all set in gold. It completes the twelve stones, each one precious.
entries.exodus 28:21: Each of the twelve stones bore the name of one of Israel's tribes. It means the whole nation was represented on the priest's heart and shoulders.
entries.exodus 28:22: Two gold cords, twisted like rope, were to be made for the chest piece. This is a detail about how the piece was to be attached and carried.
entries.exodus 28:23: Two gold rings were to be placed on the ends of the chest piece. These rings were where the cords would connect.
entries.exodus 28:24: The gold cords were to be fastened to the rings at the ends of the chest piece. This shows how the piece was held in place.
entries.exodus 28:25: The other ends of the cords were to attach to the gold settings on the front of the shoulder straps. It means the chest piece hung securely on the priest.
entries.exodus 28:26: Two more gold rings were to go on the lower inner edge of the chest piece, next to the ephod. This kept the piece from swinging loose.
entries.exodus 28:27: Two more rings were to be placed on the front of the shoulder straps, near the join above the waistband. These matched the rings on the chest piece.
entries.exodus 28:28: A blue cord was to tie the rings together so the chest piece stayed attached to the ephod. It means the priest's clothing was made to stay in place during his work.
entries.exodus 28:29: Aaron was to wear the chest piece with the tribe names over his heart whenever he entered the holy place. It means he constantly carried the people before God.
entries.exodus 28:30: The Urim and Thummim were to be kept in the chest piece so Aaron could seek God's decisions for the people. It means God provided a way for the priest to know his will.
entries.exodus 28:31: The robe worn under the ephod was to be made entirely of blue cloth. This gave the priest a distinct, recognizable appearance.
entries.exodus 28:32: The robe had a reinforced opening at the neck so it would not tear. It shows practical care was taken so the holy garment would last.
entries.exodus 28:33: Pomegranate shapes in colored yarn and gold bells were to hang around the hem of the robe. These decorated the robe and made sound as the priest moved.
entries.exodus 28:34: A gold bell and a pomegranate alternated all the way around the hem. This created a pattern of sound and beauty as the priest walked.
entries.exodus 28:35: Aaron was to wear this robe when serving, and the bells would sound as he entered and left the holy place. It means his approach to God was marked with sound, and he would not die for entering improperly.
entries.exodus 28:36: A gold plate was to be engraved with the words 'Holy to the Lord.' It marked the priest as set apart entirely for God.
entries.exodus 28:37: The plate was to be tied with a blue cord onto the front of the priest's turban. It was worn prominently for all to see.
entries.exodus 28:38: The plate on Aaron's forehead meant he bore the guilt connected with the people's holy offerings. It means the priest stood in their place so their gifts could be accepted by God.
entries.exodus 28:39: The undergarment was to be woven from fine linen, with a linen turban and a decorated sash. These were the basic, dignified garments of the priest.
entries.exodus 28:40: Aaron's sons were also to receive coats, sashes, and head coverings to give them honor and dignity. It means the whole priesthood was to be treated with respect.
entries.exodus 29:1: God tells Moses how to set Aaron and his sons apart for priestly service, starting with animals that are perfect and unblemished. For the reader, it shows that approaching God required careful preparation and the best, not leftovers.
entries.exodus 29:2: Bread made without yeast, some mixed with oil and some with oil poured on, made from fine flour, was also part of the setup. It reminds us that ordinary food, carefully prepared, can be offered to God.
entries.exodus 29:3: All the bread is placed in a basket and brought along with the ox and the two sheep. The details show that the whole ceremony was planned and orderly, not casual.
entries.exodus 29:4: Aaron and his sons are brought to the entrance of the meeting tent and washed with water. Being cleaned comes before serving, a picture of how God prepares people before they serve him.
entries.exodus 29:5: Moses dresses Aaron in the special priestly clothes, including the coat, the ephod, and the decorated band. The clothing marks him out as set apart for a holy role.
entries.exodus 29:6: A head covering and a holy crown are placed on Aaron's head. This shows his role was an honor given by God, not something he took for himself.
entries.exodus 29:7: Moses pours oil on Aaron's head to set him apart. The oil is a sign that God's Spirit and calling rest on the person chosen for the task.
entries.exodus 29:8: Aaron's sons are brought forward and dressed in their robes too. The whole family shares in the calling, each with their own part to play.
entries.exodus 29:9: Linen bands and head coverings are put on Aaron and his sons, establishing them as priests permanently by God's command. It shows that God himself defines who serves him and how.
entries.exodus 29:10: The ox is brought before the meeting tent, and Aaron and his sons lay their hands on its head. This identifies them with the animal, showing that the offering stands in their place.
entries.exodus 29:11: The ox is killed before the Lord at the entrance of the tent. The seriousness of sin is shown by the death required, even for those being set apart to serve.
entries.exodus 29:12: Some of the ox's blood is smeared on the altar's horns and the rest poured at its base. Blood is used to cleanse the altar, showing that sin and guilt must be dealt with before worship.
entries.exodus 29:13: The fat around the organs is burned on the altar. In that culture the fat was the richest part, so this means giving God the best portion.
entries.exodus 29:14: The rest of the ox, its skin and waste, is burned outside the camp because it is a sin offering. What carries sin is removed from the community, showing that sin must be taken away, not kept around.
entries.exodus 29:15: One of the sheep is brought, and Aaron and his sons lay their hands on its head. Again they identify with the animal that will be offered on their behalf.
entries.exodus 29:16: The sheep is killed and its blood is splashed on the sides of the altar. The blood marks the altar as the place where life is given to deal with sin.
entries.exodus 29:17: The sheep is cut into pieces, and the legs and inner parts are washed before being laid out with the head. Care and cleanliness are part of preparing an offering for God.
entries.exodus 29:18: The whole sheep is burned on the altar as an offering to the Lord, described as a pleasing smell. It pictures a wholehearted gift given completely to God.
entries.exodus 29:19: The second sheep is brought, and Aaron and his sons lay their hands on its head. This is the special setting-apart offering for the priests themselves.
entries.exodus 29:20: The sheep is killed, and its blood is put on the right ear, thumb, and big toe of Aaron and his sons, with the rest poured on the altar. It means their hearing, work, and walk are all to be dedicated to God.
entries.exodus 29:21: Blood from the altar and oil are sprinkled on Aaron, his sons, and their clothes to make them holy. Being set apart for God touches the person and everything connected with their service.
entries.exodus 29:22: The fat, fat tail, organs, and right leg of the setting-apart sheep are taken for the ceremony. These choice parts mark the priests as specially dedicated to God.
entries.exodus 29:23: One plain bread, one oiled cake, and one thin cake are taken from the basket set before the Lord. The bread that was offered to God is now used in the ceremony itself.
entries.exodus 29:24: All these are placed in the hands of Aaron and his sons and waved before the Lord. Lifting them up and waving them is a way of presenting the gift to God and then receiving it back.
entries.exodus 29:25: The items are taken from their hands and burned on the altar with the other offering as a pleasing smell to the Lord. What is given to God is offered fully, not half-heartedly.
entries.exodus 29:26: The breast of the sheep is waved before the Lord and becomes Moses' share. Those who lead in worship are also provided for by God.
entries.exodus 29:27: The waved breast and the lifted leg are set apart as holy for Aaron and his sons. God makes sure those who serve at the altar are cared for.
entries.exodus 29:28: This portion becomes a permanent right for the priests, taken from Israel's peace offerings and lifted up to the Lord. It shows that supporting those who serve God is a lasting practice, not an afterthought.
entries.exodus 29:29: Aaron's holy clothes are to be passed down to his sons after him, worn when they become priests. The calling continues from one generation to the next.
entries.exodus 29:30: The son who takes Aaron's place wears these clothes for seven days when he first enters the tent to serve. A period of preparation is given before full service begins.
entries.exodus 29:31: The meat of the setting-apart sheep is cooked in water in a holy place. Even the practical details of the ceremony are treated as sacred.
entries.exodus 29:32: Aaron and his sons eat the meat and the bread at the entrance of the meeting tent. Sharing a meal in God's presence is part of being set apart for him.
entries.exodus 29:33: Only the priests may eat the food used in the offerings that took away sin and made them holy. What is holy is treated with respect and not shared carelessly.
entries.exodus 29:34: Any leftover meat or bread must be burned in the morning, not eaten, because it is holy. Holy things are not to be treated as ordinary or wasted.
entries.exodus 29:35: Moses is to do all this for Aaron and his sons exactly as commanded, with the ceremony lasting seven days. Being set apart for God takes time and careful obedience.
entries.exodus 29:36: Each day an ox is offered to take away sin, and the altar is cleansed and anointed to make it holy. Even the place of worship needs to be purified before it can be used for God.
entries.exodus 29:37: For seven days the altar is made holy until it is completely set apart, and anything that touches it becomes holy. God's holiness is shown to spread to what comes into contact with him.
entries.exodus 29:38: Two year-old lambs are to be offered on the altar every single day without fail. Regular, ongoing worship is expected, not just occasional devotion.
entries.exodus 29:39: One lamb is offered in the morning and the other in the evening. Worship bookends the day, reminding the reader that God is part of daily life from start to finish.
entries.exodus 29:40: Along with each lamb, fine flour mixed with oil and a portion of wine are offered. The offering includes food and drink, showing that worship involves giving from what sustains us.
entries.exodus 28:41: God tells Moses to dress Aaron and his sons in these special clothes and pour oil on them, setting them apart to serve as priests. It means God chooses and prepares people for his service, not just anyone who decides on their own.
entries.exodus 28:42: The priests were to wear linen undergarments that covered them properly from waist to thigh. This was about modesty and decency, reminding the reader that approaching God calls for respect and care.
entries.exodus 28:43: The priests had to wear these garments whenever they entered the tent or came near the altar, or they would be guilty of an offense that could cost them their lives. It shows that God takes worship seriously and that coming to him requires the honor and preparation he asks for, a rule meant to last for generations.
entries.exodus 30:1: God tells Moses to build a small altar made of wood, used only for burning sweet-smelling incense. It shows that worship involves special, set-apart practices given by God.
entries.exodus 30:2: The altar was a square box shape with raised corners called horns, all made from the same wood. The precise measurements remind us that God cares about how worship is done.
entries.exodus 30:3: The whole altar was covered in fine gold, including its top, sides, and horns, with a gold border around it. Gold marked it as something precious and reserved for God.
entries.exodus 30:4: Two gold rings were attached to its sides so poles could be slipped through to carry it. This made the altar portable for the people's journey.
entries.exodus 30:5: The carrying poles were made of wood and covered in gold, matching the altar. Even the small details of worship were to be done with care.
entries.exodus 30:6: The altar was placed just outside the curtain that hid the ark of the law, where God said he would meet with Moses. It stood at the threshold of God's presence.
entries.exodus 30:7: Aaron was to burn sweet-smelling spices on this altar every morning when he tended the lamps. Worship was to begin each day with an offering to God.
entries.exodus 30:8: Aaron was also to burn incense each evening when he lit the lamps, and this practice was to continue for all generations. Morning and evening, the people's worship was to rise to God.
entries.exodus 30:9: Only the special incense was allowed on this altar—no other perfume, no animal sacrifices, no grain or drink offerings. This altar had one purpose, and God wanted it kept that way.
entries.exodus 30:10: Once a year Aaron was to cleanse the altar's horns with the blood of the sin offering, making it most holy to the Lord. Even the place of prayer needed cleansing, showing how seriously God takes sin.
entries.exodus 30:11: God speaks to Moses, introducing the next set of instructions. These words remind us that what follows comes directly from God.
entries.exodus 30:12: When the people were counted, each man was to give a payment for his life so that no plague would strike them during the census. Being counted before God required an offering.
entries.exodus 30:13: Each counted man was to give half a shekel of silver, measured by the sanctuary's standard, as an offering to the Lord. The amount was fixed and fair for everyone.
entries.exodus 30:14: Every man twenty years old or older who was counted had to give this offering to the Lord. The duty applied to all adults, not just a select few.
entries.exodus 30:15: Rich and poor alike were to give exactly the same half-shekel—no more, no less—as the price for their lives. Before God, every person's life is valued equally.
entries.exodus 30:16: The money collected was to fund the work of the Tent of Meeting and serve as a reminder of the people before the Lord. Their giving supported worship and reminded them their lives belonged to God.
entries.exodus 30:17: God again speaks to Moses, beginning another instruction. Each new command comes from the same God who leads his people.
entries.exodus 30:18: Moses was to make a bronze basin with a bronze stand and place it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, filled with water. It provided what the priests needed to cleanse themselves.
entries.exodus 30:19: Aaron and his sons were to use the water to wash their hands and feet. Those who served God needed to be clean before doing so.
entries.exodus 30:20: Whenever the priests entered the Tent of Meeting, they had to wash with water so they would not die, and the same applied when they came to the altar to offer fire offerings. Coming near to God required cleansing.
entries.exodus 30:21: The priests had to wash their hands and feet so they would be safe from death, and this was a permanent rule for Aaron and his descendants. Cleansing was not optional but a lasting requirement for those who serve God.
entries.exodus 30:22: God speaks to Moses once more, introducing instructions about a special oil. These commands continue God's detailed plan for worship.
entries.exodus 30:23: Moses was to gather the finest spices: about twelve pounds of liquid myrrh, half that amount of sweet cinnamon, and the same of sweet calamus. Only the best ingredients were used for this holy purpose.
entries.exodus 30:24: He was also to take about twelve pounds of cassia, measured by the sanctuary standard, along with a hin of olive oil. The recipe was precise and used costly materials.
entries.exodus 30:25: These ingredients were to be blended by a skilled perfumer into a holy anointing oil. It was made like fine perfume but set apart for God's use.
entries.exodus 30:26: The oil was to be applied to the Tent of Meeting and the ark of the law. Anointing these objects marked them as dedicated to God.
entries.exodus 30:27: The oil was also for the table and its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, and the incense altar. Every piece of the sanctuary was to be set apart for God's service.
entries.exodus 30:28: The altar of burnt offerings, its utensils, and the washing basin with its stand were also to be anointed. Nothing used in worship was left out.
entries.exodus 30:29: Anointing these objects made them most holy, so that anything touching them would become holy too. Holiness spreads from what is dedicated to God.
entries.exodus 30:30: Aaron and his sons were to be anointed with the oil to make them holy for serving as priests to God. The oil set them apart for their special role.
entries.exodus 30:31: Moses was to tell the Israelites that this oil was the Lord's holy oil for all generations. It belonged to God and was to be treated as such permanently.
entries.exodus 30:32: The oil was not to be poured on ordinary people, and no one was to make a similar blend. What is holy to God must be kept holy.
entries.exodus 30:33: Anyone who made a copy of the oil or put it on a non-priest would be cut off from the people. Misusing holy things had serious consequences.
entries.exodus 30:34: God told Moses to take equal amounts of sweet spices—stacte, onycha, galbanum—along with pure frankincense. The incense was made from carefully chosen ingredients.
entries.exodus 30:35: These were to be blended by a perfumer, mixed with salt, to make a pure and holy incense. Salt likely signified purity and lasting quality.
entries.exodus 30:36: Some of the incense was to be crushed to powder and placed in front of the ark in the Tent of Meeting, where God met with Moses, and it was most holy. It was reserved for the place of God's presence.
entries.exodus 30:37: The people were not to make this incense for their own personal use; it was to be kept holy to the Lord. What belonged to God was not for ordinary enjoyment.
entries.exodus 30:38: Anyone who made a similar incense just to enjoy its sweet smell would be cut off from the people. Treating holy things as common had serious consequences.
entries.exodus 29:41: A second lamb was to be sacrificed every evening, along with the same grain and drink offerings as in the morning. This showed that worship of God was to be steady and repeated, not a one-time event.
entries.exodus 29:42: This offering was to continue for all future generations at the entrance of the meeting tent, the place where God promised to meet and speak with his people. It reminds the reader that God wants regular, ongoing contact with his people.
entries.exodus 29:43: God promised to meet with the Israelites there, and his glorious presence would make the tent holy. The place became special because God himself showed up there.
entries.exodus 29:44: God himself would set apart the tent, the altar, and Aaron and his sons for their special role as priests. It was God who made them fit for his service, not their own effort.
entries.exodus 29:45: God promised to live among the Israelites and be their God. The reader sees that God's desire is to be close to his people, not distant from them.
entries.exodus 29:46: The people would know God as the one who rescued them from Egypt specifically so he could stay with them. God's rescue was not just to free them but to bring them into a lasting relationship with him.
entries.exodus 33:1: God tells Moses to lead the people out of Egypt toward the land he promised long ago to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and their descendants. It means God still keeps his old promises even after the people have done wrong.
entries.exodus 33:2: God promises to send an angel ahead of them to drive out the peoples already living in the land. The reader can see that God clears the way, but this verse alone doesn't mean he will be close to them.
entries.exodus 33:3: God will bring them to a rich, good land, but he says he will not travel among them because they are stubborn and he might destroy them on the way. It shows that sin puts distance between people and God, even when his gifts continue.
entries.exodus 33:4: When the people heard this bad news they mourned and stopped wearing their jewelry. It shows real sorrow over losing God's nearness, not just over losing a gift.
entries.exodus 33:5: God calls them stubborn and says that if he came among them even briefly he might destroy them, so they should remove their ornaments while he decides what to do. It means God takes their hard hearts seriously and calls for humility.
entries.exodus 33:6: So the Israelites stripped off their ornaments at Mount Horeb and did not wear them again. It marks a lasting change of attitude, showing they were willing to give up something precious to show sorrow.
entries.exodus 33:7: Moses set up the meeting tent outside the camp, away from the people, and anyone who wanted to pray to the Lord went out there. It means seeking God now required going outside the camp, a sign that fellowship with him had been disrupted.
entries.exodus 33:8: Whenever Moses walked out to the tent, everyone stood at their tent doors and watched him until he went inside. It shows the people's respect for Moses and their attention to anyone who meets with God.
entries.exodus 33:9: When Moses entered the tent, the cloud came down and stood at the entrance while the Lord spoke with him. It means God really was present and speaking, and the cloud was a visible sign of that.
entries.exodus 33:10: All the people saw the cloud at the tent door and bowed down with their faces to the ground, each at his own tent. It shows that when God's presence was visible, the people responded with worship.
entries.exodus 33:11: The Lord spoke with Moses face to face, like friends talking, and Joshua stayed behind in the tent. It means Moses had an unusually close relationship with God, and Joshua was being prepared to lead.
entries.exodus 33:12: Moses reminds God that he was told to lead the people but not told who would go with him, and he recalls God's promise of favor and personal knowledge of him. It shows Moses praying honestly and holding God to his own words.
entries.exodus 33:13: Moses asks to know God's ways so he can truly know him and be sure of his favor, and he asks God to remember that this nation is his own people. It means Moses wants more than guidance; he wants a deeper relationship with God.
entries.exodus 33:14: God answers that he himself will go with Moses and give him rest. It means God grants the nearness Moses asked for and promises relief from the burden of the journey.
entries.exodus 33:15: Moses says that if God himself will not go with them, they should not leave that place at all. It shows that God's presence mattered more to Moses than reaching the destination.
entries.exodus 33:16: Moses argues that God's going with them is exactly what marks Israel as different from every other people. It means God's presence, not their own strength, is what makes his people distinct.
entries.exodus 33:17: The Lord agrees to do what Moses asks because Moses has found favor with him and God knows him by name. It shows that God listens to prayer and values a close relationship with a person.
entries.exodus 33:18: Moses asks to see God's glory. It is a bold request to experience God's greatness and goodness more directly.
entries.exodus 33:19: God says he will show his goodness and proclaim his name before Moses, and he will be kind and merciful to whomever he chooses. It means God reveals himself freely, and mercy is his choice to give, not something anyone earns.
entries.exodus 33:20: God says Moses cannot see his face, because no one can see God fully and survive. It means God is far greater and more holy than humans can handle directly.
entries.exodus 33:21: God tells Moses there is a place near him where Moses can stand on a rock. It shows God making a way for Moses to be near him safely.
entries.exodus 33:22: When God's glory passes by, he will put Moses in a gap in the rock and cover him with his hand until he has passed. It pictures God protecting Moses from what he could not survive.
entries.exodus 33:23: God will then remove his hand, and Moses will see his back, but his face cannot be seen. It means Moses gets a partial, protected glimpse of God, because full sight of God is beyond human ability.
entries.exodus 34:1: God tells Moses to cut two new stone tablets to replace the ones he smashed, and promises to write the same words on them again. It shows God gives people a fresh start after failure.
entries.exodus 34:2: God tells Moses to be ready in the morning and come up the mountain alone to meet him at the top. It means meeting with God takes preparation and a set time.
entries.exodus 34:3: No one else, not even animals, is allowed on the mountain while God meets with Moses. It shows that this meeting with God was holy and set apart.
entries.exodus 34:4: Moses did exactly what God said, cutting the stones and climbing the mountain early with them in his hands. It shows obedience to God's instructions, done promptly.
entries.exodus 34:5: God came down in a cloud and stood near Moses, and Moses worshiped him. It means God comes close to those who seek him, and the right response is worship.
entries.exodus 34:6: God describes himself as compassionate, gracious, patient, and full of faithful love. It means God's basic character toward people is kind and patient.
entries.exodus 34:7: God shows mercy to many generations and forgives wrongdoing, yet he does not ignore sin and its effects carry on through families. It means God is forgiving but also takes sin seriously.
entries.exodus 34:8: Moses bowed down to the ground in worship right away. It shows his deep respect and gratitude toward God.
entries.exodus 34:9: Moses asks God to stay with the people and forgive them, even though they are stubborn, and to make them his own. It means we can honestly admit our faults and still ask God to stay with us.
entries.exodus 34:10: God promises to do amazing things for the people that have never been seen before, and everyone will see it. It means God's work in our lives can be something others notice.
entries.exodus 34:11: God tells the people to obey his commands and promises to drive out the nations ahead of them. It means obedience and God's help go together.
entries.exodus 34:12: God warns them not to make treaties with the people already living in the land, because it would lead them into sin. It means close ties with wrong influences can pull us away from God.
entries.exodus 34:13: They are told to tear down the altars, pillars, and idols of those peoples. It means anything set up for false worship had to be removed, not tolerated.
entries.exodus 34:14: They must worship no other god, because the Lord will not share his honor with another. It means God expects our loyalty to belong to him alone.
entries.exodus 34:15: God warns that making agreements with the local people could lead them to join in their sacrifices and feasts for other gods. It means friendships and alliances can quietly lead us into wrong worship.
entries.exodus 34:16: Taking their daughters as wives could lead the sons to worship other gods. It means the people closest to us can shape what we worship.
entries.exodus 34:17: They are told not to make metal gods for themselves. It means we should not create our own substitutes for God.
entries.exodus 34:18: They must keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread at the set time each year, eating bread without yeast for seven days. It means remembering how God rescued them from Egypt was to be a regular practice.
entries.exodus 34:19: Every firstborn male, both of people and animals, belongs to God. It means the first and best of what we have is to be given to God.
entries.exodus 34:20: A firstborn donkey could be bought back with a lamb, and every firstborn son had to be bought back; no one comes to God empty-handed. It means coming to God involves giving, not just receiving.
entries.exodus 34:21: They work six days but rest on the seventh, even during the busiest farming seasons. It means rest is required, not optional, even when there is much to do.
entries.exodus 34:22: They are to celebrate the Feast of Weeks at the first grain harvest and another feast at the end of the year. It means regular times of celebration and thanks to God.
entries.exodus 34:23: Three times a year all the men must come before the Lord. It means worship was to be a regular, shared commitment, not a rare event.
entries.exodus 34:24: God promises to protect their land and expand it while they go to worship him three times a year. It means trusting God with our time and priorities is safe.
entries.exodus 34:25: No yeast may be offered with the blood of the sacrifice, and the Passover offering must not be left until morning. It means worship is to be done God's way, with care and respect.
entries.exodus 34:26: They are to bring the firstfruits of their land to God's house and not cook a young goat in its mother's milk. It means giving God the first and best, and following his instructions even in small details.
entries.exodus 34:27: God tells Moses to write these words down because the agreement with the people is based on them. It means God's words are meant to be kept and remembered, not just heard.
entries.exodus 34:28: Moses stayed with the Lord forty days and nights without eating or drinking and wrote the Ten Commandments on the stones. It means being with God can be so consuming that other needs fade for a time.
entries.exodus 34:29: When Moses came down with the stone tablets, his face was shining from being with God, though he didn't know it. It means time with God changes a person in ways others can see.
entries.exodus 34:30: Aaron and the people were afraid to come near Moses because his face was shining. It means God's presence can be overwhelming, even when it comes through a person.
entries.exodus 34:31: Moses called them back, and Aaron and the leaders came and talked with him. It means leaders have a role in helping people approach God's messenger.
entries.exodus 34:32: Afterward all the people came near, and Moses gave them everything the Lord had commanded on the mountain. It means God's instructions are for everyone, not just the leaders.
entries.exodus 34:33: When Moses finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face. It means the shining was so intense that it needed covering when he was among the people.
entries.exodus 34:34: Whenever Moses went in to talk with the Lord he took the veil off, and when he came out he told the people what God said. It means we should be open before God and honest with others about what he tells us.
entries.exodus 34:35: The people saw Moses' face shining, so he covered it again until he went back to the Lord. It means the effect of being with God was visible, and Moses kept returning to God for more.
entries.exodus 35:1: Moses gathered the whole nation and told them these were God's own instructions, not his own ideas. It reminds the reader that what follows comes with God's authority and deserves attention.
entries.exodus 35:2: Work was allowed for six days, but the seventh day was to be kept as a special day of rest dedicated to God. Anyone who worked on that day was to be executed, showing how seriously God treated this command.
entries.exodus 35:3: The people were not even to light a fire in their homes on the Sabbath. This made the day of rest a complete break from ordinary work, even small household tasks.
entries.exodus 35:4: Moses passed on to the whole community the command God had given. The instructions that follow were for everyone, not just the leaders.
entries.exodus 35:5: People were to bring voluntary gifts to God from what they owned, including gold, silver, and bronze. Giving was to come from a willing heart, not from pressure.
entries.exodus 35:6: They were also to bring colored yarns, fine linen, and goat hair. These were the raw materials needed for making the sacred tent and its furnishings.
entries.exodus 35:7: Dyed animal skins, leather, and acacia wood were among the materials needed. Ordinary goods from daily life were to be used for God's purposes.
entries.exodus 35:8: Olive oil for lamps and spices for the sacred anointing oil and incense were also required. Even small supplies mattered for the worship God had commanded.
entries.exodus 35:9: Precious stones were to be given for the priest's special garments and chest piece. Valuable items were to be offered for the honor of God's service.
entries.exodus 35:10: Everyone with skill was invited to come and make everything the Lord had commanded. God's work called for both willing givers and willing workers.
entries.exodus 35:11: The list begins with the tabernacle itself, its tent, coverings, frames, and bases. These were the parts that made up the portable place of worship.
entries.exodus 35:12: The ark, its cover, its carrying poles, and the curtain that screened it were to be made. The ark was the most sacred object, representing God's presence among his people.
entries.exodus 35:13: The table for the sacred bread, along with its poles and utensils, was included. This table stood in the holy place and held the bread set before God.
entries.exodus 35:14: The lampstand with its lamps and oil was to be made. It provided light in the holy place where the priests served.
entries.exodus 35:15: The altar for burning incense, its poles, the anointing oil, the incense, and the curtain for the entrance were also required. Each item served a specific role in worship.
entries.exodus 35:16: The altar for burnt offerings, its bronze grating, poles, utensils, and the washing basin with its stand were to be made. These were central to the sacrifices and cleansing of the priests.
entries.exodus 35:17: The curtains for the courtyard, its pillars and bases, and the curtain for the courtyard entrance were included. These formed the outer enclosure around the tabernacle.
entries.exodus 35:18: The pegs and ropes for the tabernacle and courtyard were also needed. Even the smallest hardware mattered in building God's dwelling place.
entries.exodus 35:19: The woven garments for the priests, including Aaron's holy robes and those of his sons, were to be made. These set the priests apart for their service in the holy place.
entries.exodus 35:20: After hearing Moses, the people went back to their tents. The next verses show how they responded to what they had been told.
entries.exodus 35:21: Everyone whose heart moved them came forward with offerings for the Lord's work. God's work is supported by people who give because they want to, not because they are forced.
entries.exodus 35:22: Men and women alike brought gold jewelry as a freewill offering to the Lord. Both genders shared in giving toward God's house.
entries.exodus 35:23: Those who owned the needed fabrics, skins, and leather brought them. People gave from whatever materials they already had on hand.
entries.exodus 35:24: Those with silver, bronze, or wood brought them as offerings to the Lord. Different people contributed different things, and all of it was needed.
entries.exodus 35:25: Skilled women spun yarn with their own hands and brought the finished work. Their practical skills became an offering to God.
entries.exodus 35:26: Women with the know-how spun goat hair into cloth. Even less glamorous materials and skills were part of the sacred work.
entries.exodus 35:27: The leaders of the community gave the precious stones for the priest's garments. Those with more resources were expected to contribute accordingly.
entries.exodus 35:28: They also supplied the spices and oil needed for light, anointing, and incense. The leaders helped cover the ongoing needs of worship.
entries.exodus 35:29: Every man and woman who was willing brought freewill offerings for the work God had commanded. The whole community shared in building the place of worship.
entries.exodus 35:30: Moses told the people that God had specifically chosen Bezalel from the tribe of Judah. God himself picks the people who will do his work.
entries.exodus 35:31: God filled Bezalel with his Spirit and gave him wisdom, understanding, and skill in every kind of craft. God equips people with ability for the tasks he assigns.
entries.exodus 35:32: Bezalel was skilled at designing and working with gold, silver, and bronze. His artistic talent was a gift from God to be used for God's purposes.
entries.exodus 35:33: He was trained in cutting stones, carving wood, and every kind of craftsmanship. A wide range of practical skills was needed for the tabernacle work.
entries.exodus 35:34: God also gave Bezalel and Oholiab the ability to teach others their crafts. Skilled people were expected to pass on their knowledge so the work could be shared.
entries.exodus 35:35: God gave them expertise in weaving, designing, and all kinds of skilled work. Their abilities came from God and were to be used fully in his service.
entries.exodus 32:1: The people got impatient waiting for Moses to come back down the mountain, so they asked Aaron to make them a visible god to lead them. It shows how quickly we can turn away from God when we feel abandoned or things take too long.
entries.exodus 32:2: Aaron told the people to hand over the gold earrings from their families. He was going along with their wrong request instead of standing up for what was right.
entries.exodus 32:3: Everyone gave their gold earrings to Aaron without objection. The whole community joined in this wrong action together.
entries.exodus 32:4: Aaron melted the gold and shaped it into a calf statue, and the people declared it to be the god who brought them out of Egypt. They replaced the real God with something they had made themselves.
entries.exodus 32:5: Aaron built an altar in front of the calf and announced a festival to the Lord. He tried to mix worship of the real God with the idol they had just made.
entries.exodus 32:6: The people got up early to offer sacrifices and then sat down to eat and party wildly. Their worship turned into self-indulgence rather than honoring God.
entries.exodus 32:7: God told Moses to go down quickly because the people had corrupted themselves. God saw exactly what was happening and called it evil.
entries.exodus 32:8: God described how the people had already turned from his commands and were worshiping the metal calf. They had broken their promise to follow God alone.
entries.exodus 32:9: God told Moses that these people were stubborn and refused to change their ways. Stubbornness against God is a serious problem he sees clearly.
entries.exodus 32:10: God told Moses to step aside because his anger was burning and he wanted to destroy the people, then start over with Moses. God's anger against sin is real and serious.
entries.exodus 32:11: Moses pleaded with God, asking why his anger was burning against the people he had rescued with such power. Moses stood up for the people instead of accepting the offer to replace them.
entries.exodus 32:12: Moses worried that the Egyptians would say God brought his people out only to kill them in the mountains. He asked God to turn from his anger and not bring disaster.
entries.exodus 32:13: Moses reminded God of his promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel to make their descendants as numerous as the stars and give them the land forever. He appealed to God's own faithfulness.
entries.exodus 32:14: So the Lord changed his mind and did not carry out the punishment he had threatened. God listened to Moses's prayer and showed mercy.
entries.exodus 32:15: Moses came down the mountain carrying the two stone tablets of the law, written on both sides. He was bringing God's commands to a people who had already broken them.
entries.exodus 32:16: The tablets were made by God himself, and the writing on them was God's own writing carved into the stone. These were not human documents but directly from God.
entries.exodus 32:17: Joshua heard the loud noise from the camp and thought it sounded like a battle. He misread what was happening because he only heard the sound.
entries.exodus 32:18: Moses told Joshua it wasn't the sound of victory or defeat in war, but the sound of singing. The noise was from their wild party, not a battle.
entries.exodus 32:19: When Moses got close enough to see the calf statue and the people dancing, he was furious and smashed the stone tablets at the foot of the mountain. His anger showed how seriously the people had broken God's law.
entries.exodus 32:20: Moses burned the calf, crushed it to powder, scattered it in water, and made the Israelites drink it. He destroyed the idol completely and made them face what they had done.
entries.exodus 32:21: Moses asked Aaron what the people had done to him that led him to bring such a great sin on them. He held Aaron responsible for letting this happen.
entries.exodus 32:22: Aaron asked Moses not to be angry and said the people were prone to evil. He tried to excuse himself by blaming the people's bad tendencies.
entries.exodus 32:23: Aaron recounted that the people had asked him to make them a god because they didn't know what had happened to Moses. He described the request but avoided taking responsibility.
entries.exodus 32:24: Aaron claimed he simply told them to hand over their gold, threw it into the fire, and out came this calf. He made it sound like it happened by accident, dodging his own role.
entries.exodus 32:25: Moses saw that the people were out of control and that Aaron had let them run wild, making them a disgrace before their enemies. Bad leadership had left the people shameful and chaotic.
entries.exodus 32:26: Moses stood at the entrance to the camp and called for anyone on the Lord's side to come to him, and the Levites gathered to him. He gave people a clear choice about where they stood.
entries.exodus 32:27: Moses told the Levites that God commanded each man to take his sword and go through the camp, killing even close relatives. This was a severe judgment on the people's rebellion.
entries.exodus 32:28: The Levites did what Moses said, and about three thousand people died that day. The consequences of the idolatry were deadly and serious.
entries.exodus 32:29: Moses told the Levites they had set themselves apart for the Lord that day, even at the cost of their own sons and brothers, and that blessing was on them. Their loyalty to God had come before family ties.
entries.exodus 32:30: The next day Moses told the people their sin was great, and he would go up to the Lord to see if he could get forgiveness for them. Moses acted as a mediator, seeking mercy for a guilty people.
entries.exodus 32:31: Moses went back to the Lord and admitted that the people had committed a great sin by making a gold god. He was honest about the seriousness of what they had done.
entries.exodus 32:32: Moses asked God to forgive them, and if not, to remove his own name from God's book. He was willing to give up his own place rather than see the people rejected.
