entries.exodus 32:33: The Lord told Moses that whoever had sinned against him would be removed from his book. Each person is accountable to God for their own wrongdoing.
entries.exodus 32:34: God told Moses to lead the people on to the place he had promised, with his angel going ahead, but he would still punish them for their sin at the right time. Forgiveness did not erase all consequences.
entries.exodus 32:35: The Lord struck the people with punishment because they had worshiped the calf Aaron made. Their idolatry brought real consequences on the community.
entries.exodus 36:1: God gave certain skilled workers the ability and know-how to build the sacred tent, and they were expected to use those gifts to do the work. It means your God-given skills are meant to be put to use for him.
entries.exodus 36:2: Moses called together the skilled workers God had gifted and everyone whose heart moved them to help. It shows that God's work is done by people who willingly offer what they have.
entries.exodus 36:3: The workers received the people's gifts for building the holy place, and the people kept bringing more every morning. It means generous giving kept the work supplied day after day.
entries.exodus 36:4: The skilled workers paused their building to come together. It means they stopped to deal with something important as a group.
entries.exodus 36:5: The workers told Moses the people had given far more than the job required. It means the people's generosity had completely covered the need.
entries.exodus 36:6: Moses ordered everyone to stop bringing offerings because there was enough. It means wise leadership knows when to say 'that's enough' and stop asking.
entries.exodus 36:7: They already had more materials than needed to finish all the work. It means the supply was abundant, not just barely sufficient.
entries.exodus 36:8: The skilled craftsmen built the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine linen in blue, purple, and red, decorated with angel figures. It means the place of worship was made with care and beauty.
entries.exodus 36:9: Each curtain was the same size, twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide. It means the design was precise and uniform, not random.
entries.exodus 36:10: They sewed five curtains into one set and the other five into another set. It means the many pieces were organized into two larger sections.
entries.exodus 36:11: They attached blue loops along the outer edge of each set of curtains. It means they prepared the edges so the two sets could be joined.
entries.exodus 36:12: Each edge had fifty loops positioned to line up with the loops on the other set. It means the two halves were designed to match perfectly.
entries.exodus 36:13: They made fifty gold clasps to connect the two sets, so the tabernacle became one whole. It means the separate parts were joined into a single unified structure.
entries.exodus 36:14: They made eleven curtains of goat hair to serve as the tent covering over the tabernacle. It means a sturdy outer layer was added to protect the inner structure.
entries.exodus 36:15: Each of these curtains was thirty cubits long and four cubits wide, all identical. It means the covering was made to consistent measurements.
entries.exodus 36:16: They joined five curtains into one group and six into another. It means the covering was assembled in two sections, like the inner curtains.
entries.exodus 36:17: They put fifty loops on the outer edge of each group of curtains. It means the edges were prepared so the sections could be fastened together.
entries.exodus 36:18: They made fifty bronze clasps to join the sections and form the tent. It means the covering was held together as one piece.
entries.exodus 36:19: They made a covering of red-dyed sheepskin and another of leather to go over the tent. It means the tabernacle had outer layers for protection from weather.
entries.exodus 36:20: They made upright frames of hard wood for the walls of the tabernacle. It means the structure had a solid framework to stand on.
entries.exodus 36:21: Each frame was ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide. It means the frames were made to exact, matching dimensions.
entries.exodus 36:22: Each frame had two pegs set into it, and all the frames were made the same way. It means the parts were standardized so they would fit together.
entries.exodus 36:23: They made twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle. It means the south wall was built from a set number of identical frames.
entries.exodus 36:24: They made forty silver bases for the twenty frames, two under each frame to hold its pegs. It means each frame was firmly anchored.
entries.exodus 36:25: They made twenty frames for the north side of the tabernacle. It means the north wall matched the south wall in construction.
entries.exodus 36:26: They made forty silver bases for these frames, two under each one. It means the north side was anchored the same way as the south.
entries.exodus 36:27: They made six frames for the west side, the back of the tabernacle. It means the rear wall was built with fewer frames than the sides.
entries.exodus 36:28: They made two extra frames for the corners at the back. It means the corners were given special attention so the structure held together.
entries.exodus 36:29: These corner frames were joined at the bottom and top with a single ring, forming both corners. It means the corners were reinforced to keep the walls solid.
entries.exodus 36:30: So there were eight frames at the back with sixteen silver bases, two under each frame. It means the rear wall was fully supported.
entries.exodus 36:31: They made five wooden rods for the frames on one side of the tabernacle. It means crossbars were added to hold the wall frames steady.
entries.exodus 36:32: They made five rods for the other side and five for the back wall on the west. It means every wall had its own set of supporting rods.
entries.exodus 36:33: The middle rod ran all the way through the rings from one end to the other. It means one long rod tied the whole structure together.
entries.exodus 36:34: They covered the frames with gold, made gold rings for the rods, and covered the rods with gold. It means the structure was made beautiful and precious for God's house.
entries.exodus 36:35: They made the inner curtain of fine linen in blue, purple, and red, with angel figures designed by skilled craftsmen. It means a beautiful barrier marked off the most holy area.
entries.exodus 36:36: They made four wooden pillars covered with gold, with gold hooks and four silver bases, to hold up the inner curtain. It means the curtain was hung on a sturdy, decorated frame.
entries.exodus 36:37: They made a curtain for the entrance of the tent, of fine linen embroidered in blue, purple, and red. It means the doorway was also made with care and beauty.
entries.exodus 36:38: They made five pillars with hooks, gold tops and gold bands, and five bronze bases for the entrance curtain. It means the entrance was supported by a strong, decorated frame.
entries.exodus 37:1: Bezalel built a wooden chest for the sacred tent, sized about a metre and a quarter long and three-quarters of a metre wide and high. It was the most important piece of furniture in Israel's worship, and God gave exact instructions for it.
entries.exodus 37:2: He covered the chest with pure gold inside and out and ran a gold rim around its top edge. The inside mattered as much as the outside, a picture of being clean through and through.
entries.exodus 37:3: He cast four gold rings and attached them to the chest's four corners, two on each side. These were the fittings that would let the chest be carried safely.
entries.exodus 37:4: He made carrying poles from acacia wood and covered them with gold. Ordinary wood made precious by its covering, ready for a holy job.
entries.exodus 37:5: He slid the poles through the rings on the sides of the chest so it could be lifted and carried. The sacred chest was never to be dragged or touched directly, but carried with care.
entries.exodus 37:6: He made a solid gold lid for the chest, exactly the same length and width as the chest itself. This lid was where God would meet with his people.
entries.exodus 37:7: He hammered out two golden winged figures from a single piece of gold and set them at the two ends of the lid. They were shaped by beating, not casting, showing skilled craftsmanship.
entries.exodus 37:8: One winged figure stood at each end of the lid, made as one piece with it. The whole cover was a single unified work of gold.
entries.exodus 37:9: The figures' wings spread upward over the lid, and they faced each other with their faces toward the cover. They stood guard over the place where God's presence would rest.
entries.exodus 37:10: He built a wooden table about a metre long, half a metre wide and three-quarters of a metre high. This table held the special bread set before God each week.
entries.exodus 37:11: He covered the table with pure gold and put a gold rim all around its edge. Even a simple table for bread was made fit for a king's house.
entries.exodus 37:12: He added a hand-width border around the table and edged that border with gold. The careful detail shows how seriously God's instructions were taken.
entries.exodus 37:13: He made four gold rings and fastened them at the four corners where the table's legs were. These rings were for the carrying poles.
entries.exodus 37:14: The rings sat just under the border on the sides, so the poles could slide through and the table could be carried. Everything was designed to be moved without being damaged.
entries.exodus 37:15: He made the carrying poles from acacia wood and covered them with gold. Like the chest, the table was carried, not dragged.
entries.exodus 37:16: He made all the table's dishes, pans, bowls and jugs from pure gold. The utensils for God's house were the finest available.
entries.exodus 37:17: He made the lampstand entirely of pure gold, hammered into shape, with its base, central stem, cups, buds and flowers all one piece. It was a single work of art for giving light in God's house.
entries.exodus 37:18: Six branches extended from the lampstand's sides, three on each side. The light would spread out evenly in several directions.
entries.exodus 37:19: Each branch had three cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with a bud and a flower. The lampstand was decorated like a flowering tree, a picture of life and light.
entries.exodus 37:20: The central stem had four almond-blossom cups, each with its bud and flower. The detail was repeated carefully to match God's design.
entries.exodus 37:21: Under each pair of branches there was a bud joined to the stem, for all six branches. The whole lampstand was one connected piece, not parts stuck together.
entries.exodus 37:22: The buds and branches were all one piece of pure hammered gold. Nothing was added or bolted on; the whole thing was made as a single work.
entries.exodus 37:23: He made seven lamps for the lampstand, plus the small tools for trimming and tending them, all of gold. Even the little tools for keeping the light burning were made precious.
entries.exodus 37:24: A whole talent of pure gold, roughly thirty kilograms, went into the lampstand and its tools. It was an expensive piece of furniture, showing how much honour was given to God.
entries.exodus 37:25: He made the incense altar from acacia wood, square, about half a metre long and wide and a metre high, with horns at its corners. This was where sweet-smelling incense was burned before God.
entries.exodus 37:26: He covered the top, sides and horns with pure gold and put a gold rim around it. Every surface of the altar was made beautiful for its holy use.
entries.exodus 37:27: He made two gold rings and fixed them on opposite sides just under the rim, to hold the carrying poles. The altar too was built to be carried safely.
entries.exodus 37:28: He made the poles from acacia wood and covered them with gold. The same careful pattern was followed for every piece of furniture.
entries.exodus 37:29: He made the sacred anointing oil and the pure sweet-smelling incense, blended by a skilled perfumer. These were set apart for dedicating things to God and for worship that pleased him.
entries.exodus 39:1: Skilled workers made special colored robes for the priests to wear while serving God in the holy place. This shows that God cares about the details of how we approach him in worship.
entries.exodus 39:2: The ephod was a special priestly garment made from gold thread and fine colored fabrics. It was made carefully because it was set apart for serving God.
entries.exodus 39:3: They hammered gold into thin wire and wove it into the colored cloth. This took great skill and patience, showing that giving God our best work matters.
entries.exodus 39:4: They made shoulder straps to connect the front and back of the garment. These practical details kept the sacred clothing held together properly.
entries.exodus 39:5: The decorative waistband was made from the same fine materials and matched the rest of the garment. Everything was done exactly as God had instructed Moses.
entries.exodus 39:6: They set engraved gemstones into gold settings, with the names of Israel's tribes carved on them. Each tribe was represented before God.
entries.exodus 39:7: These stones were attached to the shoulder pieces as a reminder of the people of Israel before God. The priest carried the whole nation with him when he served.
entries.exodus 39:8: The chestpiece was made with the same fine materials and design as the ephod. It was a beautiful and unified part of the priest's outfit.
entries.exodus 39:9: The chestpiece was folded double into a square about the size of a hand span. Its simple shape held deep meaning for the priest's role.
entries.exodus 39:10: Four rows of precious stones were mounted on the chestpiece, starting with carnelian, chrysolite, and emerald. These costly stones showed how precious God's people are to him.
entries.exodus 39:11: The second row held a ruby, a sapphire, and an onyx. Each stone was carefully chosen and set in place.
entries.exodus 39:12: The third row contained a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst. The variety of stones reflected the variety among God's people.
entries.exodus 39:13: The fourth row had a topaz, a beryl, and a jasper, all set in gold. Every stone was secured with care and craftsmanship.
entries.exodus 39:14: There were twelve stones, one for each tribe, each engraved with a tribe's name. The priest represented all twelve tribes equally before God.
entries.exodus 39:15: They made twisted gold chains for the chestpiece. These chains connected the sacred pieces together securely.
entries.exodus 39:16: They made gold settings and rings and attached the rings to the ends of the chestpiece. These fittings kept the chestpiece in its proper place.
entries.exodus 39:17: The twisted chains were fastened to the rings at the ends of the chestpiece. This connected the chestpiece to the rest of the priest's garment.
entries.exodus 39:18: The other ends of the chains were attached to the front of the ephod at the shoulder pieces. This held the chestpiece firmly against the priest's chest.
entries.exodus 39:19: They made two more gold rings and placed them on the lower inner edge of the chestpiece. These rings faced the ephod to keep everything aligned.
entries.exodus 39:20: Two more gold rings were placed on the front of the ephod near the shoulder join and above the waistband. These matched the rings on the chestpiece.
entries.exodus 39:21: A blue cord tied the rings together so the chestpiece would stay in place and not come loose. This was done exactly as God had commanded Moses.
entries.exodus 39:22: The robe worn under the ephod was made entirely of blue cloth. Blue was a color associated with what is holy and set apart.
entries.exodus 39:23: The robe had a reinforced opening at the top for the head, like a soldier's collar. This practical detail kept the garment from tearing.
entries.exodus 39:24: Pomegranate-shaped decorations in blue, purple, and red were woven around the hem of the robe. These added beauty and meaning to the priest's clothing.
entries.exodus 39:25: Gold bells were placed between the pomegranates all around the hem. The bells would sound as the priest moved, marking his service before God.
entries.exodus 39:26: Bells and pomegranates alternated around the hem of the robe. This pattern was made just as God had instructed Moses.
entries.exodus 39:27: They made tunics of fine linen for Aaron and his sons. The priests wore clean, well-made clothing for their service.
entries.exodus 39:28: They made the turban, head coverings, and linen undergarments with care. Every piece of the priest's clothing was made to honor God.
entries.exodus 39:29: The sash was made of fine linen with colorful embroidery. It was made exactly as God had commanded Moses.
entries.exodus 39:30: They made a gold plate for the turban and engraved on it the words 'Holy to the LORD.' This declared that the priest belonged entirely to God.
entries.exodus 39:31: The gold plate was tied to the turban with a blue cord. This was done just as God had instructed Moses.
entries.exodus 39:32: All the work on the tent of meeting was finished, and the people had done everything exactly as God commanded. Obedience to God's instructions was complete.
entries.exodus 39:33: They brought the completed tent and all its parts to Moses. Everything was assembled and presented for inspection.
entries.exodus 39:34: They brought the outer coverings of dyed sheepskin and leather, along with the curtain for the entrance. These protected and enclosed the holy place.
entries.exodus 39:35: They brought the ark of the law with its carrying poles and its cover. The ark was the most sacred object, holding God's covenant.
entries.exodus 39:36: They brought the table with all its utensils and the special bread set before God. These items were used in worship and offering.
entries.exodus 39:37: They brought the lampstand with its lamps and utensils and the oil for lighting it. This provided light for the holy place.
entries.exodus 39:38: They brought the gold altar, the holy oil, the sweet-smelling incense, and the curtain for the tent entrance. These were all used in worship and sacrifice.
entries.exodus 39:39: They brought the bronze altar with its grating, poles, and utensils, plus the washing basin and its stand. These were used for sacrifices and cleansing.
entries.exodus 39:40: They brought the courtyard curtains, pillars, bases, entrance curtain, cords, pegs, and all the equipment needed for the tent of meeting. Every item for worship was ready.
entries.leviticus 1:1: God spoke to Moses from the tent where the people met with him. This shows that what follows comes directly from God, not from Moses' own ideas.
entries.leviticus 1:2: God told Moses to give the Israelites rules for giving offerings to him, and those offerings were to come from their own animals. It means giving to God was to come from what people already had.
entries.leviticus 1:3: If someone gave a bull as a whole burnt offering, it had to be a healthy male with nothing wrong with it, brought to the tent entrance. The point was to give God your best, not a flawed leftover.
entries.leviticus 1:4: The person placed his hands on the animal's head, and the offering was accepted on his behalf to deal with his sin. It showed that guilt was being transferred and forgiveness was being asked for.
entries.leviticus 1:5: The animal was killed in front of the Lord, and the priests splashed its blood on and around the altar at the tent entrance. Blood was central because it stood for life given up on the person's behalf.
entries.leviticus 1:6: The animal was skinned and cut into pieces. This was careful, orderly preparation, showing that the offering was handled with seriousness.
entries.leviticus 1:7: The priests were to build the fire on the altar and arrange the wood. The priests had a specific job to do in making the offering happen.
entries.leviticus 1:8: The priests laid the pieces, the head, and the fat in order on the burning wood. Everything was arranged deliberately, not thrown together.
entries.leviticus 1:9: The inner organs and legs were washed with water, and then the whole animal was burned on the altar as a pleasing smell to the Lord. Clean preparation mattered, and the whole offering was given over to God.
entries.leviticus 1:10: If the offering was a sheep or goat, it also had to be a healthy male with nothing wrong with it. The same standard of giving God your best applied to smaller animals too.
entries.leviticus 1:11: The animal was killed on the north side of the altar, and the priests put some of its blood on and around the altar. The location and the blood were both part of how the offering was made properly.
entries.leviticus 1:12: The animal was cut into pieces, and the priest arranged the parts, head, and fat on the burning wood. The offering was laid out carefully before being burned.
entries.leviticus 1:13: The inner organs and legs were washed, and then the priest burned the whole animal on the altar as a pleasing smell to the Lord. Cleanliness and completeness were both required.
entries.leviticus 1:14: If someone's burnt offering was a bird, they were to bring doves or young pigeons. This made it possible for poorer people to give an offering too.
entries.leviticus 1:15: The priest brought the bird to the altar, killed it, burned it, and drained its blood against the side of the altar. Even the smallest offering was handled with the same care and blood ritual.
entries.leviticus 1:16: The priest removed the bird's stomach and feathers and put them beside the altar where the ashes were dumped. The parts not burned were disposed of in the proper place.
entries.leviticus 1:17: The bird was opened at the wings but not torn in two, then burned on the altar as a pleasing smell to the Lord. The offering was still whole in a sense, and it was fully given to God.
entries.exodus 38:1: This describes a large square altar for burnt offerings, made of wood and about seven and a half feet wide and four and a half feet tall. It shows the people built the place of sacrifice exactly as God directed.
entries.exodus 38:2: Horns, or raised corners, were added to the altar and the whole thing was covered in bronze. The horns were a sign of strength and protection connected with the altar.
entries.exodus 38:3: All the tools used at the altar—baskets, shovels, bowls, hooks, and fire pans—were made of bronze. Everything needed for the altar's work was prepared and ready.
entries.exodus 38:4: A bronze grating was placed under the altar's ledge, reaching halfway up. This let air and ashes pass through while the fire burned on top.
entries.exodus 38:5: Four rings were made for the corners of the grating so carrying poles could be attached. This made the altar ready to be moved when the people traveled.
entries.exodus 38:6: The carrying poles were made of wood and covered with bronze. They were strong and matched the rest of the altar.
entries.exodus 38:7: The poles went through the rings on both sides so the altar could be lifted and carried, and the altar itself was hollow inside. It was built to be portable for the journey.
entries.exodus 38:8: A bronze basin and stand were made for washing, using bronze mirrors donated by women who served at the entrance of the meeting tent. Their personal items became part of the place of worship.
entries.exodus 38:9: The courtyard around the tent was enclosed with fine linen curtains a hundred cubits long on the south side. It created a set-apart space for worship.
entries.exodus 38:10: The curtains hung on twenty bronze posts set in bronze bases, with silver hooks and connecting bands. Each part had its proper material and place.
entries.exodus 38:11: The north side matched the south, with the same length of curtains on twenty bronze posts and bases, with silver hooks and bands. The courtyard was built evenly and carefully.
entries.exodus 38:12: The west side had shorter curtains, fifty cubits long, on ten posts and ten bases with silver bands. The enclosure was completed on every side.
entries.exodus 38:13: The east side, where the entrance was, measured fifty cubits across. The opening faced the sunrise.
entries.exodus 38:14: On one side of the entrance were curtains fifteen cubits long on three posts and three bases. This formed one half of the gateway area.
entries.exodus 38:15: The other side of the entrance matched the first, with fifteen cubits of curtains on three posts and bases. The entrance was balanced on both sides.
entries.exodus 38:16: All the curtains around the courtyard were made of the finest linen. The whole enclosure was made with quality material.
entries.exodus 38:17: The posts stood on bronze bases, and their tops, hooks, and bands were silver, with silver rings around every post. The courtyard was both sturdy and finely finished.
entries.exodus 38:18: The curtain at the courtyard entrance was fine linen embroidered in blue, purple, and red, twenty cubits long and five cubits high, matching the side curtains. The entrance was beautiful and set apart.
entries.exodus 38:19: The entrance curtain hung on four posts with bronze bases, and the posts had silver hooks, tops, and bands. Every detail was made as instructed.
entries.exodus 38:20: All the tent pegs for the tabernacle and the courtyard were made of bronze. Even the smallest parts were provided for.
entries.exodus 38:21: This is the record of the materials used for the tabernacle, the place of witness, counted at Moses' command by the Levites under Ithamar's direction. The work was carefully tracked and accountable.
entries.exodus 38:22: Bezalel from the tribe of Judah made everything just as the Lord had commanded Moses. He faithfully carried out God's instructions.
entries.exodus 38:23: Working with him was Oholiab from the tribe of Dan, a skilled craftsman and designer in embroidery of blue, purple, red, and fine linen. God gave the work skilled hands to complete it.
entries.exodus 38:24: The gold given for the holy place weighed twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels. The people gave generously toward God's house.
entries.exodus 38:25: The silver collected from the counted people weighed one hundred talents and one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels. Each person's contribution added up to a large offering.
entries.exodus 38:26: Every man twenty years old and older gave a half-shekel, and there were six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty of them. Everyone shared equally in giving.
entries.exodus 38:27: One hundred talents of the silver were used for the bases of the sanctuary pillars and the veil, one talent per base. The silver became the foundation of the holy place.
entries.exodus 38:28: The remaining silver was used for hooks, tops, and bands for the pillars. Nothing given was wasted.
entries.exodus 38:29: The bronze given weighed seventy talents and two thousand four hundred shekels. It was a large offering of metal for the work.
entries.exodus 38:30: From the bronze they made the bases for the meeting tent doorway, the bronze altar and its grating, and all the altar's tools. The bronze served the most active parts of worship.
entries.exodus 38:31: Bronze was also used for the courtyard bases and its entrance, and for all the pegs of the tabernacle and courtyard. The whole structure was held together with what the people gave.
entries.exodus 39:41: These were the special clothes made for worship in the sacred tent, including the outfits the priests wore while serving. It reminds the reader that approaching God was treated with care and respect.
entries.exodus 39:42: The people carried out every instruction the Lord had given through Moses, down to the details. It shows that faithful obedience means doing what God asks, not just the parts we like.
entries.exodus 39:43: Moses inspected all the work and saw it matched exactly what the Lord had commanded, so he blessed the people. It means God notices careful, complete obedience and responds with blessing.
entries.exodus 40:1: God speaks directly to Moses here, giving him the next set of instructions. It reminds the reader that God guides his people step by step rather than leaving them to guess.
entries.exodus 40:2: God tells Moses to set up the sacred tent on the first day of the new year. This marks a fresh start, showing that worship of God stands at the beginning of Israel's new year.
entries.exodus 40:3: Inside the tent, the chest holding God's law was to be placed and screened off by a curtain. This taught that God's word is central and that access to his presence is carefully ordered.
entries.exodus 40:4: The table for the sacred bread and the lampstand were to be set up with everything arranged properly, and the lamps kept burning. It shows that worship involves careful order and ongoing devotion, not just occasional effort.
entries.exodus 40:5: The gold altar for burning incense was placed just outside the inner curtain, and a curtain hung at the tent's entrance. This arranged the space so that prayer and approach to God had their proper place.
entries.exodus 40:6: The large altar for animal sacrifices stood at the entrance of the tent. It reminded the people that coming near to God required sacrifice from the very doorway.
entries.exodus 40:7: A basin filled with water was placed between the tent and the altar. It was there for washing, teaching that those who approach God must be cleansed.
entries.exodus 40:8: Moses was to set up the courtyard curtains all around and hang a curtain at its entrance. This made a clear boundary around the holy space, marking it off from ordinary life.
entries.exodus 40:9: Moses was to anoint the tent and everything in it with holy oil, setting it apart for God. It shows that things used in worship are dedicated specially to him.
entries.exodus 40:10: The altar of sacrifice and its equipment were also to be anointed and made most holy. This underlined that the place of sacrifice was especially set apart for God's purposes.
entries.exodus 40:11: The washing basin and its stand were anointed too, making them holy. Even the simple tools of cleansing were dedicated to God's service.
entries.exodus 40:12: Aaron and his sons were to come to the tent entrance and be washed with water. This showed that those who serve God must first be cleansed before they begin.
entries.exodus 40:13: Aaron was to be dressed in the holy robes and anointed so he could serve as priest. It shows that the role of priest was a gift and calling from God, not something taken on oneself.
entries.exodus 40:14: Aaron's sons were also brought forward and dressed in their coats. The whole family was included in the service, showing that God's calling extends to a household.
entries.exodus 40:15: The sons were anointed just as their father was, making their priesthood permanent for future generations. It shows that God intended a lasting line of priests to serve his people.
entries.exodus 40:16: Moses did everything exactly as the Lord commanded him. This sets an example of full obedience to God's instructions, down to the details.
entries.exodus 40:17: The tent was actually set up on the first day of the first month in the second year. This gives a real date, showing that God's instructions were carried out in history, not just in theory.
entries.exodus 40:18: Moses set up the structure piece by piece, laying the bases and standing up the frames and posts. It shows that building a place for God took patient, careful work.
entries.exodus 40:19: He spread the outer coverings over the tent just as God had ordered. Obedience in the small, practical details mattered.
entries.exodus 40:20: Moses placed the law inside the chest, added the carrying poles, and put the cover on top. The law at the heart of the chest shows that God's word was the center of Israel's worship.
entries.exodus 40:21: He brought the chest into the tent and hung the curtain in front of it, exactly as commanded. This kept the most holy place set apart and honored God's instructions.
entries.exodus 40:22: The table was placed in the tent on the north side, outside the inner curtain. Each item had its assigned place, showing order in worship.
entries.exodus 40:23: Moses arranged the bread on the table before the Lord as God had said. This was a regular act of devotion, acknowledging God's presence and provision.
entries.exodus 40:24: The lampstand was set opposite the table on the south side of the tent. The layout kept the space balanced and orderly for worship.
entries.exodus 40:25: Moses lit the lamps before the Lord, just as he had been commanded. Light in the holy place symbolized God's presence and guidance.
entries.exodus 40:26: The gold altar was placed inside the tent, in front of the inner curtain. This positioned prayer and incense close to the place of God's presence.
entries.exodus 40:27: Moses burned sweet-smelling incense on it, as the Lord had ordered. The pleasant smoke pictured prayers rising to God.
entries.exodus 40:28: He hung the curtain at the doorway of the tent. This completed the entrance, keeping the holy space properly enclosed.
entries.exodus 40:29: Moses set the altar of sacrifice at the tent entrance and offered the burnt and grain offerings on it, as commanded. Sacrifice stood at the doorway, showing that approach to God begins with offering.
entries.exodus 40:30: The water basin was placed between the altar and the tent for washing. It stood ready for the cleansing that worship required.
entries.exodus 40:31: Moses, Aaron, and Aaron's sons washed their hands and feet in it. Even the leader and the priests needed cleansing before serving God.
entries.exodus 40:32: They washed whenever they entered the tent or came near the altar, just as God had ordered Moses. This made cleansing a regular habit, not a one-time event.
entries.exodus 40:33: Moses finished the courtyard curtains and the entrance curtain, completing the whole work. The account ends with the project fully done, showing faithful follow-through.
entries.exodus 40:34: The cloud covered the tent and the Lord's glory filled the house. This was God's visible sign that he had come to dwell among his people and accepted their work.
entries.exodus 40:35: Moses could not enter the tent because the cloud rested on it and God's glory filled it. God's presence was so overwhelming that even Moses had to stay outside.
entries.exodus 40:36: Whenever the cloud lifted from the tent, the Israelites set out on their journey. God himself directed their travel, so they moved only when he led.
entries.exodus 40:37: While the cloud stayed put, the people stayed put and did not move until it lifted. This taught them patience and dependence on God's timing.
entries.exodus 40:38: The Lord's cloud rested on the tent by day and fire was in it by night, visible to all Israel throughout their journeys. God's presence stayed with his people constantly, guiding and reassuring them day and night.
entries.leviticus 2:1: This describes a gift of fine flour mixed with oil and incense, brought to God as a grain offering. It means God deserves our best, not our leftovers.
entries.leviticus 2:2: The priest burns a handful of the flour, oil, and incense as a reminder that the whole gift belongs to God. It shows that even a small, faithful act of worship is pleasing to him.
entries.leviticus 2:3: The leftover grain belongs to the priests as their food, and it is treated as very holy. It means those who serve God are to be cared for from what is given to him.
entries.leviticus 2:4: If the grain gift is baked in an oven, it must be made without yeast and mixed with oil. It teaches that worship should be done the way God asks, not however we prefer.
entries.leviticus 2:5: A grain gift cooked on a griddle must also be made of the best flour, without yeast, and mixed with oil. It means God's instructions apply to every form our giving takes.
entries.leviticus 2:6: The cooked grain is broken into pieces and oil is poured on it before it is offered. It shows that careful preparation is part of honoring God.
entries.leviticus 2:7: A grain gift cooked in a pan must be made of the best flour mixed with oil. It means the same standard of quality applies no matter how the gift is prepared.
entries.leviticus 2:8: The person brings the prepared grain gift to the Lord, and the priest carries it to the altar. It means our gifts reach God through the priest who represents him.
entries.leviticus 2:9: The priest burns a portion as a reminder, and it is described as a pleasing smell to the Lord. It means God accepts the offering given with the right heart.
entries.leviticus 2:10: The rest of the grain gift goes to the priests and is considered very holy. It means God provides for his servants through the offerings brought to him.
entries.leviticus 2:11: No grain gift offered to God may contain yeast, and yeast or honey must never be burned on the altar. It teaches that some things, though ordinary, are not fitting in worship offered to God.
entries.leviticus 2:12: Yeast and honey may be brought as first-fruit gifts, but they must not be burned on the altar. It means not everything acceptable as a gift is acceptable as an offering by fire.
entries.leviticus 2:13: Every grain gift must be seasoned with salt, which stands for God's lasting agreement with his people. It means our worship should reflect his faithfulness and be pure and lasting.
entries.leviticus 2:14: A first-fruit grain gift is made from new grain that has been dried or roasted over fire and crushed. It means the first and best of what God gives us should be offered back to him.
entries.leviticus 2:15: Oil and incense are added to this first-fruit grain gift. It means even the simplest offering is to be given with care and devotion.
entries.leviticus 2:16: The priest burns part of the grain, part of the oil, and all the incense as a reminder offering to the Lord. It means God is honored when his portion is given fully and faithfully.
entries.leviticus 3:1: This describes a peace offering from a herd animal, which had to be healthy and without defects. For the reader, it shows that gifts brought to God were to be the best, not leftovers.
entries.leviticus 3:2: The person placed a hand on the animal's head and killed it at the entrance of the meeting tent, and the priests applied its blood to the altar. This showed the offerer identifying with the sacrifice and that life belongs to God.
entries.leviticus 3:3: Part of the peace offering was burned on the altar as a gift to God, specifically the fat around the inner organs. It teaches that the offering was shared with God in a special way.
entries.leviticus 3:4: The kidneys and the fat around them and near the liver were removed for burning. These were considered the richest parts, reserved for God.
entries.leviticus 3:5: The priests burned these parts on the altar on top of the regular burnt offering, and the smell was pleasing to God. It shows worship was offered in the way God asked, not however people preferred.
entries.leviticus 3:6: A peace offering could also come from the flock, again male or female but with no defect. The point is that God accepted either sex but required the animal to be sound.
entries.leviticus 3:7: If the offering was a lamb, it was first presented before the Lord. This act of bringing it into God's presence marked it as set apart for him.
entries.leviticus 3:8: The offerer laid a hand on the lamb's head and killed it before the meeting tent, and the priests put its blood around the altar. The blood was handled carefully because it represented life.
entries.leviticus 3:9: From the peace offering, the fat tail and the fat around the inner organs were given to God as a burned offering. The best portions were set aside for him.
entries.leviticus 3:10: The kidneys and their surrounding fat, along with the fat near the liver, were removed. These specific parts were reserved for burning on the altar.
entries.leviticus 3:11: The priest burned this on the altar as food for the offering made by fire to the Lord. The language pictures the altar as God's table receiving the offering.
entries.leviticus 3:12: If the peace offering was a goat, it too was brought before the Lord. Every kind of acceptable offering had to be presented to God first.
entries.leviticus 3:13: The offerer laid a hand on the goat's head and killed it before the meeting tent, and the priests applied its blood around the altar. The same careful procedure applied to every animal.
entries.leviticus 3:14: The offerer brought the fat covering and around the inner organs as a gift burned to the Lord. The richest inner parts were given to God.
entries.leviticus 3:15: The kidneys with their fat and the fat near the liver were removed for the offering. These parts were consistently set apart for God.
entries.leviticus 3:16: The priest burned them on the altar as food for the fire offering, a pleasing smell, and all the fat belonged to the Lord. This teaches that God claims the richest portions for himself.
entries.leviticus 3:17: This was a permanent rule for all generations and homes: the people must not eat fat or blood. For the reader, it shows that God sets boundaries and that blood, which stands for life, is treated as sacred.
entries.leviticus 5:1: If you know the truth about something and are asked under oath to speak, staying silent is itself wrong. The reader learns that failing to speak up when called to testify makes you accountable for the truth.
entries.leviticus 5:2: Touching something unclean, even by accident without realizing it, still leaves a person ritually unclean. The reader sees that carelessness in daily life can make a person guilty before God, even when it was not intended.
entries.leviticus 5:3: The same applies to accidentally touching something unclean connected with a person; once you realize it, you are guilty. The reader learns that guilt begins when you become aware of what happened, and then you must deal with it.
entries.leviticus 5:4: If someone rashly swears an oath to do something good or bad without thinking it through, they are guilty once they realize it. The reader is warned that careless words spoken as promises matter and carry responsibility.
entries.leviticus 5:5: Anyone who becomes guilty in these ways must openly admit the wrong they have done. The reader learns that confession, saying the wrong out loud, is the first step toward making things right.
entries.leviticus 5:6: The guilty person brings a female lamb or goat as a sin offering, and the priest makes atonement for them. The reader sees that wrongdoing requires a real cost and that God provided a way for forgiveness.
entries.leviticus 5:7: If someone is too poor for a lamb, they may bring two doves or two young pigeons instead, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering. The reader learns that God's requirement for forgiveness does not depend on wealth.
entries.leviticus 5:8: The priest offers the sin offering first, wringing its neck without severing it completely. The reader sees that the ritual was carried out in a specific, careful way as God commanded.
entries.leviticus 5:9: The priest sprinkles some of the blood on the side of the altar and pours the rest at its base. The reader learns that blood was central to the offering that dealt with sin.
entries.leviticus 5:10: The second bird is offered as a burnt offering according to the law, and the priest makes atonement so the person is forgiven. The reader sees that forgiveness comes through the offering God prescribed, not through the person's own effort.
entries.leviticus 5:11: If someone cannot afford even two birds, they may bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, with no oil or incense because it is a sin offering. The reader learns that even the poorest person had a way to bring their sin before God.
entries.leviticus 5:12: The person brings the flour to the priest, who takes a handful and burns it on the altar as a memorial portion to the Lord. The reader sees that the offering was presented to God in a set way, even when it was only flour.
entries.leviticus 5:13: The priest makes atonement and the person is forgiven, and the rest of the flour belongs to the priest like a grain offering. The reader learns that forgiveness was fully available even to those with the least to give.
entries.leviticus 5:14: This verse simply introduces that the Lord spoke these next instructions to Moses. The reader sees that what follows is presented as God's own command given through his leader.
entries.leviticus 5:15: If someone unintentionally sins regarding the holy things of the Lord, they must bring a flawless male sheep valued in silver by the sanctuary standard. The reader learns that even accidental offenses against what belongs to God require serious restitution.
entries.leviticus 5:16: The person must pay back what was wronged plus a fifth of its value, and the priest makes atonement with the ram so they are forgiven. The reader sees that making things right includes paying back more than was taken.
entries.leviticus 5:17: If someone breaks one of the Lord's commands without knowing it, they are still guilty and responsible. The reader learns that ignorance does not erase guilt before God.
entries.leviticus 5:18: They bring a flawless male sheep of the set value as a guilt offering, and the priest makes atonement for the unintentional sin so they are forgiven. The reader sees that God provided a way to deal with even unknown wrongdoing.
entries.leviticus 5:19: This is a guilt offering because the person is truly guilty before the Lord. The reader learns that guilt before God is real and must be acknowledged and dealt with, not ignored.
entries.leviticus 4:1: God is speaking directly to Moses, giving him instructions to pass on. This shows that what follows comes from God himself, not from Moses' own ideas.
entries.leviticus 4:2: This rule is for people who sin by accident or mistake, not on purpose, breaking one of God's commands. It means God made a way for honest mistakes to be dealt with, not just deliberate rebellion.
entries.leviticus 4:3: If the high priest sins, his failure affects the whole nation, so he must bring a perfect young bull as an offering. It shows that leaders carry extra responsibility because their wrong choices can lead others astray.
entries.leviticus 4:4: The priest brings the animal to the entrance of the meeting tent, lays his hands on it, and kills it there. Laying hands on the animal symbolically puts the guilt onto it, showing that sin costs a life.
entries.leviticus 4:5: The high priest carries some of the animal's blood into the meeting tent. Blood represented life, and it was central to making things right with God.
entries.leviticus 4:6: He dips his finger in the blood and sprinkles it seven times in front of the curtain of the holy place. Seven signals completeness, and the sprinkling shows the cleansing reaching into God's holy presence.
entries.leviticus 4:7: Some blood goes on the corners of the incense altar inside the tent, and the rest is poured out at the base of the outdoor altar. This shows that the sin affected both the holy place and the everyday place of worship.
entries.leviticus 4:8: The priest removes all the fat from the animal's inner parts. The fat was considered the richest, best part, set aside for God.
entries.leviticus 4:9: He also takes the kidneys and the fat around them and near the liver. These specific inner parts were given to God as part of the offering.
entries.leviticus 4:10: The fat is handled the same way as in the peace offering and burned on the altar. This connects the sin offering to the regular pattern of worship God had already set.
entries.leviticus 4:11: The skin, flesh, head, legs, inner parts, and waste of the bull are left over. These parts were not burned on the altar.
entries.leviticus 4:12: The whole remaining animal is carried outside the camp to a clean place and burned there. Sin was taken outside the community, showing it had to be removed, not just covered over.
entries.leviticus 4:13: This covers the case where the whole nation sins unknowingly and becomes guilty without realizing it. Guilt before God can exist even when people are unaware of what they did.
entries.leviticus 4:14: Once the sin becomes known, the community must bring a young bull as a sin offering to the meeting tent. When people learn of their wrong, they are expected to respond, not ignore it.
entries.leviticus 4:15: The elders of the community lay their hands on the bull's head and kill it before the Lord. The leaders act on behalf of all the people, identifying the whole nation with the offering.
entries.leviticus 4:16: The priest carries some of the bull's blood into the meeting tent. As with the high priest's offering, the blood is brought near to God's presence.
entries.leviticus 4:17: He sprinkles the blood seven times with his finger in front of the curtain. The same careful ritual is repeated, showing the seriousness of the nation's sin.
entries.leviticus 4:18: Some blood goes on the horns of the incense altar, and the rest is poured at the base of the outdoor altar. The blood is applied in the places where God meets his people.
entries.leviticus 4:19: All the fat is removed and burned on the altar. The best parts are given to God as part of the offering.
entries.leviticus 4:20: The priest does with this bull exactly what he did with the earlier sin offering, and the result is that the people are forgiven. God's forgiveness comes through the offering he himself prescribed.
entries.leviticus 4:21: The rest of the bull is taken outside the camp and burned, just like the first one, because it is the sin offering for the whole people. The sin is carried away from the community.
entries.leviticus 4:22: This case is for a leader who sins by mistake and becomes guilty. Leaders are held to the same standard of obedience to God's commands.
entries.leviticus 4:23: Once the leader realizes his sin, he must bring a perfect male goat as his offering. Awareness of sin is meant to lead to action, not just regret.
entries.leviticus 4:24: He lays his hand on the goat's head and kills it where the burnt offering is killed. The offering is made in the proper place and in the proper way God required.
entries.leviticus 4:25: The priest puts some of the blood on the corners of the outdoor altar and pours the rest at its base. The blood is applied to the altar where daily worship happened.
entries.leviticus 4:26: The fat is burned on the altar like the peace offering, and the priest makes atonement so the leader is forgiven. Forgiveness is the stated outcome of following God's instructions.
entries.leviticus 4:27: This covers an ordinary person who sins by mistake and becomes guilty. No one is too unimportant for God to address; everyday people are included in these rules.
entries.leviticus 4:28: When the person becomes aware of the sin, they bring a perfect female goat. The offering is smaller than a leader's, but the requirement to deal with sin is the same.
entries.leviticus 4:29: The person lays a hand on the goat's head and kills it where the burnt offering is killed. The sinner personally identifies with the offering.
entries.leviticus 4:30: The priest puts some blood on the altar's corners and pours the rest at its base. The blood is handled carefully, just as in the other cases.
entries.leviticus 4:31: The fat is removed like in the peace offering and burned as a pleasing smell to the Lord, and the person is forgiven. Even a small offering, done God's way, brings real forgiveness.
entries.leviticus 4:32: If the person brings a lamb instead, it must be a perfect female. God allowed some flexibility in what animal was brought, but it still had to be without defect.
entries.leviticus 4:33: The person lays a hand on the lamb's head and kills it as a sin offering where the burnt offering is killed. The same pattern of identification and sacrifice applies.
entries.leviticus 4:34: The priest puts some blood on the altar's corners and pours the rest at its base. The blood ritual is consistent with the other sin offerings.
entries.leviticus 4:35: The fat is removed like in the peace offering and burned on the altar as an offering to the Lord, and the person is forgiven. The chapter ends by repeating the promise: following God's way brings forgiveness.
entries.leviticus 7:1: This starts the rules for the guilt offering, a sacrifice for when someone has done wrong. It tells the reader that this offering is treated as especially holy, set apart for God.
entries.leviticus 7:2: The animal for the guilt offering is killed where the whole burnt offering is killed, and the priest puts its blood on and around the altar. Blood is handled carefully because it is central to making things right with God.
entries.leviticus 7:3: All the fat of the animal, including the fat tail and the fat around the inner organs, is offered to God. The best parts are given to him rather than kept.
entries.leviticus 7:4: The priest removes the two kidneys with their fat and the fat attached to the liver. These specific parts belong to the offering.
entries.leviticus 7:5: The priest burns these parts on the altar as a fire offering to the Lord. This is what makes it a guilt offering.
entries.leviticus 7:6: Only the male priests may eat this offering, and they must eat it in a holy place. It is treated as most holy, so it is handled with care.
entries.leviticus 7:7: The guilt offering and the sin offering follow the same rule. The priest who performs the ceremony to deal with sin gets to keep the meat.
entries.leviticus 7:8: When a priest offers someone's burnt offering, he may keep the animal's hide for himself. This is part of how the priests were provided for.
entries.leviticus 7:9: Grain offerings cooked in an oven, a pot, or on a griddle belong to the priest who offers them. He receives the food he has prepared for God.
entries.leviticus 7:10: Any grain offering, whether mixed with oil or dry, is shared equally among all the priests. No priest gets more than another from these offerings.
entries.leviticus 7:11: This begins the rules for peace offerings, which are brought to the Lord. These are offerings shared between God, the priest, and the person bringing them.
entries.leviticus 7:12: If the offering is given to express thanks, the person brings unleavened cakes mixed with oil and thin cakes spread with oil, made from the finest flour. These accompany the thank offering.
entries.leviticus 7:13: Along with the thank offering, the person also brings cakes made with yeast. This is part of the peace offering given in thanks.
entries.leviticus 7:14: One portion from each kind of offering is presented to the Lord and given to the priest who puts the blood on the altar. This is the priest's share.
entries.leviticus 7:15: The meat of a thank offering must be eaten on the same day it is offered, with nothing left until morning. Thanksgiving is treated as something to be enjoyed promptly.
entries.leviticus 7:16: If the offering is brought to fulfill a vow or given freely, the meat can be eaten that day and the rest the next day. These offerings allow a little more time than the thank offering.
entries.leviticus 7:17: Any meat still left on the third day must be burned. It is not to be eaten after that point.
entries.leviticus 7:18: If someone eats the peace offering meat on the third day, the offering is not accepted and does not count for the person who brought it. The meat becomes unclean, and the person who eats it bears guilt.
entries.leviticus 7:19: Meat that touches anything unclean must not be eaten but burned. Clean people may eat the meat of the peace offerings.
entries.leviticus 7:20: Anyone who is unclean but eats the Lord's peace offering meat is cut off from the community. Being unclean and sharing in holy food do not mix.
entries.leviticus 7:21: Touching something unclean, whether from a person, an animal, or a detestable thing, and then eating the peace offering meat means being cut off from the people. Holiness is taken seriously.
entries.leviticus 7:22: The Lord speaks to Moses. This introduces the next set of instructions.
entries.leviticus 7:23: The Israelites are told not to eat the fat of oxen, sheep, or goats. The fat belongs to God and is reserved for the altar.
entries.leviticus 7:24: Fat from animals that died naturally or were killed by wild beasts can be used for other purposes but must not be eaten. Even in those cases, the fat is not food.
entries.leviticus 7:25: Anyone who eats the fat of an animal that is used as a fire offering to the Lord is cut off from the people. This rule carries serious consequences.
entries.leviticus 7:26: The Israelites must not eat any blood, whether from birds or animals, anywhere they live. Blood is not to be consumed.
entries.leviticus 7:27: Anyone who eats blood is cut off from the people. This is a firm rule with a serious penalty.
entries.leviticus 7:28: The Lord speaks to Moses again. This begins another set of instructions.
entries.leviticus 7:29: The person bringing a peace offering to the Lord must present part of it as an offering to him. The worshiper personally brings a portion to God.
entries.leviticus 7:30: The worshiper brings the fat and the breast of the animal, and the breast is waved before the Lord as a special presentation. This act sets the portion apart for God.
entries.leviticus 7:31: The priest burns the fat on the altar, but the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons. God receives the fat, and the priests receive the meat.
entries.leviticus 7:32: The right leg of the peace offering is given to the priest as a contribution. This is another share set aside for those who serve at the altar.
entries.leviticus 7:33: The priest who offers the blood and the fat of the peace offering gets the right leg as his portion. The one who does the work receives this share.
entries.leviticus 7:34: God has taken the waved breast and the lifted-up right leg from Israel's peace offerings and given them permanently to Aaron and his sons. This is the priests' lasting share.
entries.leviticus 7:35: This is the holy portion given to Aaron and his sons from the Lord's fire offerings on the day they were ordained as priests. Their support comes from what is offered to God.
entries.leviticus 7:36: The Lord commanded Israel to give this to the priests on the day he appointed them, and it is their permanent right for all generations. This provision is meant to last.
entries.leviticus 7:37: This summarizes the laws for the burnt offering, grain offering, guilt offering, ordination of priests, and peace offerings. It shows these instructions form one connected system of worship.
entries.leviticus 7:38: The Lord gave these commands to Moses on Mount Sinai when he told Israel to bring their offerings to him in the Sinai wilderness. These rules come directly from God.
entries.leviticus 9:1: This marks the start of Aaron's work as priest, eight days after he was set apart for the job. It shows that serving God begins with careful preparation and the right people present.
entries.leviticus 9:2: Aaron is told to bring animals for two kinds of offerings, one to deal with sin and one given wholly to God. The animals had to be perfect, teaching that God deserves our best, not our leftovers.
entries.leviticus 9:3: The people also bring their own offerings, including a goat for sin and perfect young animals to give to God. Everyone shares in this, showing that all people need forgiveness and a way to approach God.
entries.leviticus 9:4: More animals are brought for a shared meal offering with God, along with grain mixed with oil. Moses tells them this is the day they will actually see the Lord show up, so they bring what He asked for.
entries.leviticus 9:5: The people bring exactly what Moses commanded and gather at the entrance of the meeting tent, waiting expectantly. It pictures a community coming together, ready and watching for God to act.
entries.leviticus 9:6: Moses tells them that doing what God commanded is the path to seeing His glory. Obedience comes first, and then God reveals Himself; we don't earn His presence, but we do prepare for it.
entries.leviticus 9:7: Aaron must first offer for his own sin before he can serve on behalf of the people. Leaders need God's cleansing too, and no one stands before God on their own goodness.
entries.leviticus 9:8: Aaron steps up to the altar and begins by killing the ox for his own sin offering. He starts with himself, showing that personal honesty before God comes before leading others.
entries.leviticus 9:9: His sons hand him the blood, and he smears some on the altar's horns and pours the rest at its base. The blood stands for life given up to make things right with God.
entries.leviticus 9:10: The rich parts of the animal are burned on the altar, just as God had instructed. Doing it exactly as commanded shows that worship is on God's terms, not ours.
entries.leviticus 9:11: The parts not burned on the altar are taken outside the camp and burned. What couldn't be offered to God was removed from the community, keeping the holy and the ordinary separate.
entries.leviticus 9:12: Aaron then kills the animal for the whole offering, and his sons bring him the blood to splash around the altar. This offering was given completely to God, a picture of total dedication.
entries.leviticus 9:13: The pieces of the animal are handed to Aaron in order, including the head, and burned on the altar. The careful order shows that worship is done thoughtfully, not carelessly.
entries.leviticus 9:14: The inner organs and legs are washed first, then burned with the rest of the offering. Even the hidden parts are cleaned and given to God, reminding us that He sees and wants our whole lives.
entries.leviticus 9:15: Aaron now offers the people's sin offering, a goat, in the same way he did his own. The people's need for forgiveness is dealt with the same way as the priest's.
entries.leviticus 9:16: He presents the people's whole offering according to the prescribed procedure. Following the pattern matters, because this is about obeying God rather than improvising.
entries.leviticus 9:17: He brings the grain offering, burns a handful on the altar, and adds it to the morning offering. Daily worship builds on what was already given earlier that day.
entries.leviticus 9:18: Aaron kills the ox and sheep for the people's peace offerings, and the blood is splashed around the altar. These offerings celebrated fellowship and peace with God, not just forgiveness.
entries.leviticus 9:19: The fat portions of the animals are set aside, including the fat tail and the fat around the organs. The best and richest parts are reserved for God's altar.
entries.leviticus 9:20: The fat is placed on the breasts and then burned on the altar. The priests handle the offering carefully, making sure God's portion is given to Him.
entries.leviticus 9:21: Aaron lifts up the breast and right leg as a wave offering before the Lord, just as Moses ordered. Lifting the offering toward God was a physical way of saying it belongs to Him.
entries.leviticus 9:22: After finishing the offerings, Aaron raises his hands and blesses the people, then steps down. The priest's job ends with words of blessing, sending the people home with God's favor.
entries.leviticus 9:23: Moses and Aaron go into the meeting tent and come out blessing the people, and God's glory appears to everyone. When leaders and people obey, God's presence becomes visible to the whole community.
entries.leviticus 9:24: Fire comes from God and consumes the offering on the altar, and the people cry out and fall face down. God Himself confirms the worship, and the people respond with awe and surrender.
entries.leviticus 8:1: God speaks directly to Moses, giving him the next set of instructions. It reminds the reader that what follows comes from God, not from human invention.
entries.leviticus 8:2: God tells Moses to bring Aaron and his sons, along with the special clothes, oil, and animals needed for the ceremony. These are the supplies for setting the priests apart for their work.
entries.leviticus 8:3: The whole community is called to gather at the entrance of the meeting tent to witness this. It shows that the setting apart of priests was a public event, not a private one.
entries.leviticus 8:4: Moses obeys exactly, and the people assemble as commanded. It shows that obedience to God's instructions was the first step of the whole ceremony.
entries.leviticus 8:5: Moses tells the people that what they are about to see is commanded by God. It helps the reader understand this ritual was not Moses' idea but God's.
entries.leviticus 8:6: Moses brings Aaron and his sons forward and washes them with water. This washing shows they must be clean before they can serve God.
entries.leviticus 8:7: Moses dresses Aaron in the special priestly garments, layer by layer. The careful dressing marks Aaron as set apart for a holy role.
entries.leviticus 8:8: Moses adds the priestly pouch containing the Urim and Thummim, objects used to seek God's guidance. It shows that the priest's work included helping people know God's will.
entries.leviticus 8:9: Moses places the turban and gold plate on Aaron's head, exactly as God commanded. The gold crown marks Aaron as dedicated to God's service.
entries.leviticus 8:10: Moses pours the holy oil on the tent and everything in it to set them apart for God. This shows that the place of worship itself had to be made holy.
entries.leviticus 8:11: Moses sprinkles oil on the altar, its tools, and the washing basin seven times. The number seven suggests completeness, showing everything was fully set apart for God.
entries.leviticus 8:12: Moses pours some of the oil on Aaron's head to set him apart. This anointing marks Aaron as chosen and dedicated to serve as priest.
entries.leviticus 8:13: Moses dresses Aaron's sons in their priestly clothes, just as God commanded. They too are being set apart to serve alongside their father.
entries.leviticus 8:14: Moses brings the sin-offering ox, and Aaron and his sons lay their hands on its head. This gesture shows the people identifying with the animal that will bear their sin.
entries.leviticus 8:15: Moses kills the ox and applies its blood to the altar to cleanse it. The blood is used to remove impurity so the altar can be used for holy service.
entries.leviticus 8:16: Moses burns the fat parts of the inner organs on the altar. These choice parts are given to God as the offering's most valuable portion.
entries.leviticus 8:17: The rest of the ox—skin, flesh, and waste—is burned outside the camp. This shows that what is unclean is removed from the community's holy space.
entries.leviticus 8:18: Moses brings the first ram for the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons lay hands on it. Again they identify with the animal before it is offered.
entries.leviticus 8:19: Moses kills the ram and puts its blood on and around the altar. The blood is central to making the offering acceptable to God.
entries.leviticus 8:20: Moses cuts the ram into pieces and burns the head, parts, and fat. The offering is prepared carefully and completely for God.
entries.leviticus 8:21: After washing the inner parts and legs, Moses burns the whole ram on the altar. The text calls it a pleasing smell to God, meaning the offering was accepted.
entries.leviticus 8:22: Moses brings the second ram, the one for setting the priests apart, and Aaron and his sons lay hands on it. This offering is specifically for ordaining them to their role.
entries.leviticus 8:23: Moses kills the ram and puts some of its blood on Aaron's right ear, thumb, and big toe. This symbolizes that Aaron's hearing, work, and walk are all dedicated to God.
entries.leviticus 8:24: Moses does the same for Aaron's sons—blood on ear, thumb, and toe—and puts the rest on the altar. It shows the whole person is set apart for God's service.
entries.leviticus 8:25: Moses takes the fat portions and the right leg of the ordination ram. These choice parts are prepared for the special offering.
entries.leviticus 8:26: Moses takes three kinds of bread from the basket and places them on the fat and the leg. Bread is included in the offering, showing gratitude and fellowship with God.
entries.leviticus 8:27: Moses places all these items in the hands of Aaron and his sons and waves them before God. The gesture presents the offering to God on behalf of the priests.
entries.leviticus 8:28: Moses takes the offerings back from their hands and burns them on the altar. This completes the ordination offering as a pleasing smell to God.
entries.leviticus 8:29: Moses waves the breast of the ram before God and keeps it as his own portion. This shows that those who serve God in this work are also provided for.
entries.leviticus 8:30: Moses sprinkles oil and blood on Aaron, his sons, and their clothes to make them holy. This final act seals their dedication to God's service.
entries.leviticus 8:31: Moses tells Aaron and his sons to cook and eat the meat and bread at the tent entrance. Eating the offering shows they share in what was given to God.
entries.leviticus 8:32: Any leftover meat or bread must be burned, not kept. This teaches that what is holy is not to be treated as ordinary or wasted.
entries.leviticus 8:33: Aaron and his sons must stay at the tent entrance for seven days while the ordination is completed. This period of waiting shows their full commitment to being set apart.
entries.leviticus 8:34: Moses explains that everything done that day was commanded by God to take away sin. It reminds the reader that forgiveness comes on God's terms, not ours.
entries.leviticus 8:35: The priests must guard the tent entrance day and night for seven days to avoid death. This shows how seriously God takes the holiness of his presence.
entries.leviticus 8:36: Aaron and his sons do everything God commanded through Moses. Their obedience completes the ordination and shows the right response to God's instructions.
entries.leviticus 10:1: Two of Aaron's sons burned incense in a way God had not commanded. It means worship must be done God's way, not just however we think is best.
entries.leviticus 10:2: Fire from God killed them on the spot. It shows that God takes disobedience in worship seriously, so we should approach him with respect.
entries.leviticus 10:3: Moses tells Aaron that God will be treated as holy by those who come near him. It means God deserves honor from those who serve him, and Aaron quietly accepted this.
entries.leviticus 10:4: Moses had two relatives carry the bodies away from the holy area. It means the dead bodies had to be removed from the sacred place to keep it clean.
entries.leviticus 10:5: The two men did exactly what Moses said and carried the bodies out. It shows they obeyed quickly and carefully.
entries.leviticus 10:6: Moses told Aaron and his remaining sons not to show public mourning, so they would not also die. It means their role as priests came first, while the rest of the people could grieve.
entries.leviticus 10:7: They were told to stay at the entrance of the meeting tent because they had been set apart with holy oil. It means their special service to God required them to stay at their post.
entries.leviticus 10:8: God spoke directly to Aaron here. It sets up the instruction that follows for him and his sons.
entries.leviticus 10:9: Priests were forbidden to drink wine or strong drink before entering the meeting tent. It means they needed clear minds to serve God, and this rule was to last for all generations.
entries.leviticus 10:10: Priests had to tell the difference between what is holy and common, and between clean and unclean. It means God's people need clear guidance about what honors him and what does not.
entries.leviticus 10:11: The priests were to teach the people all the laws God gave through Moses. It means part of serving God is teaching others what he has said.
entries.leviticus 10:12: Moses told the surviving sons to eat the rest of the grain offering beside the altar. It means the priests were to receive this most holy food in the proper place.
entries.leviticus 10:13: This food was to be eaten in a holy place as the priests' rightful share. It means God provided for those who served him at the altar.
entries.leviticus 10:14: The breast and thigh from the peace offerings were for the priests and their families to eat in a clean place. It means God's provision extended to the priests' households.
entries.leviticus 10:15: The breast and thigh were to be presented before the Lord along with the fat. It means these portions were set apart for the priests and their descendants permanently.
entries.leviticus 10:16: Moses looked for the goat of the sin offering and found it had been burned up, and he was angry with the two remaining sons. It means he expected the proper procedure to be followed.
entries.leviticus 10:17: Moses asked why they had not eaten the sin offering in the holy place. It means this meal was part of how the people's sin was dealt with before God.
entries.leviticus 10:18: Since the blood was not brought into the holy place, the meat should have been eaten there. It means Moses was pointing out that the rules had not been followed.
entries.leviticus 10:19: Aaron explained that with such tragedy happening that day, eating the offering would not have been right. It means he was asking whether God would really have been pleased with that.
entries.leviticus 10:20: When Moses heard Aaron's reasoning, he accepted it and stopped being angry. It means Moses was willing to listen and reconsider when given a good explanation.
entries.leviticus 12:1: God speaks these instructions directly to Moses, showing that what follows is meant to be passed on to the people as God's guidance. For the reader, it reminds us that these rules come from God and were given for a reason.
entries.leviticus 12:2: After a woman gives birth to a boy, she is considered ritually unclean for seven days, much like during her monthly period. This was about ceremonial purity in worship, not about the baby or birth being wrong.
entries.leviticus 12:3: On the eighth day the baby boy is to be circumcised. This was the physical sign of God's covenant with Israel, marking the child as part of God's people.
entries.leviticus 12:4: The mother then waits thirty-three more days while her bleeding stops, and during this time she cannot touch sacred things or enter the holy place. This set a period of rest and separation before she could return to full worship.
entries.leviticus 12:5: If the baby is a girl, the waiting periods are doubled, two weeks plus sixty-six days. The text simply states this rule without explaining why, and it reflects the cultural setting of that time.
entries.leviticus 12:6: When her waiting period ends, the mother brings a young lamb as a burned offering and a pigeon or dove as a sin offering to the priest at the entrance of the meeting tent. These offerings marked her return to worship and dealt with any ritual impurity.
entries.leviticus 12:7: The priest offers these sacrifices to God to make atonement for her, and she is declared clean from her bleeding. This gave the woman a clear, official way to be restored to full participation in worship.
entries.leviticus 12:8: If she cannot afford a lamb, she may bring two doves or two young pigeons instead, and the priest makes atonement so she is clean. God made provision for poorer families, so no one was excluded from being restored.
entries.leviticus 6:1: God is speaking to Moses, giving him instructions to pass on to the people. This verse simply sets up the rules that follow.
entries.leviticus 6:2: If someone cheats a neighbor—by lying about property left in their care, by not repaying a debt, by stealing, or by mistreating them—God treats that as unfaithfulness to him too. It means wronging people is also an offense against God, not just a private matter.
entries.leviticus 6:3: This adds lying under oath about something found and denied. If a person does any of these wrongs, they are guilty and must answer for it.
entries.leviticus 6:4: Once they realize their guilt, they must return what they took or kept dishonestly—whether by force, by cruelty, or by holding back something entrusted to them. Real repentance starts with giving back what was wrongfully taken.
entries.leviticus 6:5: They must repay the full amount plus one-fifth extra to the rightful owner, once they are found guilty. The extra makes up for the loss and shows genuine sorrow for the wrong.
entries.leviticus 6:6: Then they bring a ram without defect to the priest as a guilt offering, valued at the set rate. Making things right with the person comes first, then the offering to God.
entries.leviticus 6:7: The priest makes atonement for them before the Lord, and they are forgiven for whatever wrong they did. God offers real forgiveness once the wrong is made right.
entries.leviticus 6:8: God continues speaking to Moses, introducing the next set of instructions. This verse just marks a new section of the law.
entries.leviticus 6:9: God gives Aaron and his sons the rules for the burnt offering: it stays on the altar fire all night until morning, and the fire must never go out. The fire's constant burning showed the people's ongoing devotion to God.
entries.leviticus 6:10: The priest puts on his linen clothes and underwear and removes the ashes from the altar, placing them beside it. Even handling leftovers from worship was done carefully and respectfully.
entries.leviticus 6:11: He then changes out of his holy clothes, puts on ordinary ones, and carries the ashes to a clean place outside the camp. The sacred and the everyday were kept distinct.
entries.leviticus 6:12: The altar fire must never go out; each morning the priest adds wood, arranges the burnt offering, and burns the fat of the peace offerings. Faithful daily attention kept worship going.
entries.leviticus 6:13: The fire on the altar must burn continually and never be allowed to go out. This constant flame pictured unbroken devotion and God's ongoing presence with his people.
entries.leviticus 6:14: This gives the rules for the grain offering, which Aaron's sons present to the Lord in front of the altar. It was a gift of thanks and honor brought to God.
entries.leviticus 6:15: The priest takes a handful of the flour, oil, and all the incense and burns it on the altar as a memorial, a pleasing smell to the Lord. A portion was offered to God to represent the whole gift.
entries.leviticus 6:16: The rest of the grain offering belongs to Aaron and his sons, who eat it without yeast in a holy place within the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. God provided for the priests through the offerings brought to him.
entries.leviticus 6:17: It must not be baked with yeast; it is the priests' share of the fire offerings and is most holy, like the sin and guilt offerings. Yeast often stood for corruption, so it was kept out of these holy gifts.
entries.leviticus 6:18: Every male descendant of Aaron may eat it as a permanent right through all generations, and anyone who touches these offerings becomes holy. Being near holy things required being set apart for God.
entries.leviticus 6:19: God speaks again to Moses, beginning a new instruction. This verse simply introduces what follows.
entries.leviticus 6:20: On the day a priest is ordained, he brings a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a grain offering, half in the morning and half in the evening. The priest's own dedication to God was marked by regular daily offering.
