entries.leviticus 6:21: It is prepared with oil on a griddle, cooked, and broken into pieces and presented as a pleasing smell to the Lord. Careful preparation showed honor toward God.
entries.leviticus 6:22: The son who succeeds him as priest must offer the same thing forever, and it must be completely burned. This kept the priesthood's dedication continuing from generation to generation.
entries.leviticus 6:23: Every grain offering brought by a priest for himself must be entirely burned, with none kept for food. Unlike other grain offerings, the priest received no share of his own offering.
entries.leviticus 6:24: God continues speaking to Moses, introducing the next set of rules. This verse just marks the start of a new section.
entries.leviticus 6:25: God gives Aaron and his sons the rules for the sin offering: it is killed before the Lord in the same place as the burnt offering and is most holy. Sin had to be dealt with seriously and in the way God prescribed.
entries.leviticus 6:26: The priest who offers the sin offering eats it in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Part of the offering provided for the priest who ministered.
entries.leviticus 6:27: Anyone who touches its meat becomes holy, and if any blood splashes on clothing, that clothing must be washed in a holy place. Contact with holy things required cleansing and care.
entries.leviticus 6:28: A clay pot used to cook the meat must be broken, but a bronze pot must be scrubbed and rinsed with water. Porous clay absorbed the holy meat, so it could not be reused for ordinary purposes.
entries.leviticus 6:29: Every male among the priests may eat it, because it is most holy. The offering was reserved for those set apart to serve at the altar.
entries.leviticus 6:30: But if any of the sin offering's blood was brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the holy place, none of that meat may be eaten—it must be burned with fire. Offerings that dealt with sin at the deepest level were not shared but completely given to God.
entries.leviticus 15:1: God is speaking here, giving instructions to both Moses and Aaron, the leader and the priest. It shows that these rules about ritual purity were meant to guide the whole community's worship.
entries.leviticus 15:2: A man with an unusual discharge from his body was considered ritually unclean under Israel's purity laws. For the reader, this shows that ancient Israel treated bodily conditions as matters of ritual status, not personal guilt.
entries.leviticus 15:3: Whether the discharge kept flowing or was blocked, the man stayed unclean either way. The point is that the condition itself, not its severity, determined his ritual status.
entries.leviticus 15:4: Anything the man lay on or sat on became unclean too. This shows how uncleanness in these laws spread through contact to everyday objects.
entries.leviticus 15:5: Anyone who touched his bed had to wash their clothes and body and stayed unclean until evening. This taught Israel that contact with uncleanness required cleansing and a waiting period.
entries.leviticus 15:6: Sitting where the unclean man had sat made a person unclean until evening, with washing required. The lesson is that uncleanness spread through ordinary contact and had to be dealt with.
entries.leviticus 15:7: Touching the man's body directly made a person unclean until evening, requiring washing. This reinforced that physical contact with the unclean condition carried ritual consequences.
entries.leviticus 15:8: If the unclean man spat on someone clean, that person became unclean until evening and had to wash. Even small contact could spread ritual uncleanness under these laws.
entries.leviticus 15:9: A saddle or leather seat the unclean man rode on became unclean. This shows the rules extended to everyday items like riding gear.
entries.leviticus 15:10: Touching anything that had been under the man made a person unclean until evening, and carrying such items required washing. The laws treated uncleanness as something that clung to objects and people.
entries.leviticus 15:11: If the unclean man touched someone without having washed his hands, that person became unclean until evening and had to wash. Handwashing mattered because uncleanness could pass on through touch.
entries.leviticus 15:12: A clay jar he touched had to be broken, while a wooden one could be washed. Porous clay could not be cleansed, so it was destroyed, showing how seriously these laws treated contamination.
entries.leviticus 15:13: Once the discharge stopped, the man waited seven days, washed his clothes, and bathed in fresh running water to become clean. Full restoration required time, washing, and running water.
entries.leviticus 15:14: On the eighth day he brought two doves or pigeons to the priest at the entrance of the meeting tent. The person did not approach God empty-handed but came with an offering.
entries.leviticus 15:15: The priest offered one bird as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering to make atonement for the man. This shows that becoming clean again involved both washing and a sacrifice before God.
entries.leviticus 15:16: A man's normal emission of semen made him unclean until evening, and he had to bathe. Even ordinary bodily functions were treated as requiring ritual cleansing.
entries.leviticus 15:17: Clothing or leather that the semen touched had to be washed and stayed unclean until evening. The laws applied to everyday items, not just to people.
entries.leviticus 15:18: When a man and woman had sexual relations, both had to bathe and were unclean until evening. This treated normal married intimacy as a temporary ritual state, not as sin.
entries.leviticus 15:19: A woman's monthly bleeding made her ritually separate for seven days, and anyone who touched her was unclean until evening. This was a ritual status, not a moral judgment on her.
entries.leviticus 15:20: Anything she lay on or sat on during her separation became unclean. Her ordinary furniture and resting places were affected by her ritual state.
entries.leviticus 15:21: Touching her bed required washing clothes and body and left a person unclean until evening. Contact with her ritual uncleanness had to be cleansed.
entries.leviticus 15:22: Touching anything she had sat on made a person unclean until evening, requiring washing. The same rule applied to her seating as to her bed.
entries.leviticus 15:23: Anyone touching her bed or seat was unclean until evening. The uncleanness attached to those objects and passed to whoever touched them.
entries.leviticus 15:24: If a man had sex with her during her period, he became unclean for seven days, and his bed became unclean too. This carried a heavier consequence than ordinary contact.
entries.leviticus 15:25: If a woman bled for many days outside her normal cycle, she stayed unclean as long as the bleeding lasted. The law covered irregular and prolonged conditions, not just the usual monthly pattern.
entries.leviticus 15:26: During that long flow, her bed and seat were unclean just as during her normal period. The same rules applied to her furniture in both cases.
entries.leviticus 15:27: Anyone touching those things became unclean until evening and had to wash. Contact with her uncleanness required cleansing, as in the normal case.
entries.leviticus 15:28: When her bleeding stopped, she waited seven days, and then she was clean. Restoration came after the condition ended and a set period passed.
entries.leviticus 15:29: On the eighth day she brought two doves or pigeons to the priest at the meeting tent. Like the man, she came with an offering to complete her cleansing.
entries.leviticus 15:30: The priest offered one bird as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering to make atonement for her. Her cleansing was completed before God through sacrifice.
entries.leviticus 15:31: God gave these rules to keep Israel from defiling his holy dwelling place and to protect them from death. The laws were about guarding worship, not about shaming people for bodily functions.
entries.leviticus 15:32: This verse summarizes the law for a man with a discharge or a normal emission that made him unclean. It introduces the closing summary of the chapter's rules.
entries.leviticus 15:33: The summary also covers a woman's bleeding, any unclean discharge, and a man who has relations with a woman during her period. These rules applied to both men and women and to intimate situations.
entries.leviticus 11:1: God speaks here to Moses and Aaron, the leaders of Israel, giving them instructions to pass on. It shows that God guides his people through chosen leaders.
entries.leviticus 11:2: God tells the Israelites which animals they are allowed to eat. This was a way of setting his people apart from the nations around them.
entries.leviticus 11:3: An animal could be eaten if it chewed its food twice over and had a split hoof. These were the marks that made it acceptable food for Israel.
entries.leviticus 11:4: The camel chews its food twice over but does not have a split hoof, so it was not to be eaten. It was off-limits for God's people.
entries.leviticus 11:5: The rock-badger was also not to be eaten because it did not have a split hoof. It was treated as unclean for Israel.
entries.leviticus 11:6: The hare was not to be eaten because its foot was not split in two. It too was unclean for the people.
entries.leviticus 11:7: The pig has a split hoof but does not chew its food twice over, so it was not to be eaten. It was unclean for Israel.
entries.leviticus 11:8: The people were not to eat these animals or even touch their dead bodies. Touching them would make a person unclean and unfit for worship.
entries.leviticus 11:9: Water creatures could be eaten if they had fins and scales. These were the signs of clean food from the water.
entries.leviticus 11:10: Any water creature without fins and scales was to be avoided. It was considered unfit and disgusting for food.
entries.leviticus 11:11: Such creatures were not to be eaten, and their dead bodies were to be avoided. They were treated as unfit for God's people.
entries.leviticus 11:12: Anything in the water without fins and scales was off-limits. The people were to treat it as unfit for food.
entries.leviticus 11:13: Certain birds, starting with eagles and ospreys, were not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit food for Israel.
entries.leviticus 11:14: Kites and falcons and similar birds were also on the list of birds not to be eaten. They were unclean for the people.
entries.leviticus 11:15: Ravens and similar birds were not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit food for Israel.
entries.leviticus 11:16: Ostriches, night-hawks, sea-hawks, and similar birds were not to be eaten. They were unclean for the people.
entries.leviticus 11:17: Little owls, cormorants, and great owls were among the birds not to be eaten. They were off-limits as food.
entries.leviticus 11:18: Water-hens, pelicans, and vultures were also not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit for God's people.
entries.leviticus 11:19: Storks, herons, hoopoes, and bats were not to be eaten. They were unclean for Israel.
entries.leviticus 11:20: Winged creatures that walk on four legs were to be avoided as food. They were considered unfit for the people.
entries.leviticus 11:21: Some winged creatures with four legs could be eaten if they had long legs for jumping. These were the exception to the rule.
entries.leviticus 11:22: Locusts of various kinds were allowed as food. They were the clean exception among jumping winged creatures.
entries.leviticus 11:23: All other winged four-legged creatures were not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit for God's people.
entries.leviticus 11:24: Touching the dead body of these creatures made a person unclean until evening. This meant they could not take part in worship until they were clean again.
entries.leviticus 11:25: Anyone who carried away such a dead body had to wash their clothes and stay unclean until evening. Cleansing required both washing and waiting.
entries.leviticus 11:26: Animals without a fully split hoof or that do not chew their food twice over were unclean. Touching them made a person unclean.
entries.leviticus 11:27: Four-footed animals that walk on the pads of their feet were unclean. Touching their dead bodies made a person unclean until evening.
entries.leviticus 11:28: Carrying away the dead body of such an animal required washing clothes and being unclean until evening. The person was restored to cleanliness after that.
entries.leviticus 11:29: Small creatures that move low on the ground, like weasels, mice, and large lizards, were unclean. They were not to be eaten or touched.
entries.leviticus 11:30: Ferrets, land crocodiles, lizards, sand-lizards, and chameleons were also unclean. They were off-limits for God's people.
entries.leviticus 11:31: Touching these creatures when dead made a person unclean until evening. They could not worship until they were clean again.
entries.leviticus 11:32: If a dead body of these creatures fell on something, that object became unclean. Wood, clothing, skin, or bags had to be put in water and were unclean until evening.
entries.leviticus 11:33: If such a dead body fell into a clay pot, everything inside became unclean and the pot had to be broken. Clay pots could not be cleaned, so they were destroyed.
entries.leviticus 11:34: Food or drink that came from such an unclean pot became unclean too. Uncleanness spread from the pot to what was in it.
entries.leviticus 11:35: If a dead body fell on an oven or cooking pot, it had to be broken. These items became unclean and could not be used.
entries.leviticus 11:36: A spring or a water storage place stayed clean even if a dead body touched it. But anyone who touched the dead body was still unclean.
entries.leviticus 11:37: If a dead body fell on seed for planting, the seed stayed clean. Dry seed was not affected by uncleanness.
entries.leviticus 11:38: But if the seed had been soaked in water and a dead body touched it, the seed became unclean. Water made the seed able to receive uncleanness.
entries.leviticus 11:39: If an animal allowed for food died on its own, anyone who touched its body was unclean until evening. Natural death made even clean animals unfit to touch.
entries.leviticus 11:40: Anyone who ate from such a dead animal or carried its body had to wash their clothes and stay unclean until evening. Cleansing required washing and waiting until evening.
entries.leviticus 11:41: Small creatures that move along the ground were not to be eaten. They were treated as unfit food for Israel.
entries.leviticus 11:42: Creatures that crawl on their belly, on four legs, or on many legs were not to be eaten. They were all considered unfit for God's people.
entries.leviticus 11:43: The people were told not to make themselves unclean by these creatures. They were to stay set apart and not become unfit through contact with them.
entries.leviticus 11:44: God says he is the Lord their God, so they must set themselves apart and be holy. Being holy means living differently because they belong to him.
entries.leviticus 11:45: God brought Israel out of Egypt to be their God, so they must be holy as he is holy. Their conduct was to reflect the God who rescued them.
entries.leviticus 11:46: This verse summarizes the whole set of rules about animals, birds, and water creatures. It shows the teaching covered every kind of creature the people might meet.
entries.leviticus 11:47: The rules were meant to teach the difference between clean and unclean, and between animals that could and could not be eaten. God's people were to know and follow that difference.
entries.leviticus 17:1: God is speaking directly to Moses, giving him instructions to pass on. This reminds the reader that these rules come from God himself, not from human invention.
entries.leviticus 17:2: Moses is told to deliver God's command to the priests and to the whole community of Israel. Everyone is expected to hear and follow it, not just the religious leaders.
entries.leviticus 17:3: This rule covers any Israelite who kills an ox, sheep, or goat, whether inside the camp or out in the open. It sets the scene for where such killing must be done.
entries.leviticus 17:4: If someone kills an animal for sacrifice but doesn't bring it to the entrance of the meeting tent, he is guilty of taking a life and must be removed from the community. The point is that worship must go through the place and way God appointed, not wherever a person chooses.
entries.leviticus 17:5: The purpose is that Israelites stop killing animals out in the open fields and instead bring them to the priest at the meeting tent as peace offerings to the Lord. It moves their worship from private, scattered practice to the one place God designated.
entries.leviticus 17:6: The priest splashes the blood on God's altar at the tent entrance and burns the fat as a pleasing offering. This shows that the priest handles the sacred parts of the sacrifice on the people's behalf.
entries.leviticus 17:7: The people must stop sacrificing to evil spirits, which they had been chasing after instead of God. This is to be a permanent rule for all their generations, showing that divided loyalty to false powers is never acceptable.
entries.leviticus 17:8: This applies to any Israelite or foreigner living among them who brings a burnt offering or any other sacrifice. The rule is stated broadly so no one can claim it doesn't apply to them.
entries.leviticus 17:9: If such a person doesn't bring the offering to the entrance of the meeting tent, he must be cut off from his people. Worship offered on one's own terms, apart from God's appointed place, is treated as a serious offense.
entries.leviticus 17:10: God says he will personally set himself against anyone, Israelite or foreigner, who eats blood, and that person will be cut off from the community. This shows how seriously God treats the eating of blood.
entries.leviticus 17:11: The reason is that the life of a creature is in its blood, and God has given blood on the altar to deal with sin. Blood cleanses from sin because it carries the life that is being offered.
entries.leviticus 17:12: Because blood is the life and is set apart for atonement, God forbids anyone in the community, including foreigners, from eating it. The reader is reminded that this is not a minor dietary rule but something tied to the sacredness of life.
entries.leviticus 17:13: Anyone who hunts an animal or bird for food must pour out its blood and cover it with earth. This treats the creature's life with respect rather than letting its blood be casually consumed.
entries.leviticus 17:14: Again the reason is given: the blood is the life of every creature, so no one may eat it, and anyone who does will be cut off. The repeated warning shows how central this principle is.
entries.leviticus 17:15: Anyone, native or foreigner, who eats an animal that died on its own or was killed by another animal must wash their clothes and bathe, staying unclean until evening, then they are clean. This shows that even accidental contact with improper food requires cleansing.
entries.leviticus 17:16: If the person refuses to wash and bathe, they carry the guilt of their sin. The reader learns that ignoring God's cleansing requirement leaves a person accountable, not merely unclean.
entries.leviticus 13:1: God is giving instructions to Moses and Aaron, the leaders and priests of Israel. This shows that caring for the health of the community was part of their God-given responsibility.
entries.leviticus 13:2: If someone notices a swelling, rash, or bright spot on their skin that might be a serious skin disease, they were to be brought to the priest to be examined. The priest, not a doctor, served as the one who checked and decided the person's status in the community.
entries.leviticus 13:3: The priest looks for signs that the problem is serious: white hair in the spot and the sore going deeper than the skin. If those signs are there, the priest declares the person unclean, meaning they must be separated from others for a time.
entries.leviticus 13:4: If the spot looks minor and the signs aren't clear, the priest doesn't decide right away but has the person stay apart for seven days to see what happens. This teaches patience rather than rushing to judgment.
entries.leviticus 13:5: After a week the priest checks again, and if the spot hasn't gotten worse or spread, the person waits another seven days. Careful watching protects both the sick person and the community.
entries.leviticus 13:6: If after the second week the spot has faded and not spread, the priest declares the person clean, and they wash their clothes and return to normal life. This gave people a clear way back into the community.
entries.leviticus 13:7: If the spot spreads after the person was examined, they must go back to the priest for another look. A change for the worse means the matter needs to be rechecked.
entries.leviticus 13:8: If the priest sees the spot has spread, he declares the person unclean because it is a real skin disease. The spreading is the key sign that this is serious.
entries.leviticus 13:9: Whenever a serious skin disease appears on someone, they are to be brought to the priest. The priest again serves as the one who confirms what is happening.
entries.leviticus 13:10: The priest checks for a white swelling, white hair, and raw, open flesh in the sore. These are signs that the disease is active and serious.
entries.leviticus 13:11: If these signs show the disease is long-standing, the priest declares the person unclean right away without waiting. Clear evidence means no need for further testing.
entries.leviticus 13:12: If the disease has spread over the person's whole skin, from head to foot, as far as the priest can see, the situation is examined as a whole. The priest looks at the total picture, not just one spot.
entries.leviticus 13:13: If the priest sees that the whole body has turned white, he declares the person clean, because the skin has fully changed and is no longer raw and open. In this case, the complete whitening is actually a good sign.
entries.leviticus 13:14: But if raw, open flesh appears anywhere on the person, that is a sign of uncleanness. Open, diseased flesh is the real problem, not just the color of the skin.
entries.leviticus 13:15: When the priest sees raw flesh, he declares the person unclean, because open diseased flesh means the disease is active. The visible condition, not rumor or fear, decides the outcome.
entries.leviticus 13:16: If the raw flesh heals and turns white again, the person is to come back to the priest. Healing is possible, and the person is not permanently shut out.
entries.leviticus 13:17: If the priest sees that the spot has turned white, he declares the person clean and free of the disease. The priest's confirmation restores the person to the community.
entries.leviticus 13:18: This covers the case of a boil or sore on the skin that has healed. Even after healing, the area needs to be checked if something new appears there.
entries.leviticus 13:19: If a white swelling or a reddish-white bright spot appears where the boil was, the priest must examine it. A new mark in an old wound could be a sign of something serious.
entries.leviticus 13:20: If the spot goes deeper than the skin and the hair in it has turned white, the priest declares the person unclean because the disease has started in the old sore. The location doesn't change the seriousness of the signs.
entries.leviticus 13:21: If the priest sees no white hair, the spot isn't deep, and it isn't bright, he has the person stay apart for seven days. When signs are unclear, waiting and watching is the wise response.
entries.leviticus 13:22: If the spot spreads during that week, the priest declares the person unclean because it is a real disease. Spreading confirms the problem.
entries.leviticus 13:23: If the bright spot stays the same size and doesn't spread, it is just the scar from the old wound, and the priest declares the person clean. Not every mark is a disease.
entries.leviticus 13:24: This covers a burn on the skin where the burned flesh becomes a bright reddish-white or white spot. Burns, like other wounds, need to be checked for signs of disease.
entries.leviticus 13:25: If the hair in the bright spot has turned white and the spot goes deeper than the skin, the priest declares the person unclean because the disease has started in the burn. The same signs mean the same conclusion, wherever they appear.
entries.leviticus 13:26: If the priest sees no white hair, the spot isn't deep, and it isn't bright, he has the person stay apart for seven days. Again, unclear cases are watched rather than decided quickly.
entries.leviticus 13:27: If on the seventh day the spot has spread, the priest declares the person unclean because it is a real disease. Spreading is the deciding sign.
entries.leviticus 13:28: If the bright spot stays the same size, doesn't spread, and fades, it is just the mark of the burn, and the priest declares the person clean. A healing burn scar is not a disease.
entries.leviticus 13:29: This begins a new case: a disease on the head or in the hair of the chin, affecting a man or a woman. Problems in hair-covered areas needed their own careful examination.
entries.leviticus 13:30: If the priest sees the sore goes deeper than the skin and has thin yellow hair in it, he declares the person unclean because it is a serious skin disease. Yellow, thin hair is a warning sign.
entries.leviticus 13:31: If the sore doesn't seem deep and there is no black hair in it, the priest has the person stay apart for seven days. Lack of clear signs means watch and wait.
entries.leviticus 13:32: On the seventh day the priest checks again: if the sore hasn't spread, has no yellow hair, and isn't deep, it still isn't confirmed. The examination continues until the signs are clear.
entries.leviticus 13:33: The person shaves their hair except over the sore, and stays apart for another seven days. Shaving helps the priest see the sore clearly without cutting into the diseased area.
entries.leviticus 13:34: If on the seventh day the sore hasn't spread and isn't deep, the priest declares the person clean, and after washing their clothes they return to normal life. Clear results mean a clear return to the community.
entries.leviticus 13:35: If the disease gets worse after the person was declared clean, the matter must be looked at again. A clean verdict isn't the end of the story if things change.
entries.leviticus 13:36: If the priest sees the sore has spread, he declares the person unclean without even checking for yellow hair. Spreading alone is enough to confirm the disease.
entries.leviticus 13:37: If the sore has stopped spreading and black hair has grown in it, the disease is gone, and the priest declares the person clean. New, normal hair is a sign of healing.
entries.leviticus 13:38: This covers bright white marks on the skin of a man or a woman. Not every white mark is serious, so each case is examined.
entries.leviticus 13:39: If the white marks are not very bright, it is only a harmless skin condition, and the priest declares the person clean. Mild skin problems don't make a person unclean.
entries.leviticus 13:40: If a man loses his hair and becomes bald, he is still clean. Baldness is not a disease and doesn't affect a person's standing in the community.
entries.leviticus 16:1: God spoke to Moses right after Aaron's two sons died for approaching God in a way he had not commanded. It reminds the reader that God takes worship seriously.
entries.leviticus 16:2: God told Moses to warn Aaron not to enter the most holy inner room whenever he liked, because God's presence there could kill him. It shows that coming near to God is not casual.
entries.leviticus 16:3: Aaron could only enter that holy place by bringing the required sacrifices, a bull for sin and a ram for a burnt offering. It teaches that approaching God requires the right offering.
entries.leviticus 16:4: Aaron had to wear simple holy linen clothes and wash his body before entering. It shows that those who come before God must be cleansed and set apart.
entries.leviticus 16:5: The people were to supply two male goats for a sin offering and one ram for a burnt offering. It shows the whole community shared in the cost of dealing with sin.
entries.leviticus 16:6: Aaron first offered a bull to cover his own sins and his family's sins. It reminds the reader that leaders too need forgiveness before serving others.
entries.leviticus 16:7: Aaron brought the two goats and presented them before the Lord at the entrance of the meeting tent. It shows that the ritual was done openly before God, not in secret.
entries.leviticus 16:8: Aaron cast lots to decide which goat belonged to the Lord and which was for Azazel, the scapegoat. It shows that God himself directed how sin would be dealt with.
entries.leviticus 16:9: The goat chosen for the Lord was sacrificed as a sin offering. It pictures sin being dealt with through a life given up.
entries.leviticus 16:10: The other goat was kept alive and sent into the wilderness to carry away the people's sin. It pictures sin being removed far away, not just covered.
entries.leviticus 16:11: Aaron sacrificed his own bull to make atonement for himself and his household. It shows that even the high priest needed cleansing before he could help others.
entries.leviticus 16:12: Aaron took burning coals and crushed incense from the altar into the most holy place. It shows careful preparation was required to enter God's presence.
entries.leviticus 16:13: The incense smoke covered the ark so Aaron would not die when he came near God's presence. It shows God's mercy in shielding a sinful man from his holiness.
entries.leviticus 16:14: Aaron sprinkled some of the bull's blood on and in front of the ark's cover seven times. It pictures blood being applied to make atonement before God.
entries.leviticus 16:15: Aaron then killed the people's sin-offering goat and sprinkled its blood in the same way inside the veil. It shows the people's sin was dealt with at the very center of worship.
entries.leviticus 16:16: Aaron cleansed the holy place from the people's uncleanness and wrongdoing, and did the same for the meeting tent among them. It shows sin contaminates even sacred space and needs cleansing.
entries.leviticus 16:17: No one else was allowed in the meeting tent while Aaron made atonement until he came out. It shows atonement was a solemn, solitary work done before God alone.
entries.leviticus 16:18: Aaron then cleansed the altar by putting blood on its horns and around it. It shows that even the place of sacrifice needed to be made clean.
entries.leviticus 16:19: Aaron sprinkled blood on the altar seven times to make it holy and clean from the people's uncleanness. It pictures thorough cleansing by blood.
entries.leviticus 16:20: After cleansing the holy place, the meeting tent, and the altar, Aaron brought the live goat forward. It shows the removal of sin followed the cleansing of sin.
entries.leviticus 16:21: Aaron laid both hands on the live goat, confessed the people's sins over it, and sent it into the wilderness. It pictures the people's guilt being placed on another and carried away.
entries.leviticus 16:22: The goat carried all their sins into a desolate land far from people. It shows sin being taken away completely, not left hanging over them.
entries.leviticus 16:23: Aaron took off the special linen clothes in the meeting tent after finishing the holy place ritual. It shows a clear ending to the sacred work before returning to normal duties.
entries.leviticus 16:24: Aaron washed, put his regular clothes back on, and offered burnt offerings for himself and the people. It shows cleansing and offering continued until sin was fully dealt with.
entries.leviticus 16:25: Aaron burned the fat of the sin offering on the altar. It shows the offering was completed as God had instructed.
entries.leviticus 16:26: The man who led the scapegoat away had to wash his clothes and body before returning to camp. It shows contact with sin, even symbolically, required cleansing.
entries.leviticus 16:27: The bodies of the sin-offering animals whose blood was used were burned outside the camp. It shows sin was taken outside the community, away from God's people.
entries.leviticus 16:28: The man who burned those bodies also had to wash before coming back to camp. It reinforces that handling sin's remains made a person unclean.
entries.leviticus 16:29: God made this an ongoing yearly command: on the tenth day of the seventh month the people were to humble themselves and do no work. It shows a regular day set aside for dealing with sin.
entries.leviticus 16:30: On that day their sin was taken away and they were made clean before the Lord. It shows God provided a real, repeated way for his people to be forgiven.
entries.leviticus 16:31: It was to be a special Sabbath of rest and self-denial, a lasting rule. It teaches that receiving forgiveness calls for humble, unhurried attention to God.
entries.leviticus 16:32: The anointed high priest who succeeded Aaron was to perform this atonement work wearing the holy linen clothes. It shows God set apart a specific person to lead this cleansing.
entries.leviticus 16:33: He was to cleanse the holy place, the meeting tent, the altar, the priests, and all the people. It shows atonement reached every part of the community's life.
entries.leviticus 16:34: This yearly atonement was a lasting command, and Moses did exactly as the Lord ordered. It shows God's people were to keep obeying his instructions for forgiveness year after year.
entries.leviticus 18:1: God is speaking directly to Moses, the leader of the Israelites. This sets up the instructions that follow as coming from God himself.
entries.leviticus 18:2: God reminds the people that he is their God, so what he says carries authority over their lives. The reader is meant to hear this as a call to take God's words personally.
entries.leviticus 18:3: God tells the Israelites not to copy the sexual and social customs of Egypt, where they used to live, or of Canaan, where they are going. Your past and your surroundings should not decide how you live.
entries.leviticus 18:4: Instead of following other cultures, the people are to follow God's own rules and live by them. God's standards, not the crowd's, are to guide the reader's choices.
entries.leviticus 18:5: God says that keeping his rules leads to life for the person who does them. Obedience is presented as the path to living well, not as a burden.
entries.leviticus 18:6: God forbids sexual relations with close relatives. Family relationships are to be kept pure and protected, not turned into sexual ones.
entries.leviticus 18:7: Having sex with your father or mother is strictly forbidden. This protects the most basic family bond from being violated.
entries.leviticus 18:8: A man may not have sex with his father's wife, since she belongs to his father. This guards the honor of the father's marriage.
entries.leviticus 18:9: Sex with a sister, whether from the same father or mother and wherever she was born, is forbidden. Brothers and sisters are to remain family, not sexual partners.
entries.leviticus 18:10: Sex with a granddaughter is forbidden because she is part of your own flesh and blood. Close family lines are not to be crossed sexually.
entries.leviticus 18:11: A daughter born to your father's wife is your sister, so sex with her is forbidden. The text treats her as full family regardless of details.
entries.leviticus 18:12: Sex with your father's sister, your aunt, is forbidden because she is a close relative. Extended family relationships are also to be protected.
entries.leviticus 18:13: Sex with your mother's sister, also an aunt, is forbidden for the same reason. The command covers relatives on both sides of the family.
entries.leviticus 18:14: A man may not have sex with his uncle's wife, since she is family. This protects the marriage of a relative.
entries.leviticus 18:15: Sex with your daughter-in-law is forbidden because she is your son's wife. A father is to honor his son's marriage, not take it.
entries.leviticus 18:16: Sex with your brother's wife is forbidden because she belongs to your brother. This protects the marriage bond between siblings' spouses.
entries.leviticus 18:17: A man may not marry a woman and also her daughter or granddaughter, because they are one family. This prevents shameful confusion within a household.
entries.leviticus 18:18: A man may not marry two sisters at the same time, which would set them against each other. This protects family peace and the dignity of each wife.
entries.leviticus 18:19: Sex is forbidden during a woman's monthly period, when she is ritually unclean. The reader is taught to respect this boundary in intimate life.
entries.leviticus 18:20: Sex with a neighbor's wife is forbidden because it makes you unclean and betrays trust. This protects other people's marriages.
entries.leviticus 18:21: God forbids giving children as burnt offerings to the god Molech and forbids dishonoring his name. Children are to be protected, and God's name is to be treated as holy.
entries.leviticus 18:22: Sex between men is forbidden and called disgusting in this text. The reader is expected to treat this as outside God's design for sexual conduct.
entries.leviticus 18:23: Sex with an animal is forbidden for both men and women and is called unnatural. This sets a clear boundary around human sexuality.
entries.leviticus 18:24: God warns the people not to defile themselves with any of these practices, because the nations being driven out did them. The reader is warned not to follow the same pattern.
entries.leviticus 18:25: The land itself became polluted by these sins, so God is punishing it and removing its inhabitants. Wrongdoing is shown to have real consequences for a whole society.
entries.leviticus 18:26: Both Israelites and foreigners living among them must keep God's rules and avoid these practices. God's standards apply to everyone in the community, not just insiders.
entries.leviticus 18:27: The previous inhabitants of the land did these disgusting things, and that is why the land became unclean. The reader sees that a society's sins can corrupt the place it lives.
entries.leviticus 18:28: If the Israelites defile the land the same way, it will throw them out just as it threw out the nations before them. The warning is that no one is exempt from the consequences.
entries.leviticus 18:29: Anyone who does these disgusting things will be cut off from their people. The text presents this as a serious penalty, showing how strongly God views these acts.
entries.leviticus 18:30: God closes by telling the people to keep his orders so they won't fall into the same defiling practices as those before them. The reader is called to stay loyal to God and avoid inherited patterns of sin.
entries.leviticus 13:41: Losing hair at the front of the head is just normal baldness, not a sickness, so the person is still considered clean. This means you don't need to worry that ordinary baldness makes you unfit.
entries.leviticus 13:42: But if a reddish-white sore appears on a bald head or forehead, that is a serious skin disease breaking out. It means a real problem can show up even where there is no hair, so it should be checked.
entries.leviticus 13:43: When the priest examines it and the sore on the bald area looks reddish-white like a serious skin disease, he must treat it as such. The point is that the priest carefully inspects before deciding anything.
entries.leviticus 13:44: The priest must declare that person unclean, because the disease is on his head. This means the priest's verdict mattered, and the person had to be treated as unclean for everyone's safety.
entries.leviticus 13:45: A person with this disease had to show signs of mourning, leave his hair loose, cover his mouth, and shout that he was unclean. This means he had to warn others to stay away and live openly as someone in sorrow.
entries.leviticus 13:46: As long as the disease lasted, the person had to live alone outside the camp. This means he was separated from the community to protect others from infection.
entries.leviticus 13:47: The same rules applied to clothing made of wool or linen that showed signs of disease. This means the concern for uncleanness wasn't only about people but also about their belongings.
entries.leviticus 13:48: The rules covered anything woven from linen or wool, and also leather and items made from skin. This means even everyday materials had to be checked for spreading damage.
entries.leviticus 13:49: If reddish or greenish marks appeared on cloth or leather, it was treated as a serious spreading disease, and the priest had to inspect it. This means suspicious spots on belongings were taken seriously, not ignored.
entries.leviticus 13:50: After the priest looked at the marked item, it was set aside for seven days. This means they waited to see whether the problem would spread before deciding what to do.
entries.leviticus 13:51: On the seventh day the priest checked again, and if the mark had spread, the item was declared unclean as a damaging disease. This means spreading damage showed the problem was serious.
entries.leviticus 13:52: The clothing or leather with the spreading disease had to be burned up completely. This means the item was destroyed so the contamination could not continue.
entries.leviticus 13:53: But if the priest saw that the mark had not spread on the cloth or leather, he did not condemn it yet. This means not every spot meant destruction; they checked carefully first.
entries.leviticus 13:54: The priest then ordered the item to be washed and set aside for another seven days. This means they gave it a fair chance to be cleaned before deciding.
entries.leviticus 13:55: If the mark stayed the same color and had not spread even after washing, the item still had to be burned, because the damage was working through it. This means washing alone doesn't fix a problem that has gotten into the material.
entries.leviticus 13:56: If the mark faded after washing, the priest had that spot cut out of the cloth or leather. This means removing the damaged part could save the rest of the item.
entries.leviticus 13:57: If the mark came back on the clothing or leather, it was a disease breaking out again, and the item had to be burned. This means a problem that keeps returning is serious and must be dealt with fully.
entries.leviticus 13:58: If the item was washed and the mark was gone, it was washed once more and then counted clean. This means careful cleaning could restore something that had been in doubt.
entries.leviticus 13:59: This sums up the rules for judging whether clothing or leather with a mark was clean or unclean. This means God gave clear guidelines so the priests could make fair and consistent decisions.
entries.leviticus 14:1: God is speaking directly to Moses, giving him instructions to pass on to the people. This shows that what follows is God's own direction, not just human custom.
entries.leviticus 14:2: This begins the rules for what happens when a person with a serious skin disease is healed and wants to be declared clean again. The person goes to the priest, who serves as the one who confirms the healing.
entries.leviticus 14:3: The priest goes outside the camp to examine the person, since the sick person had been kept away from the community. If the disease is clearly gone, the healing is confirmed.
entries.leviticus 14:4: The priest orders certain items for the cleansing ceremony: two live birds, cedar wood, red thread, and a plant called hyssop. These were common materials used in rituals of cleansing.
entries.leviticus 14:5: One bird is killed in a clay pot over fresh running water. The running water likely stands for life and purity in the ceremony.
entries.leviticus 14:6: The living bird, along with the wood, thread, and hyssop, is dipped into the dead bird's blood mixed with water. The living bird represents the person being restored to life and community.
entries.leviticus 14:7: The priest sprinkles the person seven times, declares them clean, and releases the living bird into the open field. The freed bird pictures the person being set free from their isolation.
entries.leviticus 14:8: The healed person washes their clothes, shaves, and bathes, then may return to the camp but must stay outside their own tent for seven days. Cleansing was gradual, showing that full restoration took time.
entries.leviticus 14:9: On the seventh day the person shaves off all hair and washes again. Removing all hair made sure nothing unclean remained, and then they were fully clean.
entries.leviticus 14:10: On the eighth day the person brings animals and grain offerings for the formal ceremony. These were costly gifts given to complete the cleansing before God.
entries.leviticus 14:11: The priest presents the person and their offerings at the entrance of the meeting tent, the place of worship. This brings the healed person back before God and the community.
entries.leviticus 14:12: The priest offers one male lamb and the oil as a special offering waved before the Lord. The waving was a way of dedicating the gift to God.
entries.leviticus 14:13: The lamb is killed in the same holy place where sin and burnt offerings were made. The offering is treated as very holy and belongs to the priest.
entries.leviticus 14:14: Some of the blood is put on the person's right ear, right thumb, and right big toe. This marked the person's hearing, working, and walking as set apart for God.
entries.leviticus 14:15: The priest pours some of the oil into his own left hand. The oil is used alongside the blood in the cleansing ritual.
entries.leviticus 14:16: The priest dips his right finger in the oil and sprinkles it seven times before the Lord. The number seven signals completeness in the cleansing.
entries.leviticus 14:17: More oil is placed on the same spots as the blood: ear, thumb, and toe. The oil goes over the blood, showing cleansing layered on top of the offering.
entries.leviticus 14:18: The remaining oil is poured on the person's head, and the priest makes them right with God. The oil on the head marks the person as restored and blessed.
entries.leviticus 14:19: The priest then offers the sin offering to deal with the person's uncleanness, followed by the burnt offering. Both offerings were needed to fully restore the person before God.
entries.leviticus 14:20: The burnt offering and grain offering are burned on the altar, and the priest makes the person clean. The ceremony ends with the person fully restored.
entries.leviticus 14:21: A poor person who cannot afford the full set may bring a smaller offering. God made room for people of little means to be cleansed too.
entries.leviticus 14:22: Instead of larger animals, the poor person may bring two doves or pigeons, one for each offering. This shows God's care for those who cannot pay full price.
entries.leviticus 14:23: On the eighth day the person brings these offerings to the priest at the meeting tent. The timing and place are the same as for the wealthier person.
entries.leviticus 14:24: The priest takes the lamb and the oil and waves them before the Lord. This dedicates the gifts to God on behalf of the poor person.
entries.leviticus 14:25: The lamb is killed and its blood is put on the person's right ear, thumb, and big toe, just as in the fuller ceremony. The poor person receives the same marking as anyone else.
entries.leviticus 14:26: The priest pours some oil into his left hand. The oil ritual continues exactly as before.
entries.leviticus 14:27: The priest sprinkles oil with his right finger seven times before the Lord. This repeats the sign of complete cleansing.
entries.leviticus 14:28: Oil is placed on the ear, thumb, and toe, right where the blood was put. The same spots are marked with both blood and oil.
entries.leviticus 14:29: The rest of the oil goes on the person's head to make them right with God. The poor person's cleansing is just as complete as the rich person's.
entries.leviticus 14:30: The priest offers one of the doves or pigeons the person was able to bring. The offering matches what the person can afford.
entries.leviticus 14:31: One bird is the sin offering and the other the burnt offering, along with the grain offering. The priest then makes the person clean before the Lord.
entries.leviticus 14:32: This sums up the rules for a person with skin disease who is too poor to afford the usual offerings. God provided a way for everyone to be restored.
entries.leviticus 14:33: God now speaks to both Moses and Aaron, since Aaron and the priests will carry out these rules. The instructions that follow are for life in the promised land.
entries.leviticus 14:34: God says that when the people enter Canaan, he may allow a spreading mildew-like condition to appear in a house. Even problems in buildings are under God's notice.
entries.leviticus 14:35: The owner of the house reports the problem to the priest, describing it as something like a skin disease in the house. The priest is the one who inspects it.
entries.leviticus 14:36: Before the priest goes in, everything is taken out of the house so the belongings don't become unclean. The inspection is done carefully to limit the damage.
entries.leviticus 14:37: If the priest sees green or red hollow spots that seem to go deeper than the wall's surface, the problem is serious. These signs showed the house was contaminated.
entries.leviticus 14:38: The priest leaves and shuts up the house for seven days. A waiting period was used to see whether the problem would spread.
entries.leviticus 14:39: The priest returns on the seventh day and checks whether the spots have grown. Spreading marks meant the problem was active and needed action.
entries.leviticus 14:40: If the marks have spread, the priest orders the affected stones removed and thrown in an unclean place outside town. The contaminated parts had to be taken out to protect the rest.
entries.leviticus 14:41: The inside of the house is scraped all around, and the scraped dust is dumped outside town in an unclean place. This removed any remaining contamination from the walls.
entries.leviticus 14:42: New stones are put in place of the old ones, and the house is re-plastered. The house is repaired and made whole again.
entries.leviticus 14:43: If the marks come back after the stones were removed and the house re-plastered, the problem is still active. A return of the disease meant the repair had failed.
entries.leviticus 14:44: The priest then declares the house unclean because the mark is spreading and cannot be cured. The whole house is treated as contaminated.
entries.leviticus 14:45: The house must be torn down, and its stones, wood, and plaster are carried outside town to an unclean place. A house that could not be cleansed had to be destroyed.
entries.leviticus 14:46: Anyone who goes into the house while it is shut up becomes unclean until evening. Contact with the contaminated house made a person ritually unclean for the day.
entries.leviticus 14:47: Anyone who sleeps or eats in the house must wash their clothes. Even indirect contact with the house required cleansing.
entries.leviticus 14:48: If the priest sees that the marks have not spread after the house was re-plastered, he declares it clean because the problem is gone. The house is restored to normal use.
entries.leviticus 14:49: To cleanse the house, the priest takes two birds, cedar wood, red thread, and hyssop, the same items used for a person. The house receives a ceremony like the one for a healed person.
entries.leviticus 14:50: One bird is killed over fresh running water in a clay pot. This mirrors the ritual used for cleansing a person.
entries.leviticus 14:51: The living bird, wood, thread, and hyssop are dipped in the blood and water, and the house is sprinkled seven times. The sprinkling marks the house as cleansed.
entries.leviticus 14:52: The priest uses the bird, water, wood, thread, and hyssop to make the house right with God. The same elements that cleansed a person now cleanse the building.
entries.leviticus 14:53: The living bird is released into the open field, and the house is declared clean. The freed bird pictures the contamination being carried away.
entries.leviticus 14:54: This begins a summary of all the rules about skin disease and mildew. The laws covered both people and houses.
entries.leviticus 14:55: The rules apply to skin disease on people and to mildew or contamination in clothing and houses. God's concern for cleanliness reached every part of daily life.
entries.leviticus 14:56: The rules also cover swellings, rashes, and bright spots on the skin. These were the various signs the priest had to examine.
entries.leviticus 14:57: These laws taught the people how to tell what was unclean and what was clean. Knowing the difference helped them live safely and worship God properly.
entries.leviticus 19:1: God begins speaking to Moses to give him instructions for the people. This shows that what follows comes directly from God, not from human opinion.
entries.leviticus 19:2: God tells the whole community to be holy, meaning set apart and morally pure, because he himself is holy. The reader is called to reflect God's character in everyday life.
entries.leviticus 19:3: Each person must honor their mother and father and observe God's rest days. Respecting parents and keeping God's appointed times are basic ways to honor God himself.
entries.leviticus 19:4: The people must not chase after idols or make metal images of gods. Loyalty to the one true God means rejecting anything we treat as a substitute for him.
entries.leviticus 19:5: When someone brings a peace offering to God, they must follow his instructions for it. Worship is to be done God's way, not on our own terms.
entries.leviticus 19:6: The offering meat must be eaten the same day or the next, and anything left by the third day must be burned. This teaches careful, reverent handling of what is dedicated to God.
entries.leviticus 19:7: Eating the offering on the third day is treated as disgusting and unacceptable to God. Treating holy things carelessly dishonors the one who gave them.
entries.leviticus 19:8: Anyone who eats it anyway carries guilt for treating God's holy offering with contempt and is cut off from the community. Disrespect for what is holy has serious consequences.
entries.leviticus 19:9: When harvesting grain, farmers must not strip the edges of the field or pick up what falls. God builds generosity into ordinary work by leaving room for others.
entries.leviticus 19:10: Growers must leave leftover grapes and fallen fruit for the poor and for foreigners. Those with resources are expected to provide for those without, remembering God's command.
entries.leviticus 19:11: People must not steal, lie, or deceive one another. Honesty and respect for others' property are basic requirements of life together.
entries.leviticus 19:12: Swearing a false oath in God's name dishonors him. Telling the truth matters because it reflects the God we claim to serve.
entries.leviticus 19:13: Do not oppress or rob your neighbor, and pay workers their wages promptly. Fair treatment of employees and neighbors is a matter of justice before God.
entries.leviticus 19:14: Do not curse someone who cannot hear or place a stumbling block before a blind person. Taking advantage of someone's weakness is wrong, and God is to be feared.
entries.leviticus 19:15: Judges must not favor the poor or the powerful but must judge fairly. Justice means treating each person rightly regardless of status.
entries.leviticus 19:16: Do not spread false rumors among your people or endanger a neighbor by false testimony. Words can harm, and God holds people accountable for how they use them.
entries.leviticus 19:17: Do not nurse hatred toward your fellow Israelite; instead confront them so they can stop doing wrong. Honest correction is better than silent resentment.
entries.leviticus 19:18: Do not seek revenge or hold grudges, but love your neighbor as you love yourself. This is the heart of how God's people are to treat one another.
entries.leviticus 19:19: God's people are to keep his laws, including not mixing kinds of animals, seed, or cloth. These rules marked Israel as distinct and reminded them to keep God's order.
entries.leviticus 19:20: A man who sleeps with a servant woman promised to another man must be investigated, but they are not executed because she was not free. The case is handled with justice suited to the situation.
entries.leviticus 19:21: The man must bring a guilt offering, a male sheep, to the entrance of the meeting tent. Wrongdoing requires a concrete act of making things right before God.
entries.leviticus 19:22: The priest makes atonement for him with the offering, and his sin is forgiven. God provides a way for guilt to be removed through the offering he appointed.
entries.leviticus 19:23: When the people plant fruit trees in the land, they must treat the fruit as uncircumcised and not eat it for three years. New growth is set apart and requires patient waiting.
entries.leviticus 19:24: In the fourth year all the fruit is holy, given as praise to the Lord. The first full harvest is dedicated to God in gratitude.
entries.leviticus 19:25: From the fifth year on, the fruit may be eaten, and God promises it will increase. Obedience to God's timing brings blessing and provision.
entries.leviticus 19:26: Do not eat meat with its blood still in it, and do not practice fortune-telling or seek omens. God's people are to avoid pagan practices and honor the sacredness of blood.
entries.leviticus 19:27: The people must not cut the hair at the sides of their heads or the edges of their beard. This was a visible way to reject the mourning customs of surrounding nations.
entries.leviticus 19:28: Do not cut your bodies for the dead or tattoo marks on yourselves. God's people are not to adopt the self-harming rituals of other religions.
entries.leviticus 19:29: Do not degrade your daughter by making her a prostitute, which would fill the land with shame. Parents are to protect their children's dignity and the community's moral health.
entries.leviticus 19:30: Keep God's Sabbaths and show reverence for his holy place. Rest and worship are to be treated with serious respect.
entries.leviticus 19:31: Do not consult mediums or spiritists or become unclean through them. God's people must rely on him, not on occult practices.
entries.leviticus 19:32: Stand up in the presence of the elderly and honor the aged, fearing God. Respect for older people is a practical expression of reverence for God.
entries.leviticus 19:33: Do not mistreat a foreigner living among you. How a community treats outsiders reveals its character.
entries.leviticus 19:34: Treat the foreigner like a native and love them as yourself, remembering Israel's own experience as foreigners in Egypt. Compassion for outsiders flows from remembering one's own past.
entries.leviticus 19:35: Do not use dishonest standards in measuring length, weight, or quantity. Fairness in business is required of God's people.
entries.leviticus 19:36: Use honest scales, weights, and measures, because God rescued Israel from Egypt. Honest dealings reflect gratitude to the God who delivered them.
entries.leviticus 19:37: Keep all of God's statutes and ordinances and put them into practice. Obedience is the expected response to the God who commands.
entries.leviticus 21:1: God tells Moses to instruct the priests that they must not touch or handle a dead body among their people, because doing so would make them ritually unclean. This taught the priests that their role required special purity.
entries.leviticus 21:2: An exception was allowed for the closest family members: a priest could mourn and handle the body of his mother, father, son, daughter, or brother. God made room for genuine grief within the strict rules.
entries.leviticus 21:3: A priest could also mourn for an unmarried sister who had no husband, since she was still counted as his close family. The allowance was limited to this specific case.
entries.leviticus 21:4: A leading man among the priests was not to make himself unclean in a way that would bring disgrace on himself. Those in leadership carried a higher standard because their conduct reflected on God.
entries.leviticus 21:5: Priests were forbidden to shave their heads, trim their beards, or cut their bodies as signs of mourning for the dead, which were common pagan practices. God wanted his priests to be set apart from the surrounding customs.
entries.leviticus 21:6: The priests had to be holy to God and treat his name as sacred, because they presented the offerings and the holy bread. Their job was sacred, so their lives had to match it.
entries.leviticus 21:7: A priest could not marry a prostitute, a woman of loose morals, or a divorced woman, because he was holy to his God. His marriage was expected to reflect the purity of his calling.
entries.leviticus 21:8: The people were to treat the priest as holy because he offered the bread of their God, and God himself is holy. Respect for the priest was really respect for the God he served.
entries.leviticus 21:9: If a priest's daughter disgraced herself through loose behavior and shamed her father, she was to be burned with fire. The punishment was severe because the priest's family was held to a higher standard.
entries.leviticus 21:10: The high priest, who had been anointed with holy oil and wore the holy robes, was not to let his hair hang loose or tear his clothes in mourning. His position required him to stay composed and set apart even in grief.
entries.leviticus 21:11: The high priest was not allowed to go near any dead body at all, not even his own father or mother. His duty to God's holy place came before even family mourning.
entries.leviticus 21:12: He was not to leave the holy place or treat it as ordinary, because the anointing oil of his God was on him. His whole life was dedicated to God's service without interruption.
entries.leviticus 21:13: The high priest was to marry a woman who had never had sexual relations with a man. This kept his marriage pure and fitting for his sacred role.
entries.leviticus 21:14: A priest could not marry a widow, a divorced woman, or a woman of loose behavior, but was to choose a virgin from among his own people. His family life was to be a picture of holiness.
entries.leviticus 21:15: A priest was not to have children through improper unions that would defile his family line, because God had set him apart as holy. His household was to reflect his calling.
entries.leviticus 21:16: This verse simply introduces the next instruction, showing that God continued speaking to Moses. It marks a new section of the rules for priests.
entries.leviticus 21:17: God tells Aaron that any descendant of his who had a physical defect was not to come near to offer the bread of his God. The requirement was about ceremonial fitness, not the person's worth.
entries.leviticus 21:18: Men with defects such as blindness, lameness, a disfigured nose, or an abnormal growth were not to serve at the altar. These standards set the priests apart as whole and unblemished for their sacred duties.
entries.leviticus 21:19: A man with a broken foot or hand was also excluded from serving at the altar. The rule applied to any visible physical flaw.
entries.leviticus 21:20: The list continues with hunchbacks, dwarfs, those with eye defects, skin disease, or damaged sexual organs, all barred from altar service. Physical wholeness was required for this ceremonial role.
entries.leviticus 21:21: No descendant of Aaron with any physical defect could bring the Lord's offerings, because he was considered unfit for that service. The restriction was about the office, not the person's value before God.
entries.leviticus 21:22: Even a priest with a defect could still eat the holy and most holy food of God. He was excluded from the altar but not cut off from God's provision.
entries.leviticus 21:23: Such a priest could not go behind the curtain or approach the altar, so that he would not treat God's holy places as common. God had made those places holy, and that had to be respected.
entries.leviticus 21:24: Moses passed these instructions on to Aaron, his sons, and all the Israelites. The rules were meant for everyone to hear and follow, not just the priests.
entries.leviticus 20:1: God is speaking to Moses here. This line simply introduces the instructions that follow, showing they come from God himself.
entries.leviticus 20:2: God tells Israel that anyone, native or foreigner, who gives their child to the false god Molech must be put to death by the community. The point for the reader is that child sacrifice was treated as a most serious evil.
entries.leviticus 20:3: God says he himself will oppose that man and cut him off from his people, because he defiled God's holy place and treated God's name as common. It means such sin brings both community judgment and God's personal rejection.
entries.leviticus 20:4: If the people ignore the crime and fail to act, God holds them responsible too. The reader learns that quietly tolerating terrible evil is not neutral.
entries.leviticus 20:5: God says he will set himself against that man and his family, and against everyone who joins him in the same evil. It means sin like this spreads, and God opposes the whole group that follows it.
entries.leviticus 20:6: God will oppose anyone who turns to mediums and fortune-tellers and joins in their practices. The reader is warned that seeking spiritual power outside God puts a person outside God's people.
entries.leviticus 20:7: God calls his people to set themselves apart and live clean lives, because he is the Lord their God. It means holiness is a response to who God is.
entries.leviticus 20:8: God tells them to obey his rules, reminding them that he is the one who makes them holy. The reader learns that obedience matters, and that God himself is the source of a holy life.
entries.leviticus 20:9: Anyone who curses his father or mother was to be put to death, and the guilt was his own. It shows how seriously God took respect for parents.
entries.leviticus 20:10: Both the man and the woman caught in adultery were to be put to death. The reader sees that breaking a marriage vow was treated as a capital offense in Israel.
entries.leviticus 20:11: Sex with one's father's wife was a shame on the father, and both parties were to die. The guilt rested on them, showing God's seriousness about sexual boundaries within a family.
entries.leviticus 20:12: Sex between a man and his son's wife was called unnatural, and both were to be put to death. It marks this as a grave violation of family order.
entries.leviticus 20:13: Sex between two men is called a disgusting thing here, and both were to be put to death. The text presents this as a serious offense under Israel's law.
entries.leviticus 20:14: Marrying both a woman and her mother was called shameful, and all three were to be burned so the shame would be removed from the community. It shows how strongly God wanted such practices kept out of Israel.
entries.leviticus 20:15: A man who had sex with an animal was to be put to death, and the animal destroyed. The reader sees this act treated as a serious wrong with severe consequences.
entries.leviticus 20:16: A woman who did the same with an animal was to be put to death along with the animal. The guilt was counted as theirs.
entries.leviticus 20:17: Sex between a brother and sister was called shameful, and they were to be cut off from their people. The man carried his guilt, showing God's concern for purity within the family.
entries.leviticus 20:18: Sex during a woman's monthly bleeding was forbidden, and both were to be cut off from the people. It reflects the Old Testament concern with ritual uncleanness.
entries.leviticus 20:19: Sex with a parent's sister was forbidden because she is a close relative, and the guilt would rest on them. It shows God's boundaries around close family relationships.
entries.leviticus 20:20: Sex with a father's brother's wife was a shame on the uncle, and the couple would have no children. The reader sees both guilt and a lasting consequence.
entries.leviticus 20:21: Taking a brother's wife was called unclean and a shame on the brother, and they would have no children. It shows the seriousness of violating family bonds.
entries.leviticus 20:22: God tells them to obey his rules so the land he is giving them will not throw them out. It means obedience was tied to staying safely in the land.
entries.leviticus 20:23: God warns them not to follow the customs of the nations he is driving out, because those practices made him reject those peoples. The reader learns that copying surrounding cultures can bring God's judgment.
entries.leviticus 20:24: God promises them the land of those nations as their own inheritance, a land of plenty, and reminds them he has set them apart. It means their distinct identity came from God's gift and choice.
entries.leviticus 20:25: God tells them to distinguish clean animals and birds from unclean ones and not to defile themselves with forbidden creatures. It shows that everyday choices about food were part of being set apart for God.
entries.leviticus 20:26: God says they must be holy to him because he is holy and has separated them from other nations to be his people. The reader learns that belonging to God means living differently.
entries.leviticus 20:27: Anyone practicing as a medium or fortune-teller was to be put to death by stoning, with the guilt on them. It shows how completely Israel was to reject occult practices.
entries.leviticus 22:1: This line simply introduces God speaking to Moses. It reminds the reader that what follows is presented as God's own instruction, not Moses' idea.
entries.leviticus 22:2: God tells the priests to treat the sacred offerings with respect and not handle them carelessly. For the reader, it means that things set apart for God should be treated as special, not ordinary.
entries.leviticus 22:3: Any priest who was ritually unclean yet came near the sacred offerings would be removed from priestly service. It teaches that approaching holy things requires being in the right state, not just going through the motions.
entries.leviticus 22:4: A priest with a skin disease or bodily discharge, or who had touched a dead body or other unclean thing, could not eat the sacred food until he was clean again. The point is that uncleanness, even accidental, had to be dealt with before sharing in holy things.
entries.leviticus 22:5: This continues the list: touching an unclean creature or being made unclean by another person also made a priest unclean. It shows how seriously the text treats anything that could contaminate someone serving at the sanctuary.
entries.leviticus 22:6: Anyone made unclean this way stayed unclean until evening and had to wash before eating the sacred food. For the reader, cleansing was required before coming back to holy things.
entries.leviticus 22:7: Once the sun set, the person was clean again and could eat the sacred food, since it was the priests' rightful share. It shows that uncleanness was temporary and could be resolved.
entries.leviticus 22:8: Priests were not to eat meat from animals that died naturally or were killed by wild beasts, because that would make them unclean. Even those who handled holy food had to follow the same basic food rules as everyone else.
entries.leviticus 22:9: The priests were to guard what God had entrusted to them, or they would bear guilt and could die for treating holy things as ordinary. It stresses that responsibility comes with privilege.
entries.leviticus 22:10: People outside the priestly family—guests or hired workers—were not allowed to eat the sacred food. The reader learns that holy offerings were reserved for those specifically entitled to them.
entries.leviticus 22:11: A slave bought with the priest's money, or a servant born in his household, could eat the sacred food. So the rule was about belonging to the priest's household, not about bloodline alone.
entries.leviticus 22:12: If a priest's daughter married someone outside the priestly family, she could no longer eat the sacred offerings. Her share in that holy food depended on her connection to the priestly household.
entries.leviticus 22:13: If that daughter became a widow or was divorced and had no children, and returned to her father's house, she could eat her father's food again. The text shows care for a woman in a vulnerable position while keeping the holy food restricted to the household.
entries.leviticus 22:14: If someone ate sacred food by mistake, they had to repay it plus a fifth. The reader sees that even unintentional misuse of holy things required making it right, with extra compensation.
entries.leviticus 22:15: The priests were not to let the people's holy offerings become ordinary or common. It means holy things were to be protected from misuse by those in charge.
entries.leviticus 22:16: If the priests let people eat holy offerings wrongly, guilt would fall on them. The reader learns that leaders are accountable for how holy things are handled, not just the people who bring them.
entries.leviticus 22:17: This again marks a new section of God's words to Moses. It signals that the next instructions are also presented as coming from God.
entries.leviticus 22:18: These rules applied to Israelites and to foreigners living among them who brought a burnt offering, whether promised by oath or given freely. Everyone bringing an offering had to follow the same standards.
entries.leviticus 22:19: For an offering to be accepted, it had to be a male animal without any defect, from the cattle, sheep, or goats. The reader learns that what was given to God was to be the best, not the leftovers.
entries.leviticus 22:20: An animal with any defect could not be offered, because it would not be accepted. The point is that God was not to be given what was damaged or second-rate.
entries.leviticus 22:21: The same standard applied to peace offerings, whether made to fulfill a vow or given freely: the animal had to be free of defect or damage to be accepted. It reinforces that God deserves unblemished gifts.
entries.leviticus 22:22: Blind, injured, diseased, or blemished animals could not be burned on the altar to the Lord. The reader sees that worship was not a place to dump worthless animals.
entries.leviticus 22:23: An animal with unusual proportions could be given as a freewill offering but not to fulfill a vow. So there was some flexibility for voluntary gifts, but promised offerings had to meet the full standard.
entries.leviticus 22:24: Animals with damaged or removed sexual organs could not be offered to the Lord, and such practices were forbidden anywhere in the land. The text treats certain mutilations as incompatible with what is offered to God.
entries.leviticus 22:25: Such defective animals could not be accepted even from foreigners as an offering to God, because they were not acceptable. The standard for offerings did not change based on who brought them.
entries.leviticus 22:26: This line introduces another set of instructions from God to Moses. It marks a fresh topic within the same speech.
entries.leviticus 22:27: A newborn ox, sheep, or goat had to stay with its mother for seven days and could be offered from the eighth day. The reader sees a concern for the animal's early life before it could be used in worship.
entries.leviticus 22:28: A cow or sheep was not to be killed on the same day as its young. This shows a measure of mercy even within the sacrificial system.
entries.leviticus 22:29: When giving a thank offering to the Lord, it had to be done in the proper way so it would be accepted. The reader learns that even grateful worship was to follow God's instructions, not personal preference.
entries.leviticus 22:30: The thank offering had to be eaten the same day, with nothing left until morning. It taught promptness and prevented the sacred meal from becoming ordinary leftover food.
entries.leviticus 22:31: The people were to keep God's commands and actually do them, because he is the Lord. For the reader, hearing the rules is not enough; they are meant to be obeyed.
entries.leviticus 22:32: The people were not to treat God's name as common but to honor it as holy among them. It means God's reputation and character should be respected in how his people live.
entries.leviticus 22:33: God reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt to be their God. The reader sees that all these rules rest on the fact that God had rescued them and claimed them as his own.
entries.leviticus 23:1: God begins speaking to Moses to give him instructions for the people. This shows that what follows comes directly from God, not from human ideas.
entries.leviticus 23:2: God tells Israel that these appointed festivals are his own special occasions, set apart for gathering to worship him. The reader should see that worship and rest are things God himself schedules and calls his own.
entries.leviticus 23:3: Six days are for ordinary work, but the seventh is a day of complete rest and worship, no matter where you live. This means God builds regular rest into life, and the reader is invited to treat one day a week as set apart for him.
entries.leviticus 23:4: These festivals are to be celebrated at their proper, fixed times each year. The point is that worship has a rhythm, and God's people are to keep it faithfully.
entries.leviticus 23:5: The Passover is kept on the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month. It recalls God's rescue of Israel, and the reader should see it as a yearly reminder of God's saving help.
entries.leviticus 23:6: The very next day begins the Feast of Unleavened Bread, when only bread without yeast is eaten for a week. This marks a distinct season of remembering and obedience right after Passover.
entries.leviticus 23:7: The first day of that feast is a holy gathering where no ordinary field work is done. Rest and worship come first on this special day.
entries.leviticus 23:8: Each of the seven days has an offering burned to the Lord, and the seventh day closes with another holy gathering and no field work. The week is framed by worship at both ends.
entries.leviticus 23:9: God again speaks to Moses to introduce the next set of instructions. This signals a new topic in the same ongoing conversation.
entries.leviticus 23:10: Once Israel is settled in the land and harvests grain, they are to bring the first portion of the harvest to the priest. The reader learns that the first and best of what God gives is to be handed back to him.
entries.leviticus 23:11: The priest lifts the grain before the Lord so the people may be accepted by him, on the day after the Sabbath. This act shows dependence on God for the harvest and his favor.
entries.leviticus 23:12: Along with the grain, a perfect one-year-old male lamb is offered as a burned offering. The offering is to be without defect, showing that God deserves the best.
entries.leviticus 23:13: A grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil and a drink offering of wine accompany the lamb, all as a pleasing offering to the Lord. The reader sees that worship involves giving generously and carefully.
entries.leviticus 23:14: No bread, roasted grain, or fresh grain may be eaten until this offering has been given to God. This teaches that God comes first, before the people enjoy what he has provided, and the rule is to last for all generations.
