entries.leviticus 23:15: Starting from the day after the Sabbath when the grain offering was brought, they are to count seven full weeks. This counting builds expectation toward the next festival.
entries.leviticus 23:16: Counting fifty days brings them to the day after the seventh Sabbath, when a new grain offering is presented to the Lord. This marks a second harvest festival, later called the Feast of Weeks.
entries.leviticus 23:17: From their homes they bring two loaves made from fine flour and baked with yeast, lifted before the Lord as firstfruits. Unlike other offerings, these loaves contain yeast, showing that ordinary daily bread is also brought before God.
entries.leviticus 23:18: With the bread they offer seven perfect lambs, one ox, and two rams as a burned offering, along with grain and drink offerings, all pleasing to the Lord. It is a large, joyful act of worship.
entries.leviticus 23:19: They also bring one male goat as a sin offering and two one-year-old male lambs as peace offerings. This shows that worship includes both dealing with sin and celebrating peace with God.
entries.leviticus 23:20: The priest lifts the two lambs together with the firstfruit bread before the Lord, and these become holy, belonging to the priest. The reader sees that those who lead worship are provided for from the offerings.
entries.leviticus 23:21: That same day is declared a holy gathering with no field work, a permanent rule for all generations wherever they live. Rest and worship are required, not optional.
entries.leviticus 23:22: When harvesting, they must not strip the edges of the field or pick up fallen grain; that is left for the poor and for foreigners. The reader learns that generosity to the needy is built into God's commands, and he identifies himself as their God.
entries.leviticus 23:23: God speaks to Moses once more to begin another set of instructions. This marks a fresh section in the same message.
entries.leviticus 23:24: The first day of the seventh month is a day of rest and remembrance, announced by horn blasts and a holy gathering. The reader sees a special yearly call to stop, remember God, and worship together.
entries.leviticus 23:25: No field work is done that day, and an offering by fire is brought to the Lord. The day is set apart for God alone.
entries.leviticus 23:26: God again addresses Moses, introducing the next command. This keeps the flow of instructions clear and orderly.
entries.leviticus 23:27: The tenth day of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement, a holy day when the people deny themselves and bring an offering by fire to the Lord. The reader sees a solemn yearly day for dealing with sin and humbling oneself before God.
entries.leviticus 23:28: No work at all is done that day, because it is the day sin is dealt with to make the people clean before the Lord. The seriousness of the day shows how much being right with God matters.
entries.leviticus 23:29: Anyone who does not humble themselves on that day is cut off from the people. This shows that refusing to take sin and God's command seriously has real consequences.
entries.leviticus 23:30: Anyone who works on that day will be destroyed by God from among his people. The reader is warned that God takes this day of atonement very seriously.
entries.leviticus 23:31: No work of any kind is allowed, and this is a permanent rule for all generations wherever they live. The command is meant to last and to apply wherever God's people are.
entries.leviticus 23:32: It is a Sabbath of complete rest and self-denial, kept from evening to evening on the ninth day of the month. The reader sees that this holy day runs from sunset to sunset and calls for real rest and humility.
entries.leviticus 23:33: God speaks to Moses again to introduce the final festival in this chapter. This signals another new instruction.
entries.leviticus 23:34: On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, Israel is to keep the Feast of Tents, or Booths, to the Lord for seven days. This festival remembers God's care for his people, and the reader sees a yearly time of joyful remembrance.
entries.leviticus 23:35: The first day of the feast is a holy gathering with no field work. Worship opens the festival.
entries.leviticus 23:36: Each of the seven days has an offering by fire to the Lord, and the eighth day is a special holy gathering with its own offering and no field work. The festival ends with an extra day of worship.
entries.leviticus 23:37: These are the Lord's appointed festivals, to be kept as holy gatherings where offerings by fire are brought to him, each on its proper day. The reader sees that worship is ordered and regular, not random.
entries.leviticus 23:38: These festivals are in addition to the weekly Sabbaths and to the gifts, vows, and freewill offerings the people bring to the Lord. The festivals do not replace ordinary giving and worship; they add to them.
entries.leviticus 23:39: On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, after all the land's produce is gathered, they keep the Lord's feast for seven days, with the first and eighth days as Sabbaths. The reader sees a harvest celebration framed by rest and worship.
entries.leviticus 23:40: On the first day they take fruit from beautiful trees, palm branches, leafy branches, and river willows, and they rejoice before the Lord for seven days. The reader learns that God's people are meant to celebrate with gladness and gratitude before him.
entries.numbers 1:1: God spoke to Moses in the desert at the tent of worship, about a year after the people left Egypt. It shows God still guiding his people on their journey.
entries.numbers 1:2: God told Moses to count all the Israelite men, organized by family and clan, listing each one by name. Every person mattered enough to be counted individually.
entries.numbers 1:3: They were to count men twenty and older who could serve as soldiers, with Moses and Aaron doing the counting. This was about preparing the community for its defense.
entries.numbers 1:4: God told Moses to have one leader from each tribe help with the counting. Good work is shared with trusted helpers.
entries.numbers 1:5: This begins a list of the helpers, starting with Elizur from the tribe of Reuben. God named specific people to serve.
entries.numbers 1:6: Shelumiel from Simeon was named as that tribe's helper. Each tribe had its own representative.
entries.numbers 1:7: Nahshon from Judah was named as that tribe's helper.
entries.numbers 1:8: Nethanel from Issachar was named as that tribe's helper.
entries.numbers 1:9: Eliab from Zebulun was named as that tribe's helper.
entries.numbers 1:10: From Joseph's two sons came Elishama for Ephraim and Gamaliel for Manasseh.
entries.numbers 1:11: Abidan from Benjamin was named as that tribe's helper.
entries.numbers 1:12: Ahiezer from Dan was named as that tribe's helper.
entries.numbers 1:13: Pagiel from Asher was named as that tribe's helper.
entries.numbers 1:14: Eliasaph from Gad was named as that tribe's helper.
entries.numbers 1:15: Ahira from Naphtali was named as that tribe's helper.
entries.numbers 1:16: These men were the chosen leaders and heads of their tribes. God works through people he appoints.
entries.numbers 1:17: Moses and Aaron gathered these men who had been chosen by name. They acted on God's instructions.
entries.numbers 1:18: They assembled everyone and recorded each person by family and clan, counting all men twenty and older. Careful records helped the community stay organized.
entries.numbers 1:19: Moses did exactly as God commanded and counted the people in the Sinai desert. Obedience to God's instructions was central.
entries.numbers 1:20: The counting began with Reuben, Israel's oldest son, listing men twenty and older fit for war by family.
entries.numbers 1:21: The tribe of Reuben totaled 46,500 men.
entries.numbers 1:22: Next came Simeon, counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.numbers 1:23: The tribe of Simeon totaled 59,300 men.
entries.numbers 1:24: Then Gad was counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.numbers 1:25: The tribe of Gad totaled 45,650 men.
entries.numbers 1:26: Then Judah was counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.numbers 1:27: The tribe of Judah totaled 74,600 men.
entries.numbers 1:28: Then Issachar was counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.numbers 1:29: The tribe of Issachar totaled 54,400 men.
entries.numbers 1:30: Then Zebulun was counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.numbers 1:31: The tribe of Zebulun totaled 57,400 men.
entries.numbers 1:32: Then Joseph's descendants were counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.numbers 1:33: The tribe of Ephraim totaled 40,500 men.
entries.numbers 1:34: Then Manasseh was counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.numbers 1:35: The tribe of Manasseh totaled 32,200 men.
entries.numbers 1:36: Then Benjamin was counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.numbers 1:37: The tribe of Benjamin totaled 35,400 men.
entries.numbers 1:38: Then Dan was counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.numbers 1:39: The tribe of Dan totaled 62,700 men.
entries.numbers 1:40: Then Asher was counted by family and clan, all men twenty and older able to fight.
entries.leviticus 27:1: God spoke these instructions to Moses. It shows that what follows comes from God, not from human ideas.
entries.leviticus 27:2: If someone made a special promise to give a person to God, the priests set a money value instead. This let people keep their promise in a practical way.
entries.leviticus 27:3: A man between twenty and sixty was valued at fifty pieces of silver, using the standard weight of the sanctuary. The value depended on age and ability to work.
entries.leviticus 27:4: A woman in the same age group was valued at thirty pieces of silver. The text sets a lower amount, reflecting the social system of that time.
entries.leviticus 27:5: Young people from five to twenty were valued at twenty for a male and ten for a female. The amount matched their stage of life.
entries.leviticus 27:6: Very young children from one month to five years were valued at five for a boy and three for a girl. Even the youngest could be part of such a promise.
entries.leviticus 27:7: People sixty and older were valued at fifteen for a man and ten for a woman. The value went down with age.
entries.leviticus 27:8: If someone was too poor to pay the set amount, the priest set a lower price he could afford. God's law made room for people with little money.
entries.leviticus 27:9: If someone promised an animal as an offering to God, that animal became holy and set apart. Once given, it belonged to God.
entries.leviticus 27:10: A promised animal could not be swapped for a better or worse one. If someone tried to exchange it, both animals became holy and belonged to God.
entries.leviticus 27:11: If the animal was one that could not be offered to God, it was brought to the priest. The priest handled cases involving animals unfit for sacrifice.
entries.leviticus 27:12: The priest decided what the animal was worth, good or bad, and that price stood. The priest's judgment settled the matter.
entries.leviticus 27:13: If the owner wanted the animal back, he had to pay its value plus a fifth. Getting back what was given to God cost extra.
entries.leviticus 27:14: If someone dedicated his house to God, the priest set its value, and that price was fixed. The priest's decision settled what the house was worth.
entries.leviticus 27:15: If the owner wanted his house back, he paid the set value plus a fifth. The extra amount was the cost of reclaiming it.
entries.leviticus 27:16: If someone gave part of his field to God, its value was based on how much seed it needed. The size and productivity of the land set the price.
entries.leviticus 27:17: If the field was given starting from the Jubilee year, the full set value applied. The timing of the gift affected the price.
entries.leviticus 27:18: If the field was given after the Jubilee, the priest reduced the price based on the years left until the next Jubilee. The value shrank as the time grew shorter.
entries.leviticus 27:19: If the man who gave the field wanted it back, he paid the value plus a fifth, and it became his again. Reclaiming it cost more than the original value.
entries.leviticus 27:20: If he did not buy it back, or if it had been sold to someone else, he could not get it back. The deal became permanent.
entries.leviticus 27:21: At the Jubilee that field became holy to God and belonged to the priests. It did not return to the original owner.
entries.leviticus 27:22: This rule covered a field someone had bought rather than inherited. It was not part of his family's permanent land.
entries.leviticus 27:23: The priest worked out the value up to the Jubilee, and the man paid that amount as holy to God. The payment was based on the years remaining.
entries.leviticus 27:24: At the Jubilee the field went back to the family it originally belonged to. Bought land always returned to its original owners.
entries.leviticus 27:25: All values were measured by the sanctuary shekel, which was twenty gerahs. A standard weight kept the amounts fair and consistent.
entries.leviticus 27:26: The firstborn of cattle already belonged to God, so no one could dedicate it as a special gift. It was already the Lord's.
entries.leviticus 27:27: If the animal was unclean, the owner could buy it back at the set value plus a fifth, or it was sold at that value. Either way, the priest's valuation stood.
entries.leviticus 27:28: Anything fully devoted to God could not be sold or bought back; it was most holy. Such a gift was permanent and set apart for God.
entries.leviticus 27:29: A person fully devoted to God could not be bought back and was to be put to death. This was the most serious kind of dedication.
entries.leviticus 27:30: A tenth of the land's produce and fruit belonged to God as holy. Giving a tenth was a regular way to honor him.
entries.leviticus 27:31: If someone wanted to buy back part of his tenth, he paid a fifth more. Reclaiming what was given to God cost extra.
entries.leviticus 27:32: A tenth of the herd and flock, counted as they passed under the rod, was holy to God. The tenth animal was set apart for him.
entries.leviticus 27:33: The owner could not pick out good or bad animals or swap them; if he did, both became holy. The choice was left to God, not the owner.
entries.leviticus 27:34: These are the commands God gave Moses for Israel at Mount Sinai. They were part of God's covenant instructions to his people.
entries.leviticus 23:41: God tells his people to celebrate this festival every year for seven days, and this practice is meant to continue for all generations. The reader sees that remembering God's acts is meant to be a lasting habit, not a one-time event.
entries.leviticus 23:42: During the festival, every Israelite is to live in temporary shelters for a week instead of their usual homes. This made the celebration something the whole community actually experienced, not just heard about.
entries.leviticus 23:43: The tents remind each new generation how God cared for their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt. For the reader, it shows that remembering where you came from helps you trust God in the present.
entries.leviticus 23:44: Moses passed on to the Israelites all the instructions about God's appointed festivals. It shows the reader that these celebrations came from God himself, given through a leader the people trusted.
entries.leviticus 24:1: God begins speaking to Moses with instructions for the people. This reminds the reader that what follows comes from God himself, not from human ideas.
entries.leviticus 24:2: The people were to bring pure olive oil so the lamp in the holy place would never go out. It shows that keeping worship going was a shared responsibility of the whole community.
entries.leviticus 24:3: Aaron was to keep the lamp burning from evening to morning outside the curtain of the sacred tent. This steady light stood for God's constant presence with his people, and it was a lasting rule for them.
entries.leviticus 24:4: Aaron was to keep the lamps arranged properly on the lampstand in God's presence all the time. It teaches that care and order matter in how we honor God.
entries.leviticus 24:5: The people were to take fine flour and bake twelve flat loaves, each made with a set amount of flour. The twelve loaves matched the twelve tribes of Israel.
entries.leviticus 24:6: The loaves were to be set out in two rows of six on the special table in God's presence. This was a way of presenting the people's gift before God.
entries.leviticus 24:7: Pure incense was to be placed on the rows of bread as a memorial, burned as an offering to God. It showed that the bread was set apart for him.
entries.leviticus 24:8: Fresh bread was to be set out every Sabbath as a lasting agreement between God and Israel. It was a regular reminder of their relationship with him.
entries.leviticus 24:9: The bread belonged to Aaron and his sons, who were to eat it in a holy place because it was most holy. God provided for the priests through what was offered to him.
entries.leviticus 24:10: A man whose mother was Israelite and father Egyptian got into a fight with an Israelite man near the camp. This sets the scene for the incident that follows.
entries.leviticus 24:11: The man cursed and spoke evil against God's holy name, so he was brought to Moses; his mother is named as Shelomith from the tribe of Dan. Speaking against God's name was taken very seriously.
entries.leviticus 24:12: They held him in custody until God himself gave a decision on the case. It shows they waited for God's direction rather than deciding on their own.
entries.leviticus 24:13: God then spoke to Moses to give his ruling. The decision came from God, not from human opinion.
entries.leviticus 24:14: The man was to be taken outside the camp, and those who heard his curse were to lay hands on his head before the whole community stoned him. The witnesses shared in the responsibility for the judgment.
entries.leviticus 24:15: God told Israel that anyone who curses God carries the guilt of that sin. It warns the reader that words against God are not a small matter.
entries.leviticus 24:16: Anyone, whether Israelite or foreigner, who spoke evil against the Lord's name was to be put to death by stoning. In that setting, God's name was to be treated as holy by everyone.
entries.leviticus 24:17: Anyone who takes another person's life must be put to death. It shows how seriously God values human life.
entries.leviticus 24:18: Anyone who kills an animal must pay for it, a life for a life. Even harm to animals carried a real cost that had to be made right.
entries.leviticus 24:19: If someone injures his neighbor, the same injury was to be done to him. The point was fair punishment that matched the harm done, not more.
entries.leviticus 24:20: The rule was injury for injury, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, matching the damage done. It limited revenge so punishment would fit the crime and not go beyond it.
entries.leviticus 24:21: Killing an animal required payment, but killing a person required the killer's own life. This again shows the far greater value God places on human life.
entries.leviticus 24:22: The same law applied to foreigners living among the Israelites as to native-born Israelites, because the Lord is God over all. It teaches fairness and equal treatment for outsiders.
entries.leviticus 24:23: Moses told the people God's words, and they carried out the stoning outside the camp just as the Lord commanded. The account ends by showing the people obeyed God's instruction.
entries.numbers 1:41: This records the total count of fighting men from the tribe of Asher. It shows that Asher was one of the tribes included in Israel's military census.
entries.numbers 1:42: This describes how the tribe of Naphtali was counted, listing men twenty and older who could serve in war. It reminds us that each family and tribe was carefully organized for service.
entries.numbers 1:43: This gives the total number of fighting men counted from the tribe of Naphtali. It shows the specific size of that tribe's contribution to Israel's army.
entries.numbers 1:44: Moses, Aaron, and one leader from each tribe conducted this census together. It shows that the counting was a shared, official responsibility, not one man's private action.
entries.numbers 1:45: This summarizes the whole count: all Israelite men twenty and older who were fit for military service. It shows the census focused on those able to defend the community.
entries.numbers 1:46: The grand total of fighting men was 603,550. This large number shows the size and strength of the people God had brought out of Egypt.
entries.numbers 1:47: The Levites were left out of this military count. God had a different role in mind for them than fighting.
entries.numbers 1:48: God himself spoke to Moses about this exception. It shows the decision about the Levites came directly from God, not from human planning.
entries.numbers 1:49: God told Moses not to count the tribe of Levi with the rest of Israel. They were set apart for a special purpose rather than for the army.
entries.numbers 1:50: The Levites were put in charge of the Tent of Meeting and everything in it, carrying it and caring for it as they traveled. Their job was to serve God's dwelling place among the people.
entries.numbers 1:51: The Levites were the ones to set up and take down the Tent of Meeting, and anyone else who came near it was to be put to death. This shows how seriously God treated the holiness of his dwelling.
entries.numbers 1:52: Each Israelite was to camp in his own assigned place under his family's flag. This kept the camp orderly and showed that everyone had a proper place.
entries.numbers 1:53: The Levites camped around the Tent of Meeting to guard it, so God's anger would not fall on the people. Their presence protected the community by keeping holy things treated as holy.
entries.numbers 1:54: The Israelites did everything the Lord commanded Moses. Their obedience is a model of following God's instructions carefully.
entries.leviticus 26:1: God tells his people not to make or bow down to statues and carved stones as objects of worship. For the reader, it means loyalty to God comes first, and we shouldn't give ultimate devotion to things we make.
entries.leviticus 26:2: God asks his people to keep the Sabbath rest and treat his holy place with respect. For the reader, it means setting aside regular time for God and honoring what is dedicated to him.
entries.leviticus 26:3: God says that if his people follow his rules and actually put them into practice, good things follow. For the reader, it means obedience to God is not just hearing his words but living them out.
entries.leviticus 26:4: God promises to send rain at the right season so crops grow and trees bear fruit. For the reader, it means God cares about everyday needs like food and responds to faithful living with provision.
entries.leviticus 26:5: God promises such abundance that harvesting lasts until the next planting, with plenty of food and safety. For the reader, it means God's blessing can be so full that needs are met with more than enough.
entries.leviticus 26:6: God promises peace in the land, rest without fear, and safety from wild animals and war. For the reader, it means God's blessing includes calm and security, not just material things.
entries.leviticus 26:7: God promises his people will defeat those who attack them. For the reader, it means God stands with his people against their enemies and gives them strength to face opposition.
entries.leviticus 26:8: God promises that even a small number of his people will overcome a much larger enemy force. For the reader, it means God's help matters more than numbers, and he can give victory against great odds.
entries.leviticus 26:9: God promises to look on his people with favor, bless them with children, and keep his covenant with them. For the reader, it means God delights in his people and remains faithful to his promises.
entries.leviticus 26:10: God promises so much new food that people will clear out old stored grain to make room. For the reader, it means God's provision can be so generous that it replaces what was saved before.
entries.leviticus 26:11: God promises to place his dwelling among his people and not turn away from them in disgust. For the reader, it means God wants to be near his people and does not reject them.
entries.leviticus 26:12: God promises to walk among his people, be their God, and claim them as his own. For the reader, it means God desires a close, personal relationship, not distant rule.
entries.leviticus 26:13: God reminds his people that he freed them from slavery in Egypt and broke their chains so they could walk upright. For the reader, it means God rescues people from bondage and gives them dignity and freedom.
entries.leviticus 26:14: God warns that if his people refuse to listen and fail to keep his laws, consequences follow. For the reader, it means ignoring God's instructions has real results, so listening matters.
entries.leviticus 26:15: God describes people who reject his rules, despise his judgments, and break his covenant. For the reader, it means treating God's guidance with contempt is a serious turning away from him.
entries.leviticus 26:16: God warns of terror, disease, and wasted effort, with enemies eating what his people planted. For the reader, it means rejecting God can bring fear and loss, and hard work without his blessing may come to nothing.
entries.leviticus 26:17: God warns he will turn away and let enemies defeat and rule over his people, who will flee in panic. For the reader, it means turning from God can leave people exposed and afraid, even when no real threat is near.
entries.leviticus 26:18: God says that if his people still refuse to listen after warnings, he will discipline them even more severely. For the reader, it means continued resistance to God leads to escalating consequences, not safety.
entries.leviticus 26:19: God warns he will break their proud strength and make the sky like iron and the ground like bronze, meaning no rain and no growth. For the reader, it means pride in human strength is fragile, and God can withhold blessing.
entries.leviticus 26:20: God says their strength will be spent for nothing because the land and trees will produce no food. For the reader, it means effort without God's blessing can leave people exhausted and empty-handed.
entries.leviticus 26:21: God warns that continued opposition and refusal to listen will bring even heavier punishment. For the reader, it means stubbornly resisting God only deepens the consequences.
entries.leviticus 26:22: God warns he will send wild animals that kill children and livestock, shrinking the population and leaving roads empty. For the reader, it means rejecting God can bring loss and devastation that touches families and communities.
entries.leviticus 26:23: God says that if these warnings still don't turn his people back to him, they continue opposing him. For the reader, it means discipline is meant to bring people back to God, and ignoring it hardens the heart.
entries.leviticus 26:24: God says he himself will oppose his people and punish them even more severely for their sins. For the reader, it means God takes persistent rebellion personally and will act against it.
entries.leviticus 26:25: God warns he will bring war and disease, and his people will be handed over to their enemies. For the reader, it means breaking faith with God can lead to being overwhelmed by forces they cannot control.
entries.leviticus 26:26: God warns that food will be so scarce that ten women share one oven and bread is weighed out, never enough. For the reader, it means scarcity is a real consequence of turning from God, and having some food is not the same as having enough.
entries.leviticus 26:27: God says that if his people still refuse to listen after all this and keep opposing him, he will respond further. For the reader, it means there is a limit to ignoring God's warnings, and persistence in rebellion has a cost.
entries.leviticus 26:28: God says his anger will burn against them and he will punish them even more severely. For the reader, it means God's patience is real but not endless, and continued defiance invites his judgment.
entries.leviticus 26:29: God warns that hunger will become so severe that people will eat their own children. For the reader, it means the consequences of rejecting God can reach horrifying depths, showing how serious sin is.
entries.leviticus 26:30: God warns he will destroy their places of worship, smash their altars, and pile their dead on their idols, and he will reject them. For the reader, it means false worship leads to ruin, and God will not accept devotion given to other things.
entries.leviticus 26:31: God warns he will turn their cities into ruins and destroy their sanctuaries, taking no pleasure in their offerings. For the reader, it means religious activity without real obedience does not please God.
entries.leviticus 26:32: God warns he will make their land so desolate that even their enemies will be shocked by it. For the reader, it means the results of turning from God can become a visible warning to others.
entries.leviticus 26:33: God warns he will scatter his people among other nations and leave their land empty and their cities in ruins. For the reader, it means rejecting God can lead to losing home, community, and stability.
entries.leviticus 26:34: God says the land will finally enjoy its Sabbath rests while it lies empty and the people are gone. For the reader, it means what people refused to give God will be taken anyway, and the land gets the rest it was denied.
entries.leviticus 26:35: God says the land will rest all the time it lies desolate, making up for the rests it never had while the people lived there. For the reader, it means neglected obedience cannot be avoided forever; what was withheld will be required in the end.
entries.leviticus 26:36: God warns that the survivors will be so frightened in enemy lands that the sound of a blowing leaf will make them run as if chased by a sword. For the reader, it means guilt and fear can make people panic even when no real danger is present.
entries.leviticus 26:37: God says they will stumble over one another as if fleeing a sword, even when no one is chasing them, and they will fall before their enemies. For the reader, it means fear and disunity can cause people to collapse from within.
entries.leviticus 26:38: God warns that his people will die among foreign nations and be destroyed in enemy lands. For the reader, it means turning from God can lead to losing life and place among those who do not know him.
entries.leviticus 26:39: God says the survivors will waste away in enemy lands because of their own sins and the sins of their ancestors. For the reader, it means sin's effects can carry across generations and wear people down over time.
entries.leviticus 26:40: God says his people will finally confess their sins and the sins of their ancestors, admitting they were unfaithful and opposed him. For the reader, it means honest confession is the first step back to God, and it is never too late to admit wrong.
entries.leviticus 25:1: God is speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai, the same mountain where he gave the Ten Commandments. This shows that the rules that follow come directly from God, not from human ideas.
entries.leviticus 25:2: When the Israelites settle in the land God is giving them, they must let the land rest every seventh year as a Sabbath dedicated to God. The land itself is treated as something that belongs to God and deserves rest.
entries.leviticus 25:3: For six years the people are to farm normally—planting crops and pruning vines to get a harvest. Ordinary work is expected and good during those years.
entries.leviticus 25:4: The seventh year is a year of complete rest for the land, set apart for God. The people must not plant crops or prune their vines during that year.
entries.leviticus 25:5: They must not harvest whatever grows on its own or pick grapes from unpruned vines, because it is a rest year for the land. Even volunteer crops are left alone.
entries.leviticus 25:6: Whatever the land produces by itself during that rest year becomes food for everyone—the owner, servants, hired workers, and foreigners living among them. God's rest year provides for the whole community, not just the landowners.
entries.leviticus 25:7: The same self-grown food is also for the livestock and wild animals in the land. Nothing from that year's natural growth is wasted; it feeds both people and animals.
entries.leviticus 25:8: The people are to count seven cycles of seven years, which comes to forty-nine years. This counting sets up the special fiftieth year that follows.
entries.leviticus 25:9: On the Day of Atonement in the seventh month, a loud trumpet is to be blown throughout the whole land. The trumpet announces that the special year is beginning.
entries.leviticus 25:10: The fiftieth year is set apart as holy, and freedom is proclaimed for everyone: debts are cancelled and each person returns to their family property. This year is called the Jubilee.
entries.leviticus 25:11: During the Jubilee year no one plants crops, harvests volunteer growth, or picks grapes from untended vines. It is a year of complete rest, just like the Sabbath year.
entries.leviticus 25:12: The Jubilee is holy to God, and the people are to eat only what the fields produce on their own that year. They trust God to provide rather than working the land.
entries.leviticus 25:13: In the Jubilee year, everyone returns to the property that originally belonged to their family. Land that was sold goes back to its original owners.
entries.leviticus 25:14: When buying or selling goods, people must not cheat or take advantage of each other. Fair dealing is required in all business.
entries.leviticus 25:15: The price of land is to be set based on how many years of crops remain until the next Jubilee. The closer the Jubilee, the lower the price, because fewer harvests remain.
entries.leviticus 25:16: A long time until Jubilee means a higher price, and a short time means a lower price, because what is really being sold is the crops of a set number of years. The land itself is not being sold permanently.
entries.leviticus 25:17: No one is to wrong or take advantage of another person, and everyone should live with a healthy fear of God. God himself is the reason to treat others fairly.
entries.leviticus 25:18: If the people follow God's rules and commands, they will live safely in the land. Obedience brings security.
entries.leviticus 25:19: The land will produce fruit, the people will have plenty to eat, and they will live in safety. God promises both abundance and peace to those who obey.
entries.leviticus 25:20: The people might worry and ask what they will eat in the seventh year, since they cannot plant or harvest. This is a natural question about trusting God's command.
entries.leviticus 25:21: God promises to bless them in the sixth year so that the land produces enough food for three years. God provides ahead of time for the rest year.
entries.leviticus 25:22: In the eighth year they plant again, but they eat from the old stored food until the ninth year's harvest is ready. God's provision carries them through the gap.
entries.leviticus 25:23: Land must never be sold permanently, because the land belongs to God, and the people are only guests and tenants living on it. They are caretakers, not ultimate owners.
entries.leviticus 25:24: Throughout the land, people must always have the right to buy back property that was sold. No sale of land is final.
entries.leviticus 25:25: If an Israelite becomes poor and sells some of his land, his nearest relative can buy it back for him. Family is responsible for helping a relative in trouble.
entries.leviticus 25:26: If a man has no relative to buy back his land, but later becomes wealthy enough himself, he may buy it back. Recovery is possible if his situation improves.
entries.leviticus 25:27: He must count the years since he sold it and repay the buyer for the remaining years, then he gets his property back. The repayment is fair and based on the years left.
entries.leviticus 25:28: If he cannot afford to buy it back, the land stays with the buyer until the Jubilee year, when it returns to the original owner. The Jubilee guarantees that land is never lost forever.
entries.leviticus 25:29: If someone sells a house in a walled city, he has a full year to buy it back. This gives a limited window to reverse the sale.
entries.leviticus 25:30: If the house in a walled city is not bought back within that year, it belongs permanently to the buyer and his descendants, and it does not return in the Jubilee. City houses follow different rules from farmland.
entries.leviticus 25:31: Houses in unwalled villages are treated like farmland: they can be bought back, and they return to their owners in the Jubilee. Small-town property keeps the same protections as land.
entries.leviticus 25:32: The Levites, who serve at the temple and have no tribal land, always have the right to buy back their houses. God makes special provision for those who serve him.
entries.leviticus 25:33: If a Levite does not buy back his house, it still returns to him in the Jubilee, because the Levites' houses are their permanent property among Israel. Their homes are protected.
entries.leviticus 25:34: The pasture land around the Levites' towns can never be sold, because it belongs to them permanently. Their grazing land is guaranteed forever.
entries.leviticus 25:35: If a fellow Israelite becomes poor and cannot support himself, you must help him as you would a foreigner living among you, so he can keep living. Helping the poor is a duty, not an option.
entries.leviticus 25:36: Do not charge him interest on money or goods, but fear God and let your brother keep living among you. Fair treatment of the poor is tied to respecting God.
entries.leviticus 25:37: Do not charge interest on money lent to him or on food given to him. Lending to a poor brother must not become a way to profit from his need.
entries.leviticus 25:38: God reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt and gave them the land of Canaan to be their God. Because God rescued and provided for them, they should treat others generously.
entries.leviticus 25:39: If a fellow Israelite becomes poor and sells himself to you, do not treat him like a slave you own. An Israelite servant must not be treated as property.
entries.leviticus 25:40: He is to work for you as a hired servant until the Jubilee year. His service is temporary and he must be treated with dignity, not as a slave.
entries.numbers 2:1: God speaks here to both Moses and Aaron, the two leaders of Israel. It shows that God gave direction to the whole leadership, not just one man.
entries.numbers 2:2: Each tribe was to camp under its own family flag and face the central worship tent. God wanted his people organized and focused on him at the center of their life.
entries.numbers 2:3: The tribe of Judah camped on the east side, the side of sunrise, under its flag with Nahshon as leader. Each group had a set place and a named leader.
entries.numbers 2:4: Judah's fighting men totaled 74,600. The large number shows this was a big, organized community.
entries.numbers 2:5: The tribe of Issachar camped next to Judah, led by Nethanel. Neighboring tribes stayed together as a unit.
entries.numbers 2:6: Issachar's fighting men totaled 54,400. Each tribe's size was carefully recorded.
entries.numbers 2:7: The tribe of Zebulun camped next, led by Eliab. Three tribes made up this eastern group.
entries.numbers 2:8: Zebulun's fighting men totaled 57,400. The count kept the camp orderly and ready.
entries.numbers 2:9: Judah's whole group totaled 186,400 and led the march. This largest group went first when the people moved.
entries.numbers 2:10: The tribe of Reuben camped on the south side under its flag, led by Elizur. Each side of the camp had its own assigned tribes.
entries.numbers 2:11: Reuben's fighting men totaled 46,500. The numbers show how each tribe contributed to the whole.
entries.numbers 2:12: The tribe of Simeon camped beside Reuben, led by Shelumiel. Related tribes camped near each other.
entries.numbers 2:13: Simeon's fighting men totaled 59,300. Every tribe's strength was counted and recorded.
entries.numbers 2:14: The tribe of Gad camped next, led by Eliasaph. This completed the southern group of three tribes.
entries.numbers 2:15: Gad's fighting men totaled 45,650. The exact count shows careful organization.
entries.numbers 2:16: Reuben's whole group totaled 151,450 and marched second. The camp moved in an ordered sequence, group by group.
entries.numbers 2:17: The worship tent and the Levites traveled in the middle of the marching tribes. God's presence was placed at the heart of the people as they moved.
entries.numbers 2:18: The tribe of Ephraim camped on the west side under its flag, led by Elishama. Each direction had its assigned leading tribe.
entries.numbers 2:19: Ephraim's fighting men totaled 40,500. The record kept the camp's structure clear.
entries.numbers 2:20: The tribe of Manasseh camped beside Ephraim, led by Gamaliel. These two tribes were closely related and stayed together.
entries.numbers 2:21: Manasseh's fighting men totaled 32,200. Each tribe's number mattered for organizing the march.
entries.numbers 2:22: The tribe of Benjamin camped next, led by Abidan. This completed the western group of three tribes.
entries.numbers 2:23: Benjamin's fighting men totaled 35,400. The count helped keep the camp orderly and prepared.
entries.numbers 2:24: Ephraim's whole group totaled 108,100 and marched third. The people moved in a set order, not in chaos.
entries.numbers 2:25: The tribe of Dan camped on the north side under its flag, led by Ahiezer. The last side of the camp had its own tribes and leader.
entries.numbers 2:26: Dan's fighting men totaled 62,700. The numbers show each tribe's part in the whole community.
entries.numbers 2:27: The tribe of Asher camped beside Dan, led by Pagiel. Neighboring tribes stayed together in their assigned places.
entries.numbers 2:28: Asher's fighting men totaled 41,500. The careful counting kept the camp organized.
entries.numbers 2:29: The tribe of Naphtali camped next, led by Ahira. This completed the northern group of three tribes.
entries.numbers 2:30: Naphtali's fighting men totaled 53,400. Each tribe's strength was recorded for the march.
entries.numbers 2:31: Dan's whole group totaled 157,600 and marched last under their flags. This group brought up the rear of the procession.
entries.numbers 2:32: All the Israelites together totaled 603,550. This summary shows the full size of the organized camp.
entries.numbers 2:33: The Levites were left out of this count, just as God had commanded Moses. They had a special role and were counted separately.
entries.numbers 2:34: The people did exactly what God told Moses about camping and marching. Their obedience kept the whole community ordered around God's presence.
entries.leviticus 26:41: God says that when his people were taken away to enemy lands, this happened because they had set themselves against him. If they then humble their proud hearts and accept the consequences of their sin, there is still hope for them.
entries.leviticus 26:42: When that happens, God will remember the promises he made long ago to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and he will remember the land he gave them. God's promises are not cancelled by human failure.
entries.leviticus 26:43: While the people are gone, the land will finally get its rest, which it was denied while they lived on it. They will bear the results of their sins because they rejected God's ways and turned against his laws.
entries.leviticus 26:44: Even while they are among their enemies, God will not throw them away or cancel his covenant with them completely. He remains their God, and his commitment to them holds even when they are being disciplined.
entries.leviticus 26:45: God will remember the covenant he made with their ancestors when he brought them out of Egypt in front of the nations, to be their God. He is the Lord, and he does not forget his own promises.
entries.leviticus 26:46: These are the rules and laws God gave to Israel through Moses at Mount Sinai, forming the agreement between him and his people. They show what life with God was meant to look like for them.
entries.numbers 5:1: This line simply introduces God speaking to Moses. It reminds the reader that what follows is presented as God's instruction, not Moses' own idea.
entries.numbers 5:2: People with skin disease, bodily discharge, or who had touched a dead body were to stay outside the camp. This kept ritual uncleanness away from the community's holy space.
entries.numbers 5:3: Both men and women were sent outside so the place where God dwelt among the people would not be made unclean. The concern was protecting the holiness of God's dwelling.
entries.numbers 5:4: The people obeyed exactly what God told Moses and removed these individuals from the camp. It shows the community taking God's command seriously.
entries.numbers 5:5: This again introduces God speaking to Moses. It marks the start of a new set of instructions.
entries.numbers 5:6: This covers any wrong a person commits against another, which is also a betrayal of God. The person is held guilty for what they did.
entries.numbers 5:7: The guilty person must openly confess and repay what was taken, plus one-fifth extra, to the person they wronged. Honesty and making things right are required, not just saying sorry.
entries.numbers 5:8: If the wronged person has no relative to receive the repayment, it goes to the priest, along with a ram offered to make atonement. God ensures the debt is still settled.
entries.numbers 5:9: Any sacred gift the Israelites brought to the priest belonged to that priest. This supported the priests who served at the tabernacle.
entries.numbers 5:10: Whatever a person set apart as holy and gave to a priest became the priest's own. Giving to God through the priest was a real transfer of property.
entries.numbers 5:11: This line introduces another word from God to Moses. It sets up the next topic.
entries.numbers 5:12: This begins the case of a married woman who commits sexual sin against her husband. The situation is framed as a wrong done to him.
entries.numbers 5:13: The wrong is hidden, with no witness and no catching her in the act. The law addresses suspicion when there is no proof.
entries.numbers 5:14: A husband may become suspicious of his wife, whether or not he has real reason. The law provides a way to handle that doubt rather than let it fester.
entries.numbers 5:15: The husband brings his wife to the priest with a small barley offering, without oil or incense, since it is tied to suspicion of wrongdoing. The modest offering reflects the serious, unhappy nature of the case.
entries.numbers 5:16: The priest brings the woman forward and has her stand before the Lord. The matter is placed directly before God rather than settled by the husband alone.
entries.numbers 5:17: The priest mixes holy water with dust from the tabernacle floor. This prepared water is central to the test that follows.
entries.numbers 5:18: The woman stands before the Lord with her hair loose and holds the grain offering, while the priest holds the bitter curse water. The scene is solemn and public.
entries.numbers 5:19: The priest puts the woman under oath, stating that if she has been faithful she is safe from the curse of the water. She is given a clear condition to affirm.
entries.numbers 5:20: The priest states the opposite case: if she has been unfaithful and made herself unclean. The oath covers both possibilities honestly.
entries.numbers 5:21: The priest pronounces a curse that, if she is guilty, would bring wasting of her legs and disease of her stomach. The consequences are described in vivid, physical terms.
entries.numbers 5:22: The cursed water is said to enter her body and cause these harms, and the woman agrees by saying amen. Her consent makes the oath binding.
entries.numbers 5:23: The priest writes the curses down and washes the ink into the bitter water. The words of the curse become part of what she drinks.
entries.numbers 5:24: The priest gives the woman the bitter water to drink, and it enters her body. The test is carried out as described.
entries.numbers 5:25: The priest takes the grain offering from her hands, lifts it before the Lord, and brings it to the altar. The offering is presented to God before the water is given.
entries.numbers 5:26: The priest burns a handful of the offering on the altar as a memorial, then gives the woman the water. The ritual combines offering and test.
entries.numbers 5:27: If she is guilty, the water brings the described physical harm and she becomes a curse among her people. The outcome is presented as God's judgment on the hidden sin.
entries.numbers 5:28: If she is innocent, she is cleared and will be able to have children. The test ends with her vindication and blessing.
entries.numbers 5:29: This summarizes the law for a wife suspected of unfaithfulness. It is a specific procedure for a specific situation.
entries.numbers 5:30: It also covers a husband who is suspicious of his wife and brings her to the priest. The priest carries out the prescribed procedure.
entries.numbers 5:31: The husband is not held guilty, while the wife bears the consequences of her sin if she is guilty. The law places responsibility on the person who actually did wrong.
entries.leviticus 25:41: A person who had sold himself as a servant was to be released in the Jubilee year, along with his children, and return to his own family and inherited land. God built in a fresh start for families who had fallen on hard times.
entries.leviticus 25:42: The Israelites belonged to God because he had rescued them from slavery in Egypt, so no one could own them permanently as property. Their freedom mattered to God because he had bought it.
entries.leviticus 25:43: Masters were told not to rule harshly over their Israelite servants but to treat them with respect for God. How we treat people who are under our power shows whether we take God seriously.
entries.leviticus 25:44: Israelites were allowed to buy servants from the surrounding nations as permanent property. This was a common practice in that ancient world, though it sits uneasily with us today.
entries.leviticus 25:45: They could also buy servants from foreign families living among them, and those servants became their property. The text describes the social rules of that time rather than setting an ideal for all times.
entries.leviticus 25:46: Foreign servants could be passed down to children as inherited property and serve permanently, but Israelites were never to be treated harshly. God drew a line between how his people treated outsiders and how they treated each other.
entries.leviticus 25:47: If a foreigner living among them became rich and an Israelite became poor and sold himself to that foreigner or his family, the Israelite still had hope. Poverty did not erase his place among God's people.
entries.leviticus 25:48: Even after selling himself, the Israelite kept the right to be bought back and set free, and a relative could pay the price. God made sure no one was trapped forever without hope of rescue.
entries.leviticus 25:49: An uncle, a cousin, or any close relative could buy him back, and if he earned enough money he could free himself. Family and personal effort were both ways God provided for restoring freedom.
entries.leviticus 25:50: The buy-back price was worked out by counting the years left until the Jubilee and comparing them to what a hired worker would earn. Freedom had a fair, calculated cost rather than an arbitrary one.
entries.leviticus 25:51: If many years remained before the Jubilee, he paid back a larger share of the original price. The payment matched the time still owed, so the arrangement stayed fair to both sides.
entries.leviticus 25:52: If only a few years remained, he paid back less, based on the years left. The closer the Jubilee came, the cheaper freedom became.
entries.leviticus 25:53: While he served, he was to be treated like a hired worker year by year, and his master was not to be cruel to him. God cared about how the powerful treated the vulnerable, even within a legal arrangement.
entries.leviticus 25:54: If no one bought him back, he still went free in the Jubilee year, together with his children. God made sure freedom came eventually for every Israelite servant.
entries.leviticus 25:55: The Israelites were God's servants first, because he had brought them out of Egypt, and he is the Lord their God. Their ultimate loyalty and freedom belonged to him, not to any human master.
entries.numbers 6:1: God speaks directly to Moses, starting a new set of instructions. This shows the reader that what follows comes from God himself.
entries.numbers 6:2: Any Israelite man or woman could make a special promise to set themselves apart for God for a time. It means ordinary people could choose to devote a season of their life fully to him.
entries.numbers 6:3: During that special time the person had to stay away from wine and any grape drink. This was a visible way of setting that time apart from normal life.
entries.numbers 6:4: They were to avoid everything that comes from grapes, even the seeds and skins. The point was total separation from one ordinary pleasure for the length of the promise.
entries.numbers 6:5: They were not to cut their hair at all while the promise lasted, because their uncut hair marked them as set apart for God. For the reader, it shows that devotion to God can involve visible, everyday choices.
entries.numbers 6:6: They were not allowed to go near a dead body during that time. Touching the dead made a person ritually unclean, which would break their special dedication.
entries.numbers 6:7: Even for a close family member who died, they could not break their dedication by becoming unclean. It shows that this promise to God was taken seriously above even family obligations for that period.
entries.numbers 6:8: The whole time of the promise, the person was considered holy, set apart for the Lord. Their dedication was not just a private feeling but a real status before God.
entries.numbers 6:9: If someone died suddenly right beside them, they became unclean and had to shave their head on the seventh day as part of being made clean again. It shows that even accidental uncleanness had to be dealt with.
entries.numbers 6:10: On the eighth day they brought two doves or young pigeons to the priest at the entrance of the meeting tent. This gave even a poor person a way to make things right with God.
entries.numbers 6:11: The priest offered one bird as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering to deal with the uncleanness from the death, then made the person holy again. It shows God providing a way to restore someone who was defiled.
entries.numbers 6:12: They had to start their special time over and bring a young lamb as a guilt offering, because the earlier days no longer counted. It teaches that breaking a promise to God has real consequences.
entries.numbers 6:13: This describes what the person did when their promised time of separation was finished: they came to the entrance of the meeting tent. It marks the end of the vow with a formal step.
entries.numbers 6:14: They brought three animals with no defects: a young male lamb for a burnt offering, a young female lamb for a sin offering, and a ram for a peace offering. Each offering had its own purpose in restoring and celebrating the relationship with God.
entries.numbers 6:15: They also brought a basket of bread made without yeast, cakes mixed with oil, and thin cakes with oil, along with grain and drink offerings. These gifts completed the worship and showed gratitude to God.
entries.numbers 6:16: The priest presented all these gifts before the Lord and offered the sin offering and the burnt offering. The priest acted as the go-between so the person's worship was done properly.
entries.numbers 6:17: The priest offered the ram as a peace offering together with the basket of bread, plus the grain and drink offerings. This was a shared, joyful offering celebrating peace with God.
entries.numbers 6:18: At the entrance of the meeting tent the person shaved off the hair that marked their promise and burned it on the altar fire under the peace offering. The sign of the vow was given back to God as the vow ended.
entries.numbers 6:19: After the hair was cut, the priest placed a cooked leg of the ram and two kinds of bread into the person's hands. This showed the person receiving a share of the holy offering.
entries.numbers 6:20: The priest lifted these gifts up before the Lord as a special offering, and they belonged to the priest along with other portions. Only after all this could the person drink wine again, showing the vow was truly over.
entries.numbers 6:21: This sums up the rules for someone who makes this promise, including the offerings required, and allows for giving more if they can afford it. It teaches that a promise to God must be kept as it was made.
entries.numbers 6:22: God speaks to Moses again, introducing the blessing that follows. It shows the blessing comes from God's own instruction.
entries.numbers 6:23: God tells Aaron and his sons, the priests, to bless the people of Israel with these words. It means God wanted his people regularly spoken over with words of blessing.
entries.numbers 6:24: The blessing asks God to bless his people and protect them. For the reader, it is a simple prayer that God would care for and guard them.
entries.numbers 6:25: It asks God to look on his people with favor and kindness, like a face shining with goodwill. It means asking God to show his grace toward them.
entries.numbers 6:26: It asks God to look favorably on his people and give them peace. For the reader, it is a prayer for God's approval and for wholeness in life.
entries.numbers 6:27: By speaking this blessing, the priests put God's name on the people, and God promised to bless them. It means God himself stands behind the words spoken over his people.
entries.numbers 3:1: This introduces the family line of Aaron and Moses at the time God spoke to Moses at Mount Sinai. It reminds the reader that God's words came to real people in a real place.
entries.numbers 3:2: Aaron had four sons, listed here by name with the oldest first. This shows the reader the family God set apart for priestly service.
entries.numbers 3:3: These sons of Aaron were set apart as priests by having holy oil poured on them. It means their role was officially given to them by God, not taken on their own.
entries.numbers 3:4: Two of Aaron's sons died because they offered fire to God in a way he had not commanded, and they left no children. The reader learns that God takes worship seriously and that the surviving sons carried on the priestly work.
entries.numbers 3:5: This is a simple note that God spoke directly to Moses. It reminds the reader that what follows comes from God himself.
entries.numbers 3:6: God told Moses to bring the tribe of Levi forward to serve Aaron the priest as helpers. It means God assigned a whole tribe to support the priests in their work.
entries.numbers 3:7: The Levites were to help Aaron and represent all Israel by taking care of the tent where God met with his people. The reader sees that supporting worship was a shared responsibility.
entries.numbers 3:8: The Levites were responsible for the equipment of the meeting tent and for doing the work needed for Israel's worship. It means practical service in God's house mattered and was given to specific people.
entries.numbers 3:9: God gave the Levites to Aaron and his sons as their assigned helpers from among the Israelites. The reader learns that God organizes his people so that each has a clear role.
entries.numbers 3:10: Aaron and his sons were to serve as priests, and anyone else who came near the sacred duties was to be put to death. It shows the reader that approaching God was not to be taken lightly.
entries.numbers 3:11: Again the text notes that God spoke to Moses. It signals that the next instruction is God's own command.
entries.numbers 3:12: God took the Levites for himself in place of the firstborn sons of Israel. It means God chose one tribe to represent the special claim he had on every family's firstborn.
entries.numbers 3:13: Every firstborn belonged to God because he spared Israel's firstborn when he struck Egypt's. The reader sees that God's rescue in the past shaped Israel's ongoing devotion to him.
entries.numbers 3:14: This notes that God gave the following command to Moses in the Sinai desert. It anchors the instructions in a real time and place.
entries.numbers 3:15: The Levites were to be counted by family, including every male a month old and older. It means even the youngest males were included in God's set-apart tribe.
entries.numbers 3:16: Moses obeyed and counted the Levites exactly as God commanded. The reader sees an example of careful obedience to God's instructions.
entries.numbers 3:17: Levi had three sons, named here as Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. These three lines form the structure of the Levite tribe.
entries.numbers 3:18: Gershon's sons are named, and their descendants became family groups. This shows how the tribe was organized by family.
entries.numbers 3:19: Kohath's four sons are named here. Their families would carry specific responsibilities in Israel's worship.
entries.numbers 3:20: Merari's two sons are named, completing the family lines of the Levites. The reader sees the whole tribe laid out by its ancestral households.
entries.numbers 3:21: The families descended from Gershon are identified by name. This connects the earlier family list to the actual groups being counted.
entries.numbers 3:22: The Gershonite males a month old and up totaled 7,500. The reader sees the size of this group and how carefully they were counted.
entries.numbers 3:23: The Gershonites were to camp behind the meeting tent on the west side. It means each family had an assigned place around God's dwelling.
entries.numbers 3:24: Eliasaph son of Lael was the leader of the Gershonites. It shows that each group had a responsible head.
entries.numbers 3:25: The Gershonites were to care for the tent itself, its coverings, and the curtain at its entrance. Their job was practical upkeep of the place where God met his people.
entries.numbers 3:26: They also cared for the curtains around the courtyard, the altar area, the doorway curtain, and all the cords. The reader sees that even small details of God's house were assigned to someone.
entries.numbers 3:27: The families descended from Kohath are listed by name. This identifies the group that would handle the most sacred items.
entries.numbers 3:28: The Kohathite males a month old and up totaled 8,600, and they were responsible for the holy place. It means this larger group had a serious sacred duty.
entries.numbers 3:29: The Kohathites were to camp on the south side of the meeting tent. Their location matched their assigned service.
entries.numbers 3:30: Elizaphan son of Uzziel led the Kohathite families. It shows the Kohathites also had a designated leader.
entries.numbers 3:31: The Kohathites were to carry the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the sacred utensils, and the inner curtain. These were the holiest objects, so their care was a weighty trust.
entries.numbers 3:32: Eleazar, Aaron's son, was the head over all the Levites and supervised those caring for the holy place. It means the priests had authority over the Levites' work.
entries.numbers 3:33: The families descended from Merari are named here. This identifies the third main group of Levites.
entries.numbers 3:34: The Merarite males a month old and up totaled 6,200. The reader sees this group was smaller than the others but still carefully counted.
entries.numbers 3:35: Zuriel son of Abihail led the Merarite families, and they were to camp on the north side of the tent. Each group had its leader and its place.
entries.numbers 3:36: The Merarites were to care for the tent's frames, crossbars, posts, bases, and all their equipment. Their work was the sturdy structure that held the tent together.
entries.numbers 3:37: They also cared for the courtyard posts, their bases, pegs, and cords. It means they handled the parts that kept the whole setup standing and secure.
entries.numbers 3:38: Moses, Aaron, and Aaron's sons camped on the east side in front of the meeting tent, guarding the holy place for Israel, and any outsider who came near was to die. The reader sees that the most responsible position carried the strictest warning.
entries.numbers 3:39: The total number of Levite males a month old and up was 22,000. This summary shows the full size of the tribe set apart for God's service.
entries.numbers 3:40: God told Moses to count and list all the firstborn males of Israel. This was the next step in comparing Israel's firstborn with the Levites.
entries.numbers 4:1: God speaks directly to Moses and Aaron, showing that the care of the sacred tent was commanded by him, not invented by people. For the reader, it means worship details came from God's instruction and were to be taken seriously.
entries.numbers 4:2: God tells Moses and Aaron to count the Kohathite clan within the tribe of Levi, organized by their family groups. This means each family had a recognized place and role in serving God.
entries.numbers 4:3: Only men between thirty and fifty were counted for this work, the years of full strength and maturity. It suggests that serving God in this task required grown men ready for responsibility.
entries.numbers 4:4: The Kohathites were assigned the most sacred part of the work, handling the holiest objects of the tent. Their job was a serious privilege with high responsibility.
entries.numbers 4:5: When the camp moved, Aaron and his sons first took down the inner curtain and used it to cover the sacred chest. This protected the most holy object before anyone else came near it.
entries.numbers 4:6: They layered a leather cover and a blue cloth over the chest and inserted its carrying poles. The wrapping kept the sacred object hidden and ready to be carried safely.
entries.numbers 4:7: The table for the holy bread was covered with a blue cloth, and its bowls, cups, and the bread were placed on it. Everything was prepared carefully so the table could be moved without mishandling sacred items.
entries.numbers 4:8: A red cloth and a leather cover were placed over the table, and its poles were set in place. The careful layering shows that even ordinary-seeming furniture was treated as holy.
entries.numbers 4:9: The lampstand, its lamps, trays, and oil containers were wrapped in a blue cloth. Each item had its place in the wrapping so nothing sacred was left exposed.
entries.numbers 4:10: All the lampstand items were put inside a leather cover and placed on a carrying frame. This made the load secure and kept the holy objects protected during travel.
entries.numbers 4:11: The gold altar was covered with a blue cloth and a leather cover, with its poles put in place. It too was prepared for safe carrying by the priests before others touched it.
entries.numbers 4:12: All the utensils used in the holy place were wrapped in a blue cloth, covered with leather, and set on a frame. The point is that every sacred item was handled with care and order.
entries.numbers 4:13: The ashes were removed from the altar and a purple cloth was spread over it. Cleaning came first, showing that even the altar's waste was dealt with before it was covered.
entries.numbers 4:14: All the altar's tools were laid on the cloth, then covered with a leather cover, and its poles were put in place. Everything needed for the altar's use traveled together and stayed protected.
entries.numbers 4:15: Only after Aaron and his sons finished covering the holy things could the Kohathites come to carry them, and they were forbidden to touch them on pain of death. This teaches that approaching God's holiness required respect and obedience, not casual handling.
entries.numbers 4:16: Eleazar, Aaron's son, was put in charge of the oil for light, the incense, the regular grain offering, the holy oil, and the whole tent. Leadership over the sacred supplies rested with a priest, showing that oversight mattered.
entries.numbers 4:17: God again speaks to Moses and Aaron, introducing a warning about the Kohathites. It shows God was paying close attention to how his holy things were handled.
entries.numbers 4:18: God warns that the Kohathite clan must not be wiped out from among the Levites. The concern is that careless handling of holy things could destroy them, so protection came through clear rules.
entries.numbers 4:19: Aaron and his sons were to go in first and assign each Kohathite his specific task and load. This kept the workers from guessing and protected them from deadly mistakes.
entries.numbers 4:20: The Kohathites were not even to look at the holy things for a moment, or they would die. For the reader, it shows that God's holiness is not something to be treated lightly or curiously.
entries.numbers 4:21: God speaks to Moses alone this time, beginning instructions for the Gershonite clan. It shows each group received its own orders from God.
entries.numbers 4:22: The Gershonites were also to be counted by their families and ancestral households. Like the Kohathites, they were organized for service, not left to work randomly.
entries.numbers 4:23: The Gershonites counted for service were men thirty to fifty years old, the age of full working strength. The same standard applied to them as to the other clans.
entries.numbers 4:24: This verse introduces the specific duties and loads the Gershonites were responsible to carry. Their work is defined clearly so they knew exactly what was expected.
entries.numbers 4:25: The Gershonites carried the tent curtains, the tent itself with its coverings, and the screen for the tent doorway. Their job was the outer structure, the fabric and coverings of the meeting place.
entries.numbers 4:26: They also carried the courtyard hangings, the curtain for its entrance, the cords, and all the equipment needed for these. Their work covered the outer enclosure and everything that held it together.
entries.numbers 4:27: Aaron and his sons gave the Gershonites their orders for every task and load. This means the workers served under priestly direction rather than deciding everything themselves.
entries.numbers 4:28: The Gershonites' work at the tent was done under the supervision of Ithamar, Aaron's son. Having a named supervisor kept the work accountable and orderly.
entries.numbers 4:29: The Merarite clan was also to be counted by families and ancestral households. They too had a defined place in the service of the tent.
entries.numbers 4:30: The Merarites counted were men thirty to fifty years old who were fit for the work. The same age and ability standard applied across all three clans.
entries.numbers 4:31: The Merarites carried the tent's boards, bars, pillars, and bases. Their job was the heavy structural frame, the solid parts that held the tent up.
entries.numbers 4:32: They also carried the courtyard pillars, bases, pegs, cords, and all their tools, with each item assigned by name. Naming each piece shows that even small parts of the work mattered and were tracked.
entries.numbers 4:33: The Merarites' work at the tent was done under Ithamar's direction. Like the Gershonites, they served under a priest's oversight, keeping the whole operation unified.
entries.numbers 4:34: Moses, Aaron, and the leaders began counting the Kohathites by families and ancestral households. The leaders themselves took part, showing the count was official and serious.
entries.numbers 4:35: They counted the men thirty to fifty years old who were able to do the work at the tent. The focus was on those actually fit to serve, not just everyone of that age.
entries.numbers 4:36: The total number of Kohathites counted was 2,750. The exact figure shows the record was kept carefully and the workforce was a known, real number.
entries.numbers 4:37: This was the official count of Kohathites who worked at the tent, recorded by Moses and Aaron as God commanded. It confirms the whole process followed God's order, not human preference.
entries.numbers 4:38: The Gershonites were then counted by their families. The same careful process used for the Kohathites was repeated for them.
entries.numbers 4:39: The Gershonites counted were men thirty to fifty years old who were able to do the tent work. Again, age and ability defined who was included.
entries.numbers 4:40: The Gershonite total, counted by families and ancestral households, was 2,630. The precise number shows their service was recorded and valued just as much as the others.
entries.numbers 9:1: God spoke to Moses in the desert of Sinai, in the first month of the second year after Israel left Egypt. This sets the time and place for the instructions that follow.
entries.numbers 9:2: God told Israel to celebrate the Passover at the time appointed for it. God's people were to honor him on schedule, not whenever they felt like it.
entries.numbers 9:3: They were to hold the Passover on the fourteenth day of that month at twilight, following all the rules given for it. Obedience included getting the details right.
entries.numbers 9:4: Moses passed God's command on to the people. A leader's job is to relay God's instructions faithfully.
entries.numbers 9:5: The people did exactly as God commanded through Moses, celebrating the Passover in the Sinai desert. Their obedience shows that following God's word is the right response.
entries.numbers 9:6: Some men had become ritually unclean by touching a dead body, so they could not take part in the Passover that day. They came to Moses and Aaron about it.
entries.numbers 9:7: They asked why they should be left out of bringing the Lord's offering with everyone else just because of their uncleanness. They wanted to worship and felt excluded.
entries.numbers 9:8: Moses told them to wait while he sought God's direction. It is wise to pause and ask God rather than guess when a situation is unclear.
entries.numbers 9:9: God responded to Moses with further instructions. God answers when his people seek his guidance.
entries.numbers 9:10: God said that anyone who is unclean from a dead body, or away on a long journey, could still keep the Passover to the Lord. God makes room for people whose circumstances keep them from the normal time.
entries.numbers 9:11: Such people were to celebrate it a month later, on the fourteenth day at evening, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. God provided a second chance rather than shutting them out.
entries.numbers 9:12: They were to leave none of it until morning and not break any of its bones, following the same rules as the regular Passover. The make-up observance was to be done properly, not carelessly.
entries.numbers 9:13: But anyone who was able to keep the Passover and simply refused would be cut off from the people, and his sin would remain on him. Neglecting God's worship on purpose is serious.
entries.numbers 9:14: Foreigners living among them who wanted to keep the Passover could do so, under the same rules as those born in the land. God's worship was open to outsiders on equal terms.
entries.numbers 9:15: When the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered it, and at night it looked like fire over it until morning. God visibly showed his presence with his people.
entries.numbers 9:16: This was how it always was: the cloud covered it by day and looked like fire by night. God's presence with them was constant, not occasional.
entries.numbers 9:17: Whenever the cloud lifted from the tent, the Israelites set out, and wherever it settled, they camped. God himself directed their movements.
entries.numbers 9:18: They traveled and camped at the Lord's command, and stayed put as long as the cloud rested on the tabernacle. Their schedule was set by God, not by themselves.
entries.numbers 9:19: Even when the cloud stayed a long time, they waited and did not move, obeying the Lord's order. Waiting patiently can itself be obedience.
entries.numbers 9:20: Sometimes the cloud stayed only two or three days, and they camped or moved at the Lord's command. They had to be ready to follow whenever God said.
entries.numbers 9:21: Sometimes the cloud was there only overnight, and they moved on in the morning; whenever it lifted, they went. Their plans depended on God's signal, not their own preference.
entries.numbers 9:22: Whether the cloud stayed two days, a month, or a year, they waited and did not move until it lifted. Long or short, the timing was up to God.
entries.numbers 9:23: They camped and set out at the Lord's word, keeping the orders he gave through Moses. Following God means letting him lead, however and whenever he chooses.
entries.numbers 3:41: God claims the Levites as his own special servants in place of every firstborn son of Israel, and their cattle in place of Israel's firstborn animals. This shows that God accepts a dedicated group to stand in for others.
entries.numbers 3:42: Moses obeyed and counted all the firstborn sons of Israel just as God commanded. Obedience to God's instructions is the expected response.
entries.numbers 3:43: The count of firstborn sons a month old and older came to 22,273. Each one was listed by name, showing that God cares about individuals, not just numbers.
entries.numbers 3:44: God spoke directly to Moses to give the next instruction. God guides his people step by step through his chosen leader.
entries.numbers 3:45: God says the Levites and their cattle now belong to him and take the place of Israel's firstborn sons and cattle. God has the right to set apart people for his service.
entries.numbers 3:46: There were 273 more firstborn sons than Levites, so a payment was required for those extra ones. God's arrangement made sure every firstborn was covered.
entries.numbers 3:47: Each of those 273 was to be bought back with five shekels, weighed by the standard used at the holy place. The price was fixed and fair, set by God.
entries.numbers 3:48: The money collected for the extra firstborn was to be given to Aaron and his sons, the priests. Those who serve God in his house are to be supported by the people.
entries.numbers 3:49: Moses collected the redemption money for the firstborn who were not replaced by Levites. He carried out God's command exactly.
entries.numbers 3:50: The total collected came to 1,365 shekels, weighed by the holy standard. The amount matched the 273 men at five shekels each.
entries.numbers 3:51: Moses handed the money to Aaron and his sons just as God had ordered. Faithful handling of what is given to God matters.
entries.numbers 4:41: This gives the total count of Gershon's descendants who served at the Tent of meeting, tallied as God commanded through Moses and Aaron. It shows that even the support roles in worship were carefully organized and counted before God.
