entries.numbers 20:16: They said God heard their cry and sent an angel to bring them out of Egypt, and now they were at Kadesh on Edom's border. Remembering God's past help gives courage for the present.
entries.numbers 20:17: They asked only to pass through on the main road, promising not to touch fields, vineyards, or springs. A fair and limited request is easier to consider than a vague demand.
entries.numbers 20:18: Edom refused and threatened to attack with swords if Israel came through. Not everyone will grant even a reasonable request.
entries.numbers 20:19: Israel offered to pay for any water they used and asked only to walk through on foot. Being willing to pay your way shows good faith.
entries.numbers 20:20: Edom still refused and came out with a strong army against them. Sometimes people respond to peace with force.
entries.numbers 20:21: Edom would not let Israel pass, so Israel turned and went another way. When a door is closed, choosing another path is wiser than forcing a fight.
entries.numbers 20:22: The whole community moved on from Kadesh and came to Mount Hor. Life goes on after conflict, and God leads his people forward.
entries.numbers 20:23: At Mount Hor, on the border of Edom, the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron. God sometimes gives hard news in ordinary places along the journey.
entries.numbers 20:24: God said Aaron would die and join his ancestors and would not enter the promised land, because of what happened at Meribah. Leaders are accountable to God for how they represent him.
entries.numbers 20:25: God told Moses to take Aaron and his son Eleazar up Mount Hor. Handing leadership to the next generation is part of finishing well.
entries.numbers 20:26: Moses was to remove Aaron's priestly robes and put them on Eleazar, and then Aaron would die there. Passing on your role to a successor is a gift to those who follow.
entries.numbers 20:27: Moses did exactly as the Lord said, and the people watched them go up the mountain. Obedience is visible to everyone around us.
entries.numbers 20:28: Moses transferred Aaron's robes to Eleazar, Aaron died on the mountain top, and Moses and Eleazar came back down. Even a faithful life ends, and the work continues through others.
entries.numbers 20:29: When the people learned Aaron had died, they mourned him for thirty days. Taking time to grieve shows love and respect for those who served us.
entries.numbers 23:1: Balaam tells King Balak to build seven altars and prepare seven bulls and seven rams for sacrifice. This was a setup for seeking a message from God, showing how seriously they treated the request.
entries.numbers 23:2: Balak does exactly what Balaam asked, and together they offer a bull and a ram on each of the seven altars. The two men are working together to try to get God to curse Israel.
entries.numbers 23:3: Balaam tells Balak to stay by the offerings while he goes off alone to see if God will meet him, promising to report back whatever God says. He is positioning himself to receive a message he must then pass on honestly.
entries.numbers 23:4: God comes to Balaam, and Balaam reports that he has built the seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each. He is presenting his preparations as if they earn him a hearing from God.
entries.numbers 23:5: The Lord gives Balaam the exact words to speak and sends him back to Balak to deliver them. Balaam does not get to choose the message; God controls what he says.
entries.numbers 23:6: Balaam returns and finds Balak still standing by his offering with all the leaders of Moab beside him. The king and his officials are waiting anxiously for the curse they paid for.
entries.numbers 23:7: Balaam begins his message by recalling that Balak brought him from a distant eastern land to curse Israel and be angry with them. He is setting up the surprising answer that follows.
entries.numbers 23:8: Balaam asks how he could curse people God has not cursed or be angry with people God is not angry with. He is admitting he has no power to harm those God protects.
entries.numbers 23:9: Looking down from the rocky heights, Balaam sees a people set apart who do not count themselves among the other nations. Israel is distinct because God has chosen them as his own.
entries.numbers 23:10: Balaam says no one can count Israel's people, as numerous as dust, and he wishes he could share the good end of these upright people. Instead of cursing them, he expresses a desire to be like them.
entries.numbers 23:11: Balak angrily asks Balaam what he has done, since he brought him to curse his enemies but instead he blessed them. The king is frustrated that the plan has completely backfired.
entries.numbers 23:12: Balaam replies that he must say only what the Lord puts in his mouth. He is reminding Balak that the message is not his own to change.
entries.numbers 23:13: Balak takes Balaam to another place where he can see only part of the people, hoping a different view will let him curse them from there. He thinks location might change God's answer.
entries.numbers 23:14: Balak brings Balaam to a lookout point in the Zophim region on top of Pisgah, and again they build seven altars and offer a bull and a ram on each. They repeat the same ritual, hoping for a different result.
entries.numbers 23:15: Balaam tells Balak to stand by the offering while he goes to meet the Lord. Once again he steps away to receive God's message.
entries.numbers 23:16: The Lord meets Balaam, puts his words in his mouth, and sends him back to Balak to speak them. God again takes charge of what Balaam will say.
entries.numbers 23:17: Balaam returns to find Balak waiting with the Moabite leaders, and Balak asks what the Lord has said. The king is eager to hear whether the curse finally came.
entries.numbers 23:18: Balaam calls Balak to stand up and listen carefully to what he is about to say. He is demanding the king's full attention for God's message.
entries.numbers 23:19: God is not a human being who lies or changes his mind; what he promises he will do. You can trust God's words because he does not break them like people sometimes do.
entries.numbers 23:20: Balaam says he was ordered to bless, and God has given a blessing he cannot reverse. Once God blesses someone, no human power can undo it.
entries.numbers 23:21: God sees no wrongdoing held against Jacob, and the Lord their God is with them, with the shout of a king among them. Israel is in good standing with God and enjoys his presence.
entries.numbers 23:22: It is God who brought them out of Egypt, and their strength is like that of a wild ox. God himself is the source of Israel's power and freedom.
entries.numbers 23:23: No curse or fortune-telling works against Jacob, and in time people will say what God has done for Israel. God's protection cannot be defeated by any magic or spell.
entries.numbers 23:24: Israel is pictured as a lion that rises up and will not rest until it has defeated its prey. The point is that God gives his people unstoppable strength against their enemies.
entries.numbers 23:25: Balak tells Balaam that if he won't curse them, at least he should not bless them. The king is trying to salvage something from a failed plan.
entries.numbers 23:26: Balaam reminds Balak that he already said he can only do what the Lord tells him. He will not go beyond God's instructions, even for a king.
entries.numbers 23:27: Balak suggests trying one more place, hoping God might allow a curse from there. He keeps thinking a change of location will change the outcome.
entries.numbers 23:28: Balak takes Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the desert region. This is the third attempt to find a spot from which to curse Israel.
entries.numbers 23:29: Balaam again asks Balak to build seven altars and prepare seven bulls and seven rams. The same ritual is repeated a third time.
entries.numbers 23:30: Balak does as Balaam says, offering a bull and a ram on each of the seven altars. The king follows the instructions exactly, still hoping for a curse.
